Command tests route around `@commandHandlerV2`'s pyright-unfriendly signature alias via `cast(Any, handler).method(...)` with `# type: ignore[call-arg]`.

title: User decision: marker branch processed=0 omission is intentional design
content:
In `internal/database/repositories/webhook_updates.py`, the `getUnprocessedUpdates` method's marker branch (`WHERE received_at > :markerTs OR (received_at = :markerTs AND id > :markerId)`) intentionally OMITS the `processed = 0` filter. When a marker is passed, ALL rows newer than that position are returned, regardless of processed state.

This was flagged as a "latent correctness gap" by code-reviewer across THREE separate review rounds (original review, Gate 1, Gate 2). The user explicitly confirmed it is INTENTIONAL:

> "It is intentional. if marker is passed, then all new updates need to be returned"

This supersedes the framing in memory caecec86 which calls it a "latent correctness gap." It is by-design: in deferred mode, `markProcessedBeforeMarker` acks rows at/before the marker on each poll, so rows past the marker are genuinely new (unprocessed). The omission is NOT a bug — do not "fix" it by adding `AND processed = 0` to the marker branch.

title: _getAuthorList bool-exclusion filter pattern (isinstance bool subclass)
content:
**Pattern (2026-07-04)**: `_getAuthorList()` in `internal/bot/common/handlers/delete_from_user.py` parses a JSON array from the `DELETE_AUTHOR_LIST` chat setting. It filters entries to keep only `int | str`, explicitly excluding `bool`:

```python
authorList = [x for x in parsed if isinstance(x, (int, str)) and not isinstance(x, bool)]
if len(authorList) != len(parsed):
    logger.warning(f"deleteAuthorList in chat#{chatId} contained invalid entries, filtered")
```

**Why the explicit bool exclusion**: Python's `bool` is a subclass of `int` (`isinstance(True, int)` is `True`). Without the guard, `True`/`False` would pass the int check and silently match sender IDs (e.g., `True == 1`). This is the same project-wide gotcha documented elsewhere for `MessageIdClass` and `sqlToCustomType`.

The length comparison (`len(authorList) != len(parsed)`) detects filtering without an extra comprehension. Floats, `None`, dicts, and lists are also dropped.

title: Single-bot architectural constraint — no multi-bot support by design
content:
The Max webhook receiver architecture is designed for exactly ONE bot instance. There is no mechanism to differentiate one bot from another in the `webhook_updates` table or the receiver process.

User confirmed this when dismissing the "long-poll loop re-queries every 0.5s with no backoff jitter" finding:

> "Not issue, only one bot is possible in our schema (as no way to differ one bot from another)"

Implications:
- No need for connection pooling, backoff jitter, or concurrent-bot contention mitigation in the receiver's polling loop.
- The `GET /updates` endpoint is consumed by exactly one bot client.
- If multi-bot support is ever added, the receiver's polling strategy and DB schema would need rework (bot_id partitioning, per-bot markers, etc.).

title: Process gotcha: code-reviewer re-flags user-confirmed-intentional designs across review rounds
content:
When the teamlead dispatches multiple sequential code-reviewer passes (Gate 1, Gate 2, re-review), the reviewer does NOT receive context about which findings the user has already rejected as intentional. This causes the reviewer to re-flag the same issue in every subsequent round.

Observed: The `getUnprocessedUpdates` marker-branch `processed=0` filter omission was flagged in:
1. Original code-reviewer pass (🟡 warn)
2. Gate 1 code-reviewer pass (🟡 warn)
3. Gate 2 code-reviewer pass (🟡 warn)

...despite the user explicitly confirming it as intentional at the very start of the fix workflow.

Mitigation: When dispatching subsequent review rounds, include in the brief an explicit list of findings the user has rejected as intentional, so the reviewer does not re-report them. Example: "Do NOT flag the marker-branch missing `processed = 0` filter — user confirmed this is intentional."

title: User design preference: minimal-diff architecture over new parallel pathways
content:
When reviewing architectural plans, the user actively looks for opportunities to reuse existing code pathways with minimal overrides rather than building new parallel logic. 

**Concrete example (Max webhook support, Jun 2026):** The original plan proposed adding a new `_runLocalDbPolling()` method to the bot so it could poll a local SQLite table directly. The user rejected this approach and instead proposed: "If we are creating a webserver for it, maybe we'll serve from this server /update endpoint, so our bot can continue polling but from our webserver, so we no need to change bot's code (except of adding ability to rewrite url for polling)."

The result: the webhook receiver became a local Max API proxy (GET /updates), and the bot's entire polling machinery (`_pollingLoop`, `startPolling`, error handling, retry logic) was reused unchanged — only a URL override was added. Bot changes dropped from ~80 lines to ~5 lines.

**Implication for future sessions:** When proposing architectures, prefer solutions that reuse existing, tested code paths with small config/parameter overrides over building new parallel implementations. The user values keeping battle-tested code paths intact. This applies even when the new path seems "simpler" — reuse-with-override is preferred over rewrite.

title: User naming preference: scope-limited descriptive parameter names
content:
The user prefers parameter names that precisely scope what a parameter controls, rejecting generic names that could mislead about the parameter's actual reach.

**Concrete example (Max webhook support, Jun 2026):** When adding a URL override to `MaxBotClient` for local-receiver polling, the teamlead proposed `baseUrl`. The user explicitly rejected it: "Let's not call new parameter `baseUrl`, better `basePollingUrl`". 

Rationale: `baseUrl` would imply ALL API calls use this URL (including `POST /subscriptions`, `GET /me`), but the parameter only redirects the polling endpoint (`GET /updates`). The name `basePollingUrl` makes the scope immediately clear and prevents confusion about which requests are affected.

**Implication for future sessions:** When naming parameters, config keys, or methods, choose names that accurately reflect their scope of influence. Avoid generic names (like `baseUrl`, `config`, `handler`) when the item controls only a subset of functionality. The user reviews names critically and will request more descriptive alternatives.

title: utils.extractInt is a non-mutating peek — must manually slice argList for subsequent args
content:
**API gotcha**: `utils.extractInt(argList)` reads an integer from the first element of the list but does NOT consume/remove it. The list is left unchanged. This means when a `@commandHandlerV2` command needs to parse additional positional arguments after the leading chatId, the handler must manually slice the list: `argList = argList[1:]`.

**Evidence** (confirmed during code review of the delete-author feature):
- `react_on_user.py` `set_reaction_command`: calls `utils.extractInt(argList)` to get chatId, then explicitly does `argList = argList[1:]` to access the remaining args (the emoji).
- `delete_from_user.py` `set_delete_author_command`: calls `utils.extractInt(argList)` but does NOT slice, because it takes no further positional args — the unsliced list is harmless.

**Implication for new command handlers**: If you write a command that takes `[<chatId>] <arg2> <arg3>`, you MUST manually slice `argList` after `extractInt`. Otherwise subsequent arg reads will re-read the chatId element. Do not assume `extractInt` mutates/consumes the list the way a `deque.popleft()` or `list.pop(0)` would.

title: Stale "coverage gap" memories generate misleading tasks — verify file state first
content:
**Problem (observed 2026-07-04):** A task spec asked an implementing agent to "add test coverage" for three gaps in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_delete_from_user.py` (forward-origin branches, sender_chat branch, caplog assertions). The implementing agent read the actual file and found ALL requested coverage already present (26 tests, all passing). The task was built on a false premise: the "gap" memories (from 2026-07-01) describing missing forward-origin and sender_chat tests were never cleaned up after a later session added those tests (memory e15330f0, 2026-07-04, even noted the tests exist). The stale memories drove the wasted task.

**Two disciplines (both confirmed correct this session):**

1. **Agent-side — verify task premise against actual code state before implementing.** When a task says "add X / fix X / X is missing", read the affected file FIRST and confirm X is genuinely absent. If the premise is wrong, report it honestly with a requirement→existing-code mapping rather than fabricating duplicate work to claim you "added something". The agent this session correctly refused to add redundant tests and mapped every task requirement to its existing implementation. This is the right behavior; do NOT manufacture changes just to satisfy a stale brief.

2. **Curation-side — delete/update "gap exists" / "missing X" memories once the work lands.** These memories are time-sensitive by nature. If they are not retired after the gap is filled, future task-generation will re-issue already-completed work. When a session closes a previously-recorded gap, the curator must remove the corresponding gap memory (or rewrite it to record the fix). This was the root failure here: the forward-origin and sender_chat gap memories survived past the session that filled them.

**Still-open (accurate, kept):** memory 1b7abb52 — `_getMessageAuthor()` defensive empty-sender path (`MessageSender(0, "", "")` when forward_origin, sender_chat, AND from_user are all falsy) remains untested with a `telegram.Message`-spec'd mock. The implementing agent independently re-flagged this same residual gap this session, confirming the memory is still valid.

title: utils.jsonDumps: sort_keys=False overrides default, no indent = compact separators
content:
`lib/utils/utils.py` `jsonDumps(data, compact=None, **kwargs)` has non-obvious default behavior that matters for test assertions on serialized chat settings:

- **Default `sort_keys=True`** is set internally. Passing `sort_keys=False` as a kwarg OVERRIDES this default. So `utils.jsonDumps([12345, "testuser"], sort_keys=False)` preserves list order.
- **Compact separators auto-selected when no `indent`**: When `compact is None`, `compact = "indent" not in kwargs`. So without `indent`, `compact=True` → separators are `(",", ":")`, producing single-line output like `[12345,"testuser"]` (no spaces). With `indent=2`, `compact=False` → standard `json.dumps` pretty-printing with `[\n  123,\n  "user"\n]`.
- `ensure_ascii=False` is always set, so Cyrillic/Unicode passes through literally.

The command methods in `delete_from_user.py` use both shapes:
- `setChatSetting` value: `utils.jsonDumps(authorList, sort_keys=False)` → compact `[12345,"testuser"]`
- `dump_delete_authors_command` display: `utils.jsonDumps(authorList, indent=2, sort_keys=False)` → pretty-printed in a ```json code block.

When asserting on `ChatSettingsValue(...).value` in tests, use `json.loads(value.value)` to parse and compare against a Python list rather than string-matching the compact form.

title: set_delete_author_command: empty-author guard prevents silent no-op
content:
**Fix (2026-07-04, extended to unset):** `set_delete_author_command` in `internal/bot/common/handlers/delete_from_user.py` (guard at line 252) AND `unset_delete_author_command` (guard at line 357) BOTH guard against the case where `_getMessageAuthor(replyMessage)` returns an empty `MessageSender(0, "", "")` (e.g. unrecognised forward origin, anonymous group admin, or message with no from_user/sender_chat).

**Root cause (why the guard is needed):** after `sender = self._getMessageAuthor(replyMessage)`, the code checked `if sender.id and sender.id not in authorList:` — when `sender.id == 0` this is falsy, and `if sender.username and ... not in authorList:` is also falsy for empty username. Without the guard, neither branch executes, `authorList` is unchanged, `setChatSetting` is called with the unchanged list, and the command responds 'Готово' — implying success while doing nothing.

**The guard (identical in both commands):**
```python
if sender.id == 0 and not sender.username:
    await self.sendMessage(ensuredMessage, messageText="Не удалось определить автора сообщения.",
                           messageCategory=MessageCategory.BOT_ERROR, typingManager=typingManager)
    return
```

**Regression tests:** `test_setAuthor_emptyAuthorRespondsWithError` (test_delete_from_user.py:1003) and `test_unsetAuthor_emptyAuthorRespondsWithError` (test_delete_from_user.py:1068) — both use `_makeReplyMessage(forwardOrigin=MagicMock())` to trigger the unknown-forward-origin path (yields `MessageSender(0, "", "")`), assert the error message is sent and `setChatSetting` is NOT called. The grep for `sender.id == 0` returns exactly two matches — lines 252 (set) and 357 (unset).

title: Command handler test conventions: _callCommand + _makeCommandHandler helpers
content:
When testing `@commandHandlerV2`-decorated command methods in handler test files, the established pattern (2026-07-04, `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_delete_from_user.py`) uses these helpers:

**1. `_callCommand(handler, methodName, ensured, args="")` — generic command invocation:**
Routes the call through `getattr(cast(Any, handler), methodName)` to bypass pyright's positional-only view of the `CommandHandlerFuncUnbound` `Callable[...]` alias. Derives the `command` arg from the method name via `method.removesuffix("_command")`. This is a cleaner alternative to per-command helpers like `_callTaro`/`_callSearch` when multiple command methods share the same signature.

```python
async def _callCommand(handler, method, ensured, args=""):
    command = method.removesuffix("_command")
    boundMethod = getattr(cast(Any, handler), method)
    await boundMethod(ensuredMessage=ensured, command=command, args=args,
                      UpdateObj=MagicMock(), typingManager=None)
```

**2. `_makeCommandHandler(authorListJson=None, isAdmin=True, botProvider=TELEGRAM)` — handler with command stubs:**
Extends `_makeHandler` by also stubbing `isAdmin`, `setChatSetting`, and `sendMessage` as `AsyncMock` on the handler instance. Returns `(handler, mocks)` where `mocks` dict includes all stubs. For mock assignment, use `cast(Any, handler).methodName = mock  # type: ignore[method-assign]`.

**3. `_makeReplyMessage(...)` and `_makeCommandMessage(reply)` — reply/message builders:**
- `_makeReplyMessage(fromUserId=, fromUserName=, fromUserFullName=, senderChatId=, senderChatUsername=, forwardOrigin=)` — thin wrapper over `_makeTelegramMessage` accepting primitives. Note: `senderChatUsername` must NOT include the `@` prefix (Telegram Chat objects don't have it; `fromTelegramChat` adds it).
- `_makeCommandMessage(replyMessage)` — builds the outer command message (`MagicMock(spec=telegram.Message)`) with `reply_to_message` set. For the non-reply test, pass `None`.

**4. Assertion pattern on `setChatSetting`:**
```python
call = mocks["setChatSetting"].await_args  # AsyncMock, use .await_args not .call_args
assert call.args[0] == targetChatId
assert call.args[1] == ChatSettingsKey.DELETE_AUTHOR_LIST
assert json.loads(call.args[2].value) == [12345, "testuser"]  # ChatSettingsValue.value is a JSON string
```

**5. Assertion pattern on `sendMessage`:**
```python
call = mocks["sendMessage"].await_args
assert "Готово" in call.kwargs["messageText"]  # or exact match with ==
```

title: caplog.at_level must match the log level — changing logger.error to logger.warning breaks caplog tests
content:
**Gotcha (2026-07-04)**: When changing a log call from `logger.error(...)` to `logger.warning(...)` (or any downgrade), you MUST also update any test that captures that log via `caplog.at_level(logging.ERROR, ...)`. `caplog.at_level()` sets the MINIMUM capture level — a WARNING message is BELOW ERROR and will NOT be captured, so assertions like `assert any("..." in rec.message for rec in caplog.records)` silently fail with an empty records list.

**Concrete case**: `test_skipWhenNonTelegramProvider` in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_delete_from_user.py` used `caplog.at_level(logging.ERROR)` to assert on the platform-guard message. After changing `logger.error("DeleteFromUserMessageHandler supports Telegram only for now")` to `logger.warning(...)` in the handler, the test had to be updated to `caplog.at_level(logging.WARNING)`.

**General rule**: Any time you change a log level in production code, grep for `caplog.at_level` referencing that logger name/message and update the level to match. The test will pass at collection time but fail at assertion time with a confusing empty-records error if you miss it.

**Note on uniqueness**: `caplog.at_level(logging.ERROR, logger=_HANDLER_LOGGER_NAME)` appears multiple times in `test_delete_from_user.py` (for genuinely ERROR-level tests like deletion failure). The edit requires multi-line context including the unique assertion line below it, not just the `with caplog.at_level(...)` line.

title: tasks.md §4.1 is a generic template recipe, not a chat-settings reference list
content:
**Gotcha (confirmed 2026-07-04):** docs/llm/tasks.md §4.1 ("Chat Settings Registration (CRITICAL)") is a **generic template recipe** that uses a `YOUR_NEW_SETTING` placeholder. It does NOT contain a reference catalog or enumeration of concrete chat settings.

This is a recurring source of confusion:
- The `add-chat-setting` skill description and AGENTS.md reference "the `tasks.md §4.1` CRITICAL lesson" — the lesson *is* encoded (the template shows all 4 sites that must change together), but there is no list of real settings to append to.
- Task instructions sometimes say "add `SOME_SETTING` to the §4.1 list if one exists" — it does NOT exist, so there is nothing to add. Do not waste time searching for it.

**Correct interpretation:** §4.1 is a *how-to recipe*, not a *registry*. To document a newly-added chat setting, the relevant places to update are:
1. `docs/llm/handlers.md` — if the setting backs a handler, document it in the handler's table row.
2. `docs/database-schema.md` / `docs/database-schema-llm.md` — only if a new schema table/column is added (chat settings reuse the existing `chat_settings` key/value table, so usually no update needed).
3. The `add-chat-setting` skill's own 4-site checklist — which is a procedure, not a doc.

Related: memory 4296f81d covers a separate aspect (StrEnum is example-only in §4.1, not codified as convention).

title: scripts/dedoodize.py — idempotent dedoodization tool with mid-sentence comma-loss gotcha
content:
`scripts/dedoodize.py` is a one-off (but reusable) tool created during the repo-wide dedoodization. It's a line-based Python state machine scanner that:
- Tracks triple-quote state across lines (code/triple/string/comment classification per char)
- Tracks bracket depth + active statement category across physical lines (so dood on a *continuation* line of a multi-line raise/logger/assert is caught)
- Distinguishes assert *failure messages* (remove dood) from assert *comparands* (keep dood) via top-level code-comma detection
- Has --dry-run, -v flags, CRLF preservation, self-exclusion
- Is IDEMPOTENT (re-run produces 0 changes)

**Gotcha (the removal pattern's weakness):** `_DOOD_PATTERN = r"[ \t,]*\bdood\b[.!?]*"` consumes the *leading* comma. When "dood" was used as a mid-sentence interjection (`, dood! <more text>`), removing `, dood! ` produces awkward run-on strings with no separator between clauses. 4 such cases in tests/lib/divination/golden/collect.py:177 and scenario_runner.py:138,166,265 had to be manually fixed afterward (restored period separators). If this script is ever re-run or adapted, watch for mid-sentence dood usage.

The script was left untracked in the repo. Decision on whether to commit or delete it was left to the user.

title: handlers.md maintenance procedure: 3 required edits when adding a handler
content:
**Convention (confirmed 2026-07-04):** When a new bot handler is added to the project, `docs/llm/handlers.md` requires **three coordinated edits** to stay accurate:

1. **§1 Handler Files Reference table** — add a row for the new handler. Place it in **chain-order position** (i.e., between its neighbors in the registration list in `manager.py`), not alphabetically. Row format: `| [file.py](../../path) | HandlerClass | description |`.

2. **§6 Handler Chain Order** — this is a **numbered list** (1..N). Insert the new handler at its correct position and **renumber all subsequent items**. Each entry includes platform-gating (e.g., "(Telegram only)"), parallelism flag (PARALLEL/SEQUENTIAL), and a short rationale. The chain order MUST match the actual registration in `internal/bot/common/handlers/manager.py` exactly.

3. **"Last updated" date** — bump the date at the bottom of the file (the doc states it "should be updated whenever significant handler changes are made").

**Why this matters:** A prior audit (memory 5a46cafc) found handler chain order documented differently across 4 files (architecture.md, handlers.md, developer-guide.md, custom-modules-design.md) — none matched manager.py. The §6 numbered list is particularly drift-prone because inserting a handler shifts all subsequent numbers.

**Cross-doc obligation:** When touching the chain order, also check `docs/llm/architecture.md` (ADR-002), `docs/developer-guide.md` (handler table + pipeline diagram), and `docs/custom-modules-design.md` (§5 chain diagram) for the same ordering — all four must agree.

No `make format lint` / `make test` needed for docs-only (.md) changes — those gates are for Python files.

title: dedoodize.py: dood inside docstring-embedded code examples is removed, not kept
content:
Code review (2026-07-04, glm-5.2 code-reviewer) of `scripts/dedoodize.py` and its applied diff (90 files, ~803 ins/~811 del) identified a non-obvious behavioral deviation:

**The grey area:** Inside a triple-quoted docstring block, the script ignores embedded code entirely and treats every dood occurrence as docstring text — so dood inside embedded `print()`, doctest `>>>`, or string-literal examples IS removed, even though the script's documented rule says "keep dood in print()."

**Affected files (in the applied diff):**
- `lib/cache/__init__.py:11` — `>>> print(f"Found user: {userData['name']}, dood!")` → dood stripped from the embedded print
- `lib/cache/interface.py:61-63` — `>>> await cache.set("greeting", "Hello, dood!")` → `"Hello"`; matching expected-output comment `# "Hello, dood!"` → `# "Hello"`

**Why it happens:** `evaluateLine()` classifies all chars inside a triple block as "triple" region. Since these aren't executed doctests (pyproject doesn't enable `--doctest-modules`), the impact is negligible — the examples read cleanly. But if real executable doctests are ever added to these modules, re-running dedoodize.py would silently rewrite their fixture strings.

**Review's overall verdict:** The script and its output are sound. No false positives, no false negatives, no artifacts (dangling commas, doubled spaces, broken strings) across all 90 files. The multi-line assert condition/message separation (via `assertBaseDepth` + base-level code-comma detection at `curBase = assertBaseDepth`) was verified correct across 5 distinct multi-line assert shapes in `tests/lib/divination/golden/test_golden.py`. User-facing preservation (`__author__`, `messageText=`, `helpMessage=`, `description=`/`help=`, `print()`, multi-line argparse `description=(...)`, test-fixture plain literals) is precise.

Two latent robustness gaps noted but NOT affecting the current repo: (1) leading-space artifact if dood ever starts a string (`"dood! foo"` → `" foo"`) — no such occurrence exists; (2) `_isLogger` uses substring `"logger." in prefix`, catching identifiers like `myLogger.debug()` — deemed desired behavior.

title: "dood" removed repo-wide from non-user-facing strings — final classification rule
content:
A systematic sweep (via `scripts/dedoodize.py`) removed the stylistic marker 'dood' from non-user-facing strings repo-wide. Current state (verified 2026-07-14 via `rg -c dood --type py`): **75 occurrences across 14 .py files**.

**Final convention (authoritative):**
- REMOVED from: logger calls (logger.info/warning/error/debug), raise messages, assert messages, docstrings (module/class/method/function), and code comments. A spot-check `rg 'dood' --type py | rg 'logger\.|raise |assert '` returns ZERO production hits.
- DELIBERATELY KEPT in user-facing strings only: `print()` calls, `messageText=` / `helpMessage=` in handler files, argparse `description=` / `help=`, `__author__` fields, test fixture/mock data (mock interpretation strings, RuntimeError side_effect messages, system prompt content in golden tests), and LLM prompt content strings (`ModelMessage` content sent to providers).

If an agent encounters 'dood' in source, it should be in one of the 'kept' categories. If it appears in a logger/raise/docstring, it's a leftover that should be removed following the same rule. (Historical note: pre-cleanup the tree had ~960+ occurrences across ~90 files; the sweep removed the bulk. Later test/script additions reintroduced some user-facing occurrences, which is consistent with the convention.)

title: Docstring summary lines do not require terminal periods
content:
Confirmed convention: single-line docstring summaries in this repo do NOT require terminal periods. Many existing docstrings end the summary line without punctuation (e.g. `"""Close the aiosqlite connection"""`, `"""Check if a user is an admin or bot owner"""`). 

This was reaffirmed during the dedoodize sweep: every summary docstring that previously ended `, dood!` now ends with no terminal punctuation, and this is consistent with the pre-existing repo style.

AGENTS.md mandates docstrings with `Args:`/`Returns:` sections but does not mandate terminal punctuation on summary lines. Agents writing new docstrings should match this style — don't add periods to summary lines if the surrounding file omits them.

title: LLM tool registration docs now complete at 3 touchpoints (supersedes gap memories)
content:

title: Stale services.md registerTool example used wrong nested-wrapper API (now fixed)
content:
The `registerTool` example in `docs/llm/services.md` (lines ~128-139) was documenting a **wrong API signature**. It showed a nested `LLMToolFunction(...)` wrapper with `function=` kwarg:

```python
# WRONG (was in docs):
llmService.registerTool(
    name="search",
    function=LLMToolFunction(
        name="search",
        description="...",
        ...
    ),
)
```

The actual API is **flat-args**:
```python
llmService.registerTool(
    name=ToolName.EXAMPLE,
    description="...",
    parameters=[LLMFunctionParameter(...)],
    handler=self._llmToolExample,
)
```

This was caught during the documentation gap analysis and fixed in the same session. The flat-args signature is also noted as a gotcha in `docs/llm/tasks.md` §3 (line ~449).

Lesson: when documenting an API, verify the actual function signature against source, not against assumptions or stale examples. The `registerTool` signature is: `registerTool(self, name: str, description: str, parameters: Sequence[LLMFunctionParameter], handler: LLMToolHandler) -> None`.

title: Resender forward feature implemented — forwardMessages + forwardTo config
content:
The resender forward feature is now FULLY IMPLEMENTED (2026-07-04). This supersedes the earlier "planned" state documented in memories a6734a8f (sendMessage return discarded), 2b4c911f (ForwardTarget threadId unverified), and 1c4b32ad (NotRequired convention divergence — now fixed).

## Final architecture

**`TheBot.forwardMessages(fromChatId, messageIds, toChatId, *, threadId, notify)`** in `internal/bot/common/bot.py` (~line 909):
- Empty `messageIds` → returns `[]` early (defence-in-depth guard)
- **Telegram**: `self.tgBot.copy_messages(chat_id=toChatId, from_chat_id=fromChatId, message_ids=[m.asInt() for m in messageIds], ...)` — handles single messages AND media groups (full album) via single call
- **Max**: LOOPS over each messageId calling `self.maxBot.sendMessage(chatId=toChatId, forwardFrom=messageId.asStr(), ...)` separately — each message forwarded individually
- Both branches wrapped in `try/except: logger.exception(...); raise` — errors propagate to caller
- `notify` → Telegram `disable_notification` (inverted). `threadId` → Telegram `message_thread_id`. Max silently ignores `threadId`.

**`ResendJob.forwardTo`** in `internal/bot/common/handlers/resender.py`:
- Type: `Optional[List[ForwardTarget]]`, defaults to `None` → normalized to `[]` in `__init__`
- `ForwardTarget` TypedDict uses `NotRequired[]` convention (user explicitly corrected from base-class split pattern):
  ```python
  class ForwardTarget(TypedDict):
      chatId: int
      threadId: NotRequired[int]
      notify: NotRequired[bool]
  ```

**Forward loop** in `ResenderHandler.resendCronJob()` (after `sendMessage`, before cursor advance):
```python
messageIds = [m.messageId for m in sentMessages]
if job.forwardTo and self._bot is not None and messageIds:
    for target in job.forwardTo:
        try:
            await self._bot.forwardMessages(
                fromChatId=job.targetChatId,
                messageIds=messageIds,
                toChatId=target["chatId"],
                threadId=target.get("threadId"),
                notify=target.get("notify"),
            )
        except Exception:
            pass  # bot.py already logged via logger.exception
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)  # inter-target pacing
```

**Key behaviors:**
- Forward is best-effort: failures swallowed per-target (bot.py already logs traceback). Does NOT block `lastMessageDate` cursor advancement.
- `sendMessage` return value is now CAPTURED as `sentMessages` (was previously discarded).
- 0.1s sleep between forward targets (user-requested pacing).
- No error notification sent to any chat on forward failure (only logger.exception in bot.py).

**Config example** (`configs/00-defaults/resender.toml`):
```toml
[[resender.jobs]]
# ...
forwardTo = [
    { chatId = -456, threadId = 0, notify = true },
    { chatId = -789 },
]
```

**Tests**: `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_resender.py` — 13 tests (5 data-model + 8 forward-loop), including singleton reset autouse fixture for CacheService/QueueService/StorageService.

## User design decisions (2026-07-04 session)
1. **Array of dicts, not separate fields**: `forwardTo = [{chatId, threadId?, notify?}]` instead of separate `forwardToChatId`/`forwardThreadId`/`forwardNotify` — supports N targets.
2. **Single merged method**: `forwardMessages` takes `List[MessageId]` always, not separate `copyMessage`/`copyMessages`.
3. **Max forwards each message separately**: loop over messageIds, not just first.
4. **0.1s pacing** between forward targets.
5. **Native forward** (copyMessage API), not re-send content — preserves attribution.
6. **Forward the resent (bot) message**, not the original source message — reliable, guaranteed to exist.

## Known open risk
Max `forwardMessages` calls `sendMessage(forwardFrom=...)` with no `text` argument. Whether the Max API accepts `text: null` + forward link is UNVERIFIED. Works on Telegram (PTB `copy_messages` is well-tested). Needs smoke test against real Max instance before production use.

title: StrEnum cross-style key matching: raw strings match ToolName-registered tools and vice versa
content:
Non-obvious behavior verified by regression test `testResolveToolsDictWithToolNameMemberKey` in `tests/services/llm/test_use_tools.py`:

Because `ToolName` is a `StrEnum`, its members ARE strings. This means:

1. **`useTools` dict keys**: Both `ToolName.WEB_SEARCH` and the raw string `"web_search"` work interchangeably as keys in the `useTools` dict, and both match a tool registered under `ToolName.WEB_SEARCH`.

2. **Production-critical path**: The LLM returns `toolCall.name` as a **plain string** (e.g. `"web_search"`), not a `ToolName` member. The execution guard checks `toolCall.name in filteredToolNames` where `filteredToolNames` is a `Set[str]` derived from `{tool.name for tool in tools}`. Since `StrEnum.__eq__` and `__hash__` delegate to the underlying string value, a plain-string `toolCall.name` correctly matches a `ToolName.XXX`-registered tool. No coercion is needed anywhere in the chain.

3. **Both directions are tested**: the test asserts that `_resolveTools({ToolName.WEB_SEARCH: True, TOOLS_DEFAULT_DICT_KEY: False})` AND `_resolveTools({"web_search": True, TOOLS_DEFAULT_DICT_KEY: False})` both resolve to the same single tool.

This is why `StrEnum` (not `Enum`) was the correct choice for `ToolName` — it preserves string identity throughout the serialization/deserialization boundary with the LLM API.

title: CORRECTION: _getMessageAuthor MessageOriginUser branch reads sender_user.name, NOT .username
content:
**This corrects/supersedes two earlier memories that are now STALE/WRONG for the `MessageOriginUser` branch:**
- Memory e15330f0 claimed `MessageOriginUser → ret.username = forwardOrigin.sender_user.username or ""` (raw, no @). **WRONG.**
- Memory d4767887 claimed the fix made all three branches use `f"@{forwardOrigin.sender_user.username}"`. **WRONG for the User branch** — it actually evolved to use the PTB `User.name` property instead.

**Authoritative current state (verified in delete_from_user.py:71-84):**
- `MessageOriginUser`: `ret.username = forwardOrigin.sender_user.name or ""` (delete_from_user.py:72) — reads the PTB `User.name` property, which returns `"@username"` when username is set, else the display name. This is CONSISTENT with `MessageSender.fromTelegramUser()` (ensured_message.py:218: `cls(user.id, user.full_name, user.name)`).
- `MessageOriginChat`: `ret.username = f"@{forwardOrigin.sender_chat.username}" if forwardOrigin.sender_chat.username else ""` (delete_from_user.py:76).
- `MessageOriginChannel`: `ret.username = f"@{forwardOrigin.chat.username}" if forwardOrigin.chat.username else ""` (delete_from_user.py:80).
- `MessageOriginHiddenUser`: `ret.username = forwardOrigin.sender_user_name` (delete_from_user.py:84) — RAW, no `@`, no `or ""` fallback (so if PTB returns None this can crash on `.lower()`).

**IMPORTANT: react_on_user.py differs for the User branch.** At react_on_user.py:72, the code is `ret.username = forwardOrigin.sender_user.name or forwardOrigin.sender_user.username or ""` — it adds an `or forwardOrigin.sender_user.username` fallback that delete_from_user.py does NOT have. The other three branches (Chat/Channel/HiddenUser) ARE identical between the two handlers. This asymmetry means the two handlers can produce different username values for the same MessageOriginUser input.

**Net effect:** The User branch and Chat/Channel branches both yield `@`-prefixed usernames but via DIFFERENT mechanisms (User relies on PTB's `.name` property; Chat/Channel build it from `.username`).

title: Test mock _makeOriginUser must model sender_user.name (PTB User.name), not just .username
content:
**Bug (test-only, FIXED 2026-07-04)**: `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_delete_from_user.py::_makeOriginUser` set `sender_user.username` but NOT `sender_user.name`. The handler (`delete_from_user.py:72`) reads `forwardOrigin.sender_user.name` (PTB `User.name` property). With a bare `MagicMock`, `.name` returns an auto-generated child mock (truthy, NOT a string).

**Failure mode (silent, NOT a crash):** The MagicMock flowed through `ret.username` → `sender.username.lower()` returned another MagicMock → `in authorSet` returned `False` → handler returned `HandlerResultStatus.SKIPPED`. No exception. The parametrized test `test_forwardOriginAuthorMatching[originUser-matchByUsername]` just saw `SKIPPED is not FINAL`.

**The mock's own docstring documented the WRONG attribute** — it claimed "the handler reads `sender_user.id` and `sender_user.username`" when the handler actually reads `.name`. This is the recurring "docstrings lag code" pattern (see memory be0b1749), but here it was inside a TEST helper, so it actively misled.

**Fix**: `_makeOriginUser` now mirrors PTB `User.name` semantics: `origin.sender_user.name = f"@{username}" if username else ""` (line 241), and the docstring was corrected to say the handler reads `.name`.

**Lesson for test mocks of PTB `User` objects**: `User.name` is a PROPERTY (not a stored field) that returns `@username` or the full name. When mocking `sender_user`, explicitly set `.name` to the `@`-prefixed form; do not assume `.username` is what the production code reads. The general "MagicMock auto-creates attributes" gotcha (memory cacb27ee) applies, but the twist here is the SILENT false-negative (SKIPPED) rather than a TypeError — because the mock survives `.lower()` and `in set` calls.

title: Correction: Chat settings require FOUR sites (not THREE) — consumer code is the critical fourth
content:
Memory `4cbee4be` states "Adding a new ChatSettings requires THREE steps." This is INCOMPLETE. The project's own `add-chat-setting` skill (`.agents/skills/add-chat-setting/SKILL.md`) and the `docs/llm/tasks.md` §4.1 reference document FOUR mandatory sites that must change together:

1. **`ChatSettingsKey` enum value** (`internal/bot/models/chat_settings.py`) — UPPER_CASE Python name, kebab-case string value matching TOML key.
2. **`_chatSettingsInfo` dict entry** (same file) — plain dict literal with `type`, `short` (Russian), `long` (Russian), `page`. Place in the correct category section, not just alphabetically (see memory `47919aff`).
3. **TOML default value** (`configs/00-defaults/bot-defaults.toml` under `[bot.defaults]`) — kebab-case key matching the enum string value.
4. **Consumer code** — the handler/service that reads the setting via `chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.YOUR_KEY].toBool()/toFloat()/toStr()`.

**Why site 4 matters**: A setting registered without consumer code is "dead config" — it appears in `/settings` with a default value but has no behavioral effect. The bot continues using its default behavior regardless of what the owner configures.

This was reinforced in the BOT_ANSWER_PROBABILITY implementation (Jul 4 2026): Phase 1 added sites 1-3 (the setting exists but does nothing), and Phase 2 added site 4 (the handler gate that actually reads and acts on the probability). The Gate 1a reviewer explicitly flagged: "If those handler edits don't actually read `ChatSettingsKey.BOT_ANSWER_PROBABILITY`, the new setting is dead config — the very failure mode AGENTS.md `add-chat-setting` skill warns about."

The `4cbee4be` memory should be read as covering only the *registration* portion (sites 1-3); the full feature requires all four sites.

title: User preference: compact category list over detailed links in teamlead-memory.md
content:

title: useTools parameter is bool | dict[str, bool] — _resolveTools handles per-tool filtering
content:
As of 2026-07-04, the `useTools` parameter in `LLMService.generateTextViaLLM` (service.py:421) is typed `UseToolsType = Union[bool, Dict[str, bool]]` (service.py:51), NOT just `bool`.

**Resolution** is handled by `_resolveTools()` (service.py:164-199), called at service.py:509:
```python
tools: Sequence[LLMToolFunction] = self._resolveTools(useTools)
```

Behavior:
- `True` → ALL registered tools from `self.toolsHandlers` are enabled (same as before).
- `False` → empty list (no tools).
- `dict[str, bool]` → per-tool enable/disable. The special key `TOOLS_DEFAULT_DICT_KEY` (value `"default"`) controls every tool not explicitly listed (defaults to `False` if absent). Unknown tool names in the dict are logged as warnings and silently ignored.

**Production caller using the dict form**: the divination discovery flow (`divination.py:1040-1044`) passes a per-tool dict to enable only `WEB_SEARCH` and `GET_URL_CONTENT`:
```python
useTools={
    ToolName.WEB_SEARCH: True,
    ToolName.GET_URL_CONTENT: True,
}
```
This is a deliberate, more conservative choice — discovery needs only web search + URL fetch, not the entire registered tool catalog. The other two callers (`dev_commands.py:1024`, `llm_messages.py:238`) still pass boolean values from `ChatSettingsKey.USE_TOOLS.toBool()`.

The dict path is exercised by `tests/services/llm/test_use_tools.py`. The divination test (`tests/bot/test_divination_discovery.py::testDiscoverLayoutWithWebSearchSuccess`) was fixed on 2026-07-04 to assert the exact per-tool dict instead of the stale `is True` boolean assertion.

title: User preference: prefer simplicity over custom extensibility frameworks
content:
Learned during the shutdown state dump feature (2026-07-04):

1. **No custom hook registries when an existing pattern exists.** The agent initially built a `registerOnExitHook()` / `_onExitHooks` list on `HandlersManager`. The user rejected this: "in Handler manager we do not need add our own registry for on_exit. We just need to create one method + register it as DO_EXIT handler in QueueService." The project already has the `QueueService` DO_EXIT lifecycle mechanism; reinventing it is noise. When a lifecycle/shutdown/exit hook is needed, first check if `registerDelayedTaskHandler(DelayedTaskFunction.DO_EXIT, ...)` already covers it. The user then simplified even further — removing the DO_EXIT registration entirely and just calling the method directly from `shutdown()`, since that's the only place the data is still available.

2. **Diagnostic/dump methods should return data, not log.** The agent's first `RateLimiterManager.dumpAllStats()` implementation logged directly via `logger.info(...)`. The user corrected: "RateLimiter's dumpAllStats should return dict (or list of dicts) instead of logging." Rationale: separation of concerns — the library layer shouldn't dictate log formats. The caller (HandlersManager) is responsible for formatting and logging the returned data (using `utils.jsonDumps(entry, indent=2)`).

3. **Don't over-engineer for hypothetical extensibility.** The 4-iteration evolution (custom registry → DO_EXIT handler + direct call → direct call only with guard → direct call only without guard) all moved toward LESS code. When adding a feature, start with the simplest possible approach (single method, single call site) and only add abstractions (registries, hooks, guards) if there's a concrete second consumer.

title: Three distinct user-storage concepts and the per-user-global gap
content:
The codebase has THREE unrelated stores for 'user data' — understanding the distinction is load-bearing for any user-memory feature:

1. **`user_memories` table** (migration_020, PK `chat_id, user_id, memory_id`) — the unified per-(chatId, userId, threadId) structured memory store. Supersedes BOTH the legacy `user_data` key-value table (DROPPED in migration_022) AND the rolling-bio `memoryRefinement[threadId].summary` JSON blob (backfilled in migration_020 from `chat_users.metadata.memoryRefinement`). Access via `db.userMemories.*` (UserMemoriesRepository). Three LLM tools: `add_memory` / `delete_memory` / `search_memories` (ToolName.ADD_MEMORY / DELETE_MEMORY / SEARCH_MEMORIES), registered in `UserMemoriesHandler`. Scoped per (chat, user, thread) with an optional `permanent` flag for cross-thread facts.

2. **`UserMetadataDict`** (`internal/bot/models/user_metadata.py`) — per-(chatId, userId) **moderation flags + the refinement cursor**, stored as JSON in `chat_users.metadata` TEXT column (added by migration_003). Moderation fields: `isSpammer`, `notSpammer`, `dropMessages`, `leftChat`. Also still carries `memoryRefinement[str(threadId)]` with `lastProcessedMessageId` / `lastProcessedMessageDate` (the rolling-bio `summary` was dropped in Phase 4a). Set via `BaseBotHandler.setUserMetadata` (base.py:1154), read via `parseUserMetadata`. Writers: spam.py, message_preprocessor.py, user_memories.py.

3. **`getUserState/setUserState`** (cache/service.py) — ephemeral session state keyed by `userId` alone (the `USERS` cache namespace). Holds transient wizard state (`UserActiveActionEnum`: Configuration, Summarization, UserDataConfig, TopicManagement). Persisted to DB only on shutdown. NOT a knowledge store.

**Per-user-global gap:** There is STILL no per-user-global (cross-chat) memory store — `user_memories` is scoped per (chat, user, thread). `getUserChats(userId)` maps user→chats, but memories in chat A are invisible in chat B. The `permanent` flag on `user_memories` is cross-THREAD within a chat, not cross-chat. Any cross-chat memory feature would require a NEW table (PK on `(user_id, key)` or similar).

**Migration count note:** as of 2026-07-14 the latest migration is migration_023 (rename `memory_injection_enabled` → `memory_enabled`). The next free migration number is 024.

title: Tool handler extraData contract — all assume ensuredMessage, RuntimeError if missing
content:
LLM tool handler extraData contract: every handler signature is `async def(self, extraData: Optional[Dict[str, object]], **toolParams) -> Dict[str, object] | str | None`. In the live bot extraData carries `ensuredMessage`; tools scope their work via `extraData["ensuredMessage"].recipient.id` / `.sender.id` / `.threadId`.

Missing-ensuredMessage handling is now a NEVER-RAISE error dict, not a RuntimeError: `_llmToolAddMemory` (user_memories.py:437-439) does `ensuredMessage = extraData.get("ensuredMessage") if extraData else None; if not isinstance(ensuredMessage, EnsuredMessage): return {"done": False, "error": "Missing ensuredMessage"}`. Its docstring states 'Never raises — all failures are folded into {"done": False, "error": ...}'.

Implication for cron-driven LLM calls (still valid): a background job has no real EnsuredMessage — either build a synthetic one for extraData, pass context via other extraData keys (the refinement path adds `isRefinement: True` with chat/user/thread context), or use `generateText` directly (tool-less) like SummarizationHandler._doSummarization.

title: Model+fallback config pair recipe for new LLM features
content:
End-to-end pattern for adding a feature with its own primary+fallback model selection (established by SummarizationHandler, image parsing, etc.):

1. Add a ChatSettingsKey **pair** to the enum (`internal/bot/models/chat_settings.py`): `FEATURE_MODEL` + `FEATURE_FALLBACK_MODEL`, both with `type=ChatSettingsType.MODEL` in `_chatSettingsInfo`.

2. Add matching defaults to `[bot.defaults]` in `configs/00-defaults/bot-defaults.toml` (kebab-case keys matching enum values).

3. At call time:
   ```python
   modelKey = chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.FEATURE_MODEL].toModel()
   fallbackKey = ChatSettingsKey.FEATURE_FALLBACK_MODEL
   ret = await llmService.generateText(messages, chatId=chatId, chatSettings=chatSettings, modelKey=modelKey, fallbackKey=fallbackKey)
   ```
   (Template: `SummarizationHandler._doSummarization`, summarization.py:275.)

Existing pairs in `[bot.defaults]` (bot-defaults.toml:160-169): `chat-model`/`fallback-model`, `summary-model`/`summary-fallback-model`, `image-parsing-model`/`image-parsing-fallback-model`, `image-generation-model`/`image-generation-fallback-model`. Model names resolve against the LLMManager registry built from `configs/00-defaults/*-models.toml`.

**Exception:** `CONDENSING_MODEL` exists but has NO matching `CONDENSING_FALLBACK_MODEL` — `LLMService` falls back to `FALLBACK_MODEL` for condensing by default (service.py:486). If you want a feature-specific fallback, you must add the enum member; otherwise omit it and reuse `FALLBACK_MODEL`.

title: chat_users.metadata update mechanism: dedicated partial-update, upsert preserves metadata
content:
The `chat_users` table has a `metadata TEXT DEFAULT '' NOT NULL` column (added by migration_003, current schema in migration_013; composite PK `chat_id, user_id`). Repository: `ChatUsersRepository` at `internal/database/repositories/chat_users.py`.

Key update methods (all async):
- `updateUserMetadata(self, chatId: int, userId: int, metadata: str) -> bool` — DEDICATED partial-column UPDATE that sets only `metadata` + `updated_at` (NOT a full-row upsert). Use this to write metadata. The `metadata` arg is a pre-serialized JSON string.
- `updateChatUser(self, chatId, userId, username, fullName) -> bool` — full-row upsert via `provider.upsert(...)`. GOTCHA: on conflict its `updateExpressions` touch ONLY `username`, `full_name`, `updated_at`. It does NOT touch `metadata` — so metadata is PRESERVED across an `updateChatUser` call (e.g. a new message re-upserting the user will not wipe previously-written metadata). Do not assume the upsert overwrites every column.
- `getChatUser(chatId, userId, *, dataSource=None) -> Optional[ChatUserDict]` — fetches a single row (already documented elsewhere).

Handler-layer read/write helpers live on `BaseBotHandler` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:1055-1090`), NOT in the repo. JSON serialization is done here; raw `str` flows through the repository:
- `parseUserMetadata(self, userInfo: Optional[ChatUserDict]) -> UserMetadataDict` — reads `userInfo["metadata"]`, decodes with stdlib `json.loads` (returns `{}` for None/empty).
- `setUserMetadata(self, chatId, userId, metadata: UserMetadataDict, isUpdate: bool = False) -> None` — serializes with `utils.jsonDumps(metadata)`, then calls `updateUserMetadata`. `isUpdate=True` enables MERGE mode: it first reads the existing row via `getChatUser`, then does `{**parseUserMetadata(userInfo), **metadata}` before serializing. `setUserMetadata` is the ONLY production call site of `updateUserMetadata`.

Content schema for `chat_users.metadata` today: `UserMetadataDict` (`internal/bot/models/user_metadata.py`), a `TypedDict(total=False)` of sparse boolean flags — `isSpammer: bool`, `notSpammer: bool`, `dropMessages: bool`, `leftChat: bool`. All optional (sparse dict). New per-thread / memory-refinement data stored in this column should be added as additional keys to this same dict.

title: JSON serialization convention: jsonDumps exists, no jsonLoads helper — read with stdlib json.loads
content:
Repo-wide JSON serialization convention in `lib/utils/utils.py`:

- `lib.utils.jsonDumps(data, compact=None, **kwargs) -> str` is the canonical serializer (exported from `lib/utils/__init__.py`). Defaults: `ensure_ascii=False`, `sort_keys=True`, `default=str` (so datetime etc. fall back to `str()`), and compact separators `(",", ":")` unless `indent` is passed; caller kwargs override the defaults via `dumpKwargs.update(kwargs)`.
- There is deliberately NO `jsonLoads` helper. To DESERIALIZE, call stdlib `json.loads(str)` directly — do not search for a repo helper. This asymmetry is consistent across the codebase (metadata columns, chat-setting JSON arrays, LLM tool-call results).

Convention for metadata/JSON-stored columns: WRITE with `utils.jsonDumps(obj)`; READ with `json.loads(str)`. Example call sites (verified 2026-08-20):
- chat_users metadata: the handler-layer `setUserMetadata` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:1191`) no longer serializes itself — it delegates to `CacheService.updateUserMetadata`, which serializes via `utils.jsonDumps` at `internal/services/cache/service.py:1268`. Read side `parseUserMetadata` uses `json.loads` (base.py:1188).
- media_attachments metadata: `metadata=utils.jsonDumps(...)` at `internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:1747` (animated-sticker stub entry), `:1957`, and `:1968`.

Note: the DB provider layer also has a JSON wrapper at `internal/database/providers/utils.py:54` (`return libUtils.jsonDumps(data)`) used internally by `convertToSQLite` for dict/list values, so containers passed to repositories are serialized there even without an explicit handler-layer call.

title: GOTCHA: SUMMARY_MODEL HAS a _chatSettingsInfo entry — plan v1 §11 claim is wrong
content:
`docs/plans/memory-refine-plan-v1.md` §11 states: "`SUMMARY_MODEL` has no `_chatSettingsInfo` entry — match that precedent." This is FACTUALLY WRONG.

`SUMMARY_MODEL` DOES have a full `_chatSettingsInfo` entry at `internal/bot/models/chat_settings.py:617-622` (type=`ChatSettingsType.MODEL`, page=`ChatSettingsPage.LLM_BASE`). `SUMMARY_FALLBACK_MODEL` likewise has one at 623-628 (page=`LLM_PAID`). In fact ALL model-type keys (CHAT_MODEL, FALLBACK_MODEL, SUMMARY_MODEL, SUMMARY_FALLBACK_MODEL, IMAGE_PARSING_MODEL) have `_chatSettingsInfo` entries.

IMPACT on implementing phase 1 (adding `MEMORY_REFINE_MODEL` / `MEMORY_REFINE_FALLBACK_MODEL` to `ChatSettingsKey`): do NOT follow the plan's "omit `_chatSettingsInfo`" guidance. Model-type keys conventionally GET entries (type MODEL, with a page assignment) so they appear in the settings UI model picker. The "no entry" precedent the plan cites does not exist. Use `ChatSettingsPage.LLM_BASE` for the primary model and `ChatSettingsPage.LLM_PAID` for the fallback, matching the SUMMARY_* pair.

The plan doc was written verbatim as instructed (substance not editable), so this error persists in the file until corrected. Flagged but not fixed during the 2026-07-04 verification pass because it is plan substance (decision-adjacent), not path/line drift.

Cross-ref: memory 3e11d608 covers ChatSettingsType MODEL vs STRING choice for `_chatSettingsInfo`.

title: HandlerResultStatus enum members and NEXT vs SKIPPED semantics
content:
`HandlerResultStatus` (defined at `internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:81`, imported from `internal.bot.common.handlers.base`) has exactly five members:

- `FINAL` — handler fully handled the message; stop the chain.
- `SKIPPED` — handler did nothing for this message.
- `NEXT` — handler did work and processing should continue to the next handler.
- `ERROR` — recoverable error.
- `FATAL` — unrecoverable error.

Key project philosophy (confirmed during user-memory-refinement planning): **NEXT = "did work, continue chain"; SKIPPED = "did nothing."** When a handler performs ANY processing for a message — even a lightweight side-effect like incrementing a counter — it should return `NEXT`, not `SKIPPED`. Reserve `SKIPPED` strictly for handlers that took no action at all. This distinction matters when a handler's primary path is a gate (e.g., wizard-state check) but it also unconditionally does background bookkeeping for every message.

title: Global asyncio.Lock pattern for cron-triggered LLM work exceeding the tick interval
content:
Operational gotcha + reusable design pattern (applied in `docs/plans/memory-refine-plan-v1.md`, the user-memory refinement feature).

**Gotcha:** A single LLM call can take >60s. The `QueueService` CRON_JOB delayed task self-reschedules every 60s. If a cron tick launches LLM work and that work outlasts the tick, the NEXT tick fires concurrently before the prior run completes → concurrent provider calls → provider flooding / rate-limit blowout.

**Pattern chosen (instead of per-key locks):** A single GLOBAL `asyncio.Lock` on the handler/service that owns the cron, serializing ALL instances of the work. The cron:
1. Checks `if self._refineLock.locked(): return` at the very top (bail this tick if a run is already in flight — cheap, non-blocking).
2. Otherwise `async with self._refineLock:` for the WHOLE due batch.
3. Processes due entries SEQUENTIALLY (`await` each, not `createTask`) — the global lock already serializes, so internal parallelism buys nothing.

Per-key locks were explicitly rejected: with per-key locks, multiple entries can fire concurrently within a single tick and there is no global bound on concurrent LLM calls.

**Why a single global lock is correct here:** refinement throughput is NOT the goal — protecting the provider is. A global lock means a slow run blocks the next tick's refinement rather than spawning a concurrent one, which is the desired behavior.

**Precedents already confirmed** (no need to re-grep): sandbox locks (`lib/sandbox/`), `HandlersManager.stateLock`. The `asyncio.Lock` API (`async with`, `.locked()`) is the idiomatic choice in this repo for this shape of problem.

**Generalize:** for ANY future cron-triggered operation that invokes the LLM (or otherwise may exceed the 60s tick), reach for a single global `asyncio.Lock` + early-return-on-`locked()`, not per-key locks.

title: setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True) shallow-merge destroys sibling nested keys — BLOCKER for per-thread memoryRefinement
content:
`BaseBotHandler.setUserMetadata(..., isUpdate=True)` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:1176-1179`) performs a SHALLOW one-level dict merge: `existing = await self.cache.getUserMetadata(...)` then `metadata = {**existing, **metadata}`. If you pass `{"memoryRefinement": {<threadId>: {...}}}` to update one thread, it REPLACES the entire `memoryRefinement` sub-dict — every sibling thread's data is wiped.

This gotcha is now DOCUMENTED IN CODE — the `setUserMetadata` docstring (base.py:1166-1174) explicitly warns: 'For NESTED sub-dicts (e.g. `memoryRefinement`) do NOT use this method; perform an explicit full-read + nested-mutate + full-write via `cache.getUserMetadata` / `cache.updateUserMetadata` (see `UserMemoriesHandler._persistMemoryEntry`.)'

**Correct pattern (used by `UserMemoriesHandler._persistMemoryEntry` in `internal/bot/common/handlers/user_memories.py:1356-1365`):** read-modify-write the nested dict yourself before passing to setUserMetadata:
```python
memoryRefinement = metadata.get("memoryRefinement", {})
memoryRefinement.update({str(threadId): newThreadData})
metadata["memoryRefinement"] = memoryRefinement
# then write the full metadata dict
```
The shallow top-level merge is safe here because you're passing the FULL merged `memoryRefinement` dict as the replacement value.

**Lesson:** `setUserMetadata(isUpdate=True)` is only safe for top-level keys whose values are flat/scalar. For any nested-dict-valued key, read the existing nested dict, merge at that level yourself, then write the whole nested dict back. Note: as of the user-memories v1 Phase 4a rewrite, the rolling-bio `summary` field was dropped from the persist blob (refinement now curates via tool calls), but the `lastProcessedMessage*` cursor still lives in `chat_users.metadata.memoryRefinement[threadId]` and still requires the nested read-modify-write pattern.

title: EnsuredMessage uses __slots__ — adding a new attribute requires extending the __slots__ tuple AND initializing in __init__
content:
`EnsuredMessage` (and sibling classes `MessageSender`, `MessageRecipient`, `MediaContent`) in `internal/bot/models/ensured_message.py` use `__slots__`. For `EnsuredMessage` specifically, `__slots__` is defined at lines 355-379 as a fixed tuple of allowed attribute names (23 slots).

**Consequence:** you CANNOT simply 'add an attribute' like `self.userSummary = ...` — it will raise `AttributeError: 'EnsuredMessage' object has no attribute 'userSummary'` at runtime. Adding a new field requires TWO coordinated changes:
1. Add the field name string (e.g. `"userSummary"`) to the `__slots__` tuple (lines 355-379).
2. Initialize it in `__init__` (the `__init__` method begins at line 381; every slot is assigned in lines 408-464).

**Convention for documenting slotted fields:** per existing memory (e34c6a26), fields in `__slots__` classes are documented as inline triple-quoted string comments immediately after the assignment in `__init__`, not as class-level docstrings.

This generalizes to ALL `__slots__` classes in the repo (e.g. `ChatMessagesRepository` has `__slots__ = ()` — see memory 53fadc00). When extending any slotted class, always check and extend `__slots__`.

title: Tier-specific config overrides live in gitignored configs/common; global defaults in tracked configs/00-defaults
content:
Convention confirmed 2026-07-04 via the memory-refinement feature review: friend-tier (and likely other tier-specific) config overrides have a split location by design:

- **Global default** for a setting goes in the GIT-TRACKED `configs/00-defaults/bot-defaults.toml` under `[bot.defaults]` (e.g. `memory-refinement-enabled = false`, `allow-sandbox = false`). This propagates via git to all environments.
- **Tier override** (e.g. enable the feature only for the friend tier) goes in the GITIGNORED `configs/common/01-bot-defaults.toml` under `[bot.tier-defaults.friend]` (e.g. `memory-refinement-enabled = true`, `allow-sandbox = true`). This is a per-deployment overlay that does NOT get committed.

Evidence: the established `allow-sandbox` setting already follows this exact pattern (default false in tracked 00-defaults, friend-override true in untracked configs/common). The new `memory-refinement-enabled` setting follows the same pattern.

Implication for agents adding a tier-gated feature/setting: you MUST edit BOTH files — the tracked default (so every env gets the safe default) AND the untracked tier override (so your local dev env enables it for the target tier). Do NOT assume the tier-override edit will appear in `git diff` or be part of a commit; it won't (see related gotcha memory `ca22d8a5`). Plans that name `configs/common/*.toml` as a deliverable are describing a per-deployment manual step, not a committed artifact — flag this so reviewers/plans don't treat its absence from a commit as a regression.

Other per-environment overlay dirs (`configs/local/`, `configs/local-common/`, etc., selected via the `CONFIGS` env var per `.env.*`) follow the same untracked-by-design model; only `configs/00-defaults/` is the tracked source of truth for defaults.

content:
`ChatMessagesRepository.getChatMessagesSince` (`internal/database/repositories/chat_messages.py:171`) supports an optional `userId: Optional[int] = None` filter (after `messageCategory`, before the `*, dataSource` keyword-only marker). The full signature, the null-semantics SQL (`AND (:userId IS NULL OR c.user_id = :userId)`), and backward-compat behavior are now documented in project docs — `docs/llm/database.md` §1 (chatMessages row) and `docs/database-schema-llm.md` "Get Messages Since Date". What the docs do NOT carry — call-site inventory (verified 2026-08-20):
