title: LLM tool never-raise contract: tool-execution loop has no try/except
content:
The LLM tool-execution never-raise contract (verified against code 2026-07-14):

**The tool-execution loop (`internal/services/llm/service.py:642-668`) has NO try/except around tool handler invocations.** The loop body is:
```python
for toolCall in ret.toolCalls:
    toolRet = ""
    if toolCall.name in filteredToolNames:
        toolRet = await self.toolsHandlers[toolCall.name].call(extraData, **toolCall.parameters)
    else:
        toolRet = {"done": False, "error": f"Tool {toolCall.name} not available, ..."}
```

**`LLMToolFunction.call` (`lib/ai/models.py:295-319`) is a bare passthrough** — `return self.function(*args, **kwargs)` with zero exception handling.

**Propagation chain:** If a tool handler raises, the exception propagates up through `generateTextViaLLM` → `_generateTextViaLLM` (llm_messages.py) → `_sendLLMChatMessage`'s try/except, which catches it, logs 'Error while sending LLM request', sends the user `f"Error while sending LLM request: {type(e).__name__}"`, and returns `LLMReplyOutcome.ERROR`.

**Consequence:** An unhandled raise in a `_llmTool*` handler does NOT crash the process, but it DOES abort the entire LLM generation for that turn — the user sees an error message instead of a reply. **Tool handlers MUST catch their own exceptions** and return an error dict (e.g. `{"error": "..."}`) rather than letting exceptions escape.

This contract is documented in the `add-llm-tool` skill (`.agents/skills/add-llm-tool/SKILL.md`).

title: 5th coordination site for memory-refinement LLM tools: _runSingleRefinement useTools dict
content:
The standard '4 sites must change together' pattern for LLM tools (ToolName StrEnum, registerTool call, _llmTool* handler, chat-time gating in _sendLLMChatMessage) has a **5th coordinated site for memory-refinement destructive tools** (verified current, 2026-08-21): `_runSingleRefinement` builds its OWN useTools dict at internal/bot/common/handlers/user_memories.py:1306-1312 — `{ADD_MEMORY: True, DELETE_MEMORY: True, SEARCH_MEMORIES: True, SEARCH_MESSAGES: True, GET_CURRENT_DATETIME: True}` — bypassing chat-time gating entirely (the refinement LLM can call tools that chat-time cannot; chat-time sets DELETE_MEMORY/ADD_MEMORY/SEARCH_MEMORIES False in llm_messages.py:286-302 per D3).

**Implication for a new destructive memory tool:** gate it False in _sendLLMChatMessage's useTools (Site 4) AND enable it True in the refinement pass's useTools dict (user_memories.py:1306) — or the refinement LLM can't call it.

**Skill status (CORRECTED):** the `add-llm-tool` skill NOW documents this 5th site — a callout block at .agents/skills/add-llm-tool/SKILL.md:350-351 ('Memory-refinement tools: a 5th coordinated enablement site') plus a checklist item (:445). The earlier claim that the skill omitted it is outdated.

Context: the refinement pass invokes generateTextViaLLM directly with extraData {"isRefinement": True} (:1313-1317); `isRefinement` is a real key at internal/services/llm/models.py:42, read at user_memories.py:448. For non-memory tools, the standard 4 sites suffice.

title: str-returning LLM tools exist in production: _llmToolGetCurrentDateTime returns jsonDumps
content:
Convention reality check verified 2026-07-11: **str-returning LLM tool handlers are NOT just legacy/example code — they exist in production.**

The `LLMToolHandler` type alias (`internal/services/llm/service.py:38`) is:
```python
LLMToolHandler: TypeAlias = Callable[..., Awaitable[Union[str, Dict[str, Any], None]]]
```
So the type system permits `str`, `Dict[str, Any]`, or `None`.

**Live production handlers returning JSON strings (not dicts):**
- `internal/bot/common/handlers/common.py:165-183` — `_llmToolGetCurrentDateTime` returns `utils.jsonDumps({"datetime": ..., "timestamp": ..., "timezone": "UTC"})`. This is a registered, shipping tool (registered at common.py:75).
- `internal/bot/common/handlers/example.py:130` — `_llmToolExample` returns `utils.jsonDumps(...)`.

**The modern convention is to return `Dict[str, Any]`** (newest handlers like `user_memories.py` do this), and the `add-llm-tool` skill recommends dict returns. But the absolute prohibition ("❌ Never return a JSON string") found in the skill is overstated — `common.py:_llmToolGetCurrentDateTime` is a counterexample that a developer reading the skill would find and be confused by, or worse, "fix" unnecessarily.

**Practical guidance:** Prefer `Dict[str, Any]` returns for new tools. If you see an existing tool returning a JSON string, it works fine — the service serializes either form. Don't rewrite it unless you're already touching that code.

title: make format lint validates only .py files — does NOT lint markdown or embedded doc code blocks
content:
`make format lint` runs `flake8`, `isort`, `black`, `pyright`, and an `import main` check — all of which operate on `.py`/`.pyi` files ONLY. It does NOT validate, lint, or format `.md`/`.txt` documentation files, and it does NOT check code blocks embedded inside markdown documentation.

Confirmed by the Makefile targets (line numbers verified 2026-08-20):
- `format` (Makefile:67-75): `isort .` + `black .`, then iterates `lib/ext_modules/*/` — all Python-only.
- `lint` (Makefile:59-64): `flake8 .` + `isort --check-only --diff .` + an `import main` circular-import check + `pyright`. flake8/isort/black/pyright all parse Python AST; none processes markdown.
- `check` (Makefile:105-108): adds `black --check --diff .` — also Python-only.
- `check-docs` (Makefile:111-112): runs `scripts/check_docs.py` — the ONLY gate that touches markdown (local link integrity).

**Still-inaccurate claim in agent tooling (verified at its new location 2026-08-20):** `.agents/skills/update-project-docs/SKILL.md:177` says '`make format lint && make test` still green — this catches code examples that drifted.' This overstates what the gates catch. `make format lint` catches only Python-AST drift (a renamed import, a bad function signature); it cannot detect a stale code snippet embedded inside a `.md` file. Only `make test` can catch a doc-embedded example if that exact code happens to exist as a pytest test case elsewhere — and per the docs-only convention (memory dd5a9470), pure docs changes may legitimately skip `make test` entirely, leaving doc-embedded examples unverified by any automated gate.

**NEW (2026-08-20):** update-project-docs SKILL.md:179 now codifies the docs-only substitute gate: "If you are `docs-writer` (or another agent restricted from running `make format`/`make test`), substitute `make lint && make check-docs` as your verification gate." The docs-writer agent prompt (`.opencode/agents/docs-writer.md:163`) likewise says "Do NOT run `make test` — no code changed under your watch" and its step 4 (docs-writer.md:172) correctly frames `make lint` as 'validates the repo still imports and lints clean after your changes' (a sanity check, not a doc-content validator).

**What `make format lint` IS useful for after doc edits:** it validates the repo still imports cleanly and no Python was accidentally broken — a sanity check, not doc-content validation. For markdown-link integrity use `make check-docs`; for doc-embedded code examples there is currently NO automated validation (see memory cff99f91).

title: Bash permission pattern styles: suffixed-wildcard preferred over two-line form
content:
Styles observed for bash permission patterns in `.opencode/agents/*.md` frontmatter when allowing a command both bare and with arguments:

**Style A — Two-line:** `"ls": allow` (bare) AND `"ls *": allow` (with args).
**Style B — Suffixed-wildcard:** `"git diff*": allow` — glob semantics where `*` matches zero or more characters, so one rule covers both `git diff` and `git diff HEAD`.
**Style C — Exact-match (for containment-critical commands):** `"make lint": allow` matches ONLY the bare string; combined/redirect forms need explicit variants like `"make lint 2>&1": allow`.

**Current state (verified 2026-08-20):**
- `docs-writer.md` (lines 80-92) uses Style B EXCLUSIVELY: `make lint*`, `make check-docs*`, `rg*`, `grep*`, `ls*`, `git diff*`, `git log*`, `git show*`, `git status*`, `git ls-files*`, `wc*`.
- `code-reviewer.md` (lines 83-124) uses a MIX: Style B for git inspection subcommands (`git diff*`, `git log*`, `git show*`, `git rev-parse*`, etc.), Style A two-line for `ls`/`ls *`, `sort`/`sort *`, `wc`/`wc *`, and Style C exact for `make lint`, `make test`, `make check-docs`, `pwd`, bare `git tag`, bare `git branch` — plus explicit `2>&1` variants (lines 121-123) and `"./venv/bin/pytest *"` wildcard.

**Recommendation:** When authoring new agent bash allow-lists, prefer the suffixed-wildcard form (`"cmd*"`) — a single rule covers bare and arg'd invocations. Reserve exact-match (+ explicit variants) for commands where wildcarding would over-permit (e.g. `make` targets, where `make test*` would also match hypothetical mutating targets, and `git branch` where the bare form is listing but `git branch X` creates a branch).

Refines prior memory 140bc9e7: 'both bare and globbed forms are needed' is incorrect for suffixed-wildcard globs — `"cmd*"` matches bare `cmd` too.

title: Agent authoring principle: cross-check prompt-suggested commands against bash permission allow-list
content:
When authoring or reviewing `.opencode/agents/*.md` definitions, the system prompt's suggested commands MUST be cross-checked against the agent's own `bash:` permission allow-list. A common failure mode is a prompt that instructs the agent to use a command form (especially piped commands) that the permission map rejects at runtime.

**Specific risks to check:**
1. **Pipelines:** `ls -1 … | grep … | wc -l` won't match per-command patterns (`"ls *": allow` etc.) — piped strings are evaluated as a whole. Reframe to structured tools (Glob/Grep/Read) or adjust patterns.
2. **Exact vs. glob:** If the prompt says "run `make format lint`" but the allow-list only has `"make lint": allow` (without `"make format lint"`), the combined command is denied.
3. **Asymmetric allow-lists:** Allowing `"make format lint"` but not standalone `"make format"` is meaningless for containment — `make format lint` executes the `format` target anyway and can rewrite `.py` files via black/isort subprocesses, bypassing the edit/write permission gate.

**Also check prompt-permission alignment for:**
- `task:` delegation — the prose "you may delegate to X/Y" must match the `task:` map's allows.
- `edit:`/`write:` scope — if the prompt says "don't edit .opencode/ or .agents/", but the permission allows `*.md`, the restriction is soft-only (matches architect.md's convention, but is not hard-enforced).

**Origin:** Discovered during the docs-writer.md review, where Method step 2 instructed piped recounts that the bash allow-list would deny.

title: code-reviewer bash allowlist: make lint/test are exact-match-only, need wildcards for flags/pipes
content:
The code-reviewer agent's bash allowlist uses exact-match patterns for the make quality gates. As of 2026-08-07 the allowlist (lines 118-124) contains: `"make lint"`, `"make test"`, `"make check-docs"` (exact), plus explicit `"make lint 2>&1"`, `"make test 2>&1"`, `"make check-docs 2>&1"` entries, and `"./venv/bin/pytest *"` (wildcard). Consequences:

- `make lint` — ALLOWED (exact match)
- `make lint 2>&1` — ALLOWED (explicit variant added 2026-08-07; previously DENIED — this specific gap was closed)
- `make lint 2>&1 | tail -40` — STILL DENIED (falls through to `"*": deny` because the pipe makes the whole command string not match any pattern)
- `make test -x foo` or any other flag suffix — DENIED (no matching pattern)
- `./venv/bin/pytest tests/foo.py -v` — ALLOWED (wildcard matches)

Originally confirmed live (2026-07-11): `make lint 2>&1 | tail -40` was denied despite `"make lint": allow` — which motivated adding the bare `2>&1` variants. Piped and suffixed forms that don't exactly match a pattern still fall through to the catch-all deny.

General opencode permission-matching gotcha (confirms memories 2cb79249, ee0d2f60, 1907e1d3): opencode matches the WHOLE command string against bash patterns; patterns are exact-match unless they end in `*`. If the agent is expected to run a command with flags or pipes, either use a suffixed wildcard (`"make lint*"`) or enumerate the exact variant (`"make lint 2>&1"`).

title: Provider return-type aliases for no-Any compliance in test helpers
content:
When type-annotating test helper FUNCTIONS (not stub classes) that accept a database provider or return results from `executeFetchOne`/`executeFetchAll`, import and use the concrete exported type aliases from `internal.database.providers.base`:

- `BaseSQLProvider` — for helper params that take the provider instance.
- `QueryResultFetchOne` (defined as `Dict[str, Any] | None`) — the return type of `executeFetchOne`.
- `QueryResultFetchAll` (defined as `Sequence[Dict[str, Any]]`) — the return type of `executeFetchAll`.
- `QueryResult` — the union of the above plus `None`.

This satisfies AGENTS.md's "no Any" rule WITHOUT writing `Any` in your own annotations — you reference the project's own exported aliases, so the `Any` is upstream in the project's definitions, not in your code.

Discovered during migration_023 test typing (Fix 4 of the Gate-1 review). The precedent file `tests/database/test_migration_020_user_memories.py` does NOT have provider-typed helpers — it inlines `provider = testDatabase.getProvider()` in each test body and types `db: Database` in helpers. So when writing new migration test helpers that take a provider directly (e.g. `_insertChatSetting(provider, ...)`, `_fetchSetting(provider, ...) -> QueryResultFetchOne`), there's no direct precedent to copy — you must discover and import these aliases yourself.

Import pattern:
```python
from internal.database.providers.base import BaseSQLProvider, QueryResultFetchOne
```

This is distinct from test STUB CLASSES overriding abstract `BaseSQLProvider` methods (covered by a separate memory) — those must match the abstract signature including `QueryResult` return type.

title: Permission-enforced path containment: explicit directory-denies ahead of broad allow
content:
When an agent prompt restricts editing certain directories (e.g., "do not edit agent definitions under `.opencode/`" or "do not edit skills under `.agents/`"), a prose-only restriction is insufficient if the `edit`/`write` permission map would technically allow those files. For example, `"*.md": allow` would also match `.opencode/agents/foo.md` and `.agents/skills/foo/SKILL.md`.

**Pattern for hard containment** — add explicit path-denies for sensitive directories AHEAD of the broad allow in the edit and write maps:

```yaml
edit:
  "*": deny
  ".opencode/**": deny   # blocks editing agent definitions
  ".agents/**": deny      # blocks editing skills
  "*.md": allow
  "*.txt": allow
write:
  "*": deny
  ".opencode/**": deny
  ".agents/**": deny
  "*.md": allow
  "*.txt": allow
```

This was applied to `.opencode/agents/docs-writer.md` (Finding 5 of a code review). The agent prompt said "do not edit `.opencode/` or `.agents/`" but the permission map only had `"*.md": allow`, which would have permitted those paths. The fix makes the containment permission-enforced, preventing the docs-writer from accidentally editing its own definition or the skills.

**Ordering note:** The denies are placed before the `*.md` allow. OpenCode permission maps for `task` use "last matching rule wins" semantics (per memory d2e226e6). The edit/write ordering semantics are less clear — this implementation assumes specificity-based or first-match-wins resolution where `.opencode/**` (a more specific glob) overrides `*.md` for paths under `.opencode/`. If edit/write maps also use last-match-wins, the deny would need to come AFTER the allow to take effect. Verify the actual semantics before relying on this pattern in other agents.

title: code-reviewer allowlist fixed: make format/make format lint removed, patterns widened to wildcards
content:
UPDATED 2026-08-20. The code-reviewer agent's bash allowlist at `.opencode/agents/code-reviewer.md` had `make format` and `make format lint` entries that REWRITE source (black+isort via Makefile), contradicting the agent's review-only identity. Fix applied and confirmed stuck:

- `"make format"` / `"make format lint"` are ABSENT from the current allowlist.
- Quality-gate entries (lines 118-124): EXACT-MATCH `"make lint"`, `"make test"`, `"make check-docs"` (lines 118-120) PLUS explicit `"make lint 2>&1"`, `"make test 2>&1"`, `"make check-docs 2>&1"` (lines 121-123, added 2026-08-07 — supersedes the earlier `"make check-docs*"` wildcard), and `"./venv/bin/pytest *"` wildcard (line 124). Rationale for the `2>&1` entries: opencode bash patterns are exact-match unless they end in `*`, so base `"make lint": allow` does not cover `make lint 2>&1`.
- Prose is aligned: code-reviewer.md instructs the reviewer that it CAN and SHOULD run `make lint`/`make test`/`make check-docs`/`./venv/bin/pytest` to self-verify findings (lines 140, 143, 174, 255, 272, 276).
- The task block is `"*": deny` + `"code-analyst": allow` only (lines 127-129) — the reviewer can delegate read-only analysis to code-analyst.

GATES (Makefile, read-only vs. rewriting):
- `make lint`: flake8, isort --check-only --diff, import check, pyright — READ-ONLY. Safe for review-only.
- `make format`: isort + black — REWRITES SOURCE. Unsafe for review-only.
- `make test`: pytest. Read-only w.r.t. source. Safe.

Design principle reinforced: the permission gate must ENFORCE the agent's identity, not just the prompt prose. If an agent is 'review-only', the bash allowlist must not contain any command that authors or edits source.

title: OpenCode bash allowlist patterns are exact-match unless they end with wildcard *
content:
Discovered while fixing the code-reviewer allowlist. OpenCode bash permission patterns in agent config (`.opencode/agents/*.md`) are EXACT-MATCH unless the pattern ends with `*`. This means:

- `"make lint": allow` matches ONLY the exact command `make lint` — NOT `make lint 2>&1`, `make lint 2>&1 | tail`, `make lint -v`, or any piped/flagged variant.
- `"make lint*": allow` matches `make lint`, `make lint 2>&1 | tail`, `make lint -v`, etc. — any command starting with `make lint`.
- `"./venv/bin/pytest *": allow` matches `./venv/bin/pytest <anything>` but NOT bare `./venv/bin/pytest` (note the space before `*`).

When allowlisting a command that the agent may combine with flags, pipes, or redirections, use the `*` suffix form. Otherwise the exact-match-only entry causes commands to fall through to the catch-all `"*": deny`.

This is a property of opencode's permission matching, not documented in the project's own AGENTS.md. Apply it when designing allowlists for any agent.

title: make test killed by tool timeout (120s) before its own timeout 5m completes
content:
When running `make test` via a tool/shell command, the default command timeout (120000ms = 2 minutes) is SHORTER than `make test`'s own internal guard (`timeout 5m` = 5 minutes). The command will be killed by the tool timeout before the suite finishes.

The full test suite takes ~108 seconds on this machine (3121 tests), which is right at the 120s boundary — sometimes it completes, sometimes the tool kills it first. For `make test`, always set a tool timeout of at least 300000ms (5 minutes) to match `make test`'s internal `timeout 5m`.

This is separate from the known issue that `make test-failed` has NO internal timeout guard at all (see other memory). The relevant distinction:
- `make test` internal guard: `time timeout 5m pytest ...` (5 min)
- Tool command default timeout: 120000ms (2 min) — too short for full suite
- Fix: use a larger tool timeout (≥300000ms) when invoking `make test`

title: Doc-sync convention: dated changelog rows in live docs are frozen; avoid dead tokens in current-behavior prose
content:
During a refactor that renames or removes identifiers (e.g., the 2026-07-11 ChatSettingsKey consolidation that removed REGENERATE_EMBEDDINGS, MEMORY_EMBEDDINGS_ENABLED, MEMORY_RETRIEVAL_MODE, etc. and renamed MEMORY_INJECTION_ENABLED → MEMORY_ENABLED), when syncing live docs/llm/ markdown to reflect the new state:

**1. Dated changelog/history sections within LIVE, actively-maintained docs are frozen.** This is distinct from the already-recorded conventions about SUPERSEDED-banner files (909dc68a), docs/plans/ immutability (71b4f7f4), and docs/archive/ policy (561b6201) — those cover whole files/directories. This covers *sections* inside docs that are otherwise current. For example, `docs/llm/memories/chat-history-search.md` contains "Post-Review Fixes — Round 1 (2026-06-21)" and "Post-Review Fixes — Round 2 (2026-06-28)" sections with table rows and bullet points that reference now-removed identifiers (e.g., "REGENERATE_EMBEDDINGS self-reset attempted then reverted"). These are historically accurate point-in-time records of what happened on those dates — LEAVE THEM AS-IS. Do not rewrite history to purge old names from dated changelog entries.

**2. In CURRENT-behavior prose (not dated changelog), update ALL references** to removed/renamed identifiers. A single identifier may appear many times in a file; update every occurrence. Relocate by reading content (line numbers drift).

**3. Even explanatory parentheticals in current-behavior prose should avoid spelling out dead token names** — e.g., do NOT write "(renamed from MEMORY_INJECTION_ENABLED)" or "(the former REGENERATE_EMBEDDINGS was removed)". Instead describe the change generically: "(renamed in the chatSettings consolidation)", "(the former one-shot re-embedding trigger was removed)". This is because the verification bar is strict zero-hits on the dead tokens via rg, with the ONLY exception being genuinely historical dated-changelog rows.

**4. Verification approach:** After edits, run two rg checks — one for dead enum/constant tokens, one for dead TOML-key strings — across the edited file set. Target is zero hits. Remaining hits should ONLY be documented historical-changelog exceptions, explicitly noted in the summary. Then `make lint` (docs-only changes pass cleanly since flake8/isort/pyright don't touch .md files; the `import main` circular-import check is the only code-path exercised).

This was applied successfully to 4 docs (chat-history-search.md, architecture.md, handlers.md, database.md) during the 2026-07-11 consolidation doc sync, leaving 4 dated-changelog rows in chat-history-search.md as documented exceptions.

title: Docs convention: example code uses object, but source-reporting must faithfully report Any
content:
Convention distinction verified during add-llm-tool SKILL.md review (2026-07-11):

**Example/template code in documentation must use `object`, not `Any`** — this directly mirrors the repo's no-`Any` rule (AGENTS.md hard rules). Example signatures in skill files and docs should read `Dict[str, object]`, `**kwargs: object`, `-> Dict[str, object]`.

**BUT documentation that *describes* existing source code must faithfully report what the source actually says — even if the source uses `Any`.** Do NOT "fix" `Any` to `object` in prose describing a real type alias, because that would make the documentation lie about the source.

**Concrete case:** The `add-llm-tool` SKILL.md describes the `LLMToolHandler` type alias (service.py:38) as `str | Dict[str, Any] | None`. This is correct and should NOT be changed to `Dict[str, object]` — the actual source is `Union[str, Dict[str, Any], None]`. Meanwhile, the same skill's *example* tool signatures use `Dict[str, object]`, which is also correct because those are templates for new code, not descriptions of existing code.

**Rule of thumb:** If the doc is showing you what to *write* → use `object`. If the doc is telling you what *already exists* → report the real type verbatim, including `Any`.

This distinction could trip up future agents who reflexively "fix" every `Any` they see in docs — doing so to source-reporting prose introduces factual errors.

title: Grep drift audits have blind spot for prose tuple mentions — pair patterns with broader search
content:
During the 2026-07-11 getChatSettings drift-sweep verification, the prescribed grep patterns (`getChatSettings.*tuple` and `\[0\].*value|value.*\[0\]`) structurally cannot catch unqualified "(value, updatedBy) tuple" references in natural-language or illustrative dialogue text. 

Concrete instance: `.opencode/agents/debugger.md:48` (illustrative routing-example dialogue) still contains "caller-side handling of the (value, updatedBy) tuple" — an unqualified tuple claim not surfaced by either pattern because the phrase "tuple" isn't adjacent to "getChatSettings" and the sentence doesn't use a `[0]` shape. The reviewer flagged this as a cosmetic NIT (illustrative dialogue, not a prescriptive gotcha) and the sweep was deemed complete for active instructional docs.

LESSON for future drift audits: when auditing for a recurring drift pattern via grep, also run a broad natural-language grep for the concept by its prose name alone (e.g., `rg "tuple" .opencode/ docs/ .agents/ AGENTS.md --type md` then manually filter), not just the adjacency patterns. The prescribed patterns catch the structured/formal occurrences; the broad search catches prose/illustrative ones.

The sweep also confirmed an acceptable-location categorization convention for classifying grep hits in future audits:
- **(a) DB-repo-scoped docs** (docs/llm/database.md, docs/database-schema*.md, docs/database-README.md, write-regression-test/SKILL.md:304) — inherently repository-layer; tuple claims correct for that layer.
- **(b) Frozen historical docs** (docs/archive/, docs/plans/) — immutable snapshots.
- **(c) Immutable logs** (.opencode/memory.jsonl) — append-only memory log.
- **Irrelevant** — list/dict/string indexing in code/tests (e.g., `value[0] == "-"` in lib/utils/utils.py).

Every remaining grep hit in the verified sweep fell into one of these categories.

title: Edit/write permission map resolution semantics still ambiguous — architect.md does not disambiguate
content:
Follow-up to memory e9dba44a (path-denies pattern). The code-reviewer reviewing `.opencode/agents/docs-writer.md` Finding 5 claimed that opencode edit/write permission maps resolve by "most-specific-glob-wins" (not first-match-wins), citing as evidence that `architect.md` ships `"*": deny` ahead of `"*.md": allow` and works correctly.

**This inference is NOT conclusive.** architect.md (`"*": deny` → `"*.md": allow` → `"*.txt": allow`) is consistent with BOTH resolution strategies:
- Most-specific-match: `*.md` is more specific than `*`, so allow wins. ✓
- Last-match-wins (same as `task` maps per memory d2e226e6): `*.md` comes after `*`, so allow wins. ✓

The actual disambiguating test case is docs-writer.md itself, which places specific denies BEFORE broad allows:
```yaml
edit:
  "*": deny
  ".opencode/**": deny
  ".agents/**": deny
  "*.md": allow
  "*.txt": allow
```
For path `.opencode/agents/foo.md`, ALL of `"*"`, `.opencode/**`, and `*.md` match. Resolution depends entirely on strategy:
- Most-specific-match → `.opencode/**` (most specific) wins → **DENY** (the deny works as intended).
- Last-match-wins → `*.md` (last matching rule in order) wins → **ALLOW** (the deny is INEFFECTIVE; docs-writer can still edit `.opencode/**/*.md`).

**Practical consequence:** The path-denies in docs-writer.md may or may not actually block edits to `.opencode/`/`.agents/` depending on the (still-unverified) resolution strategy. If opencode uses last-match-wins uniformly (as it does for `task`), then denies must be placed AFTER the allows, not before. This should be empirically tested before relying on deny-before-allow patterns. Until verified, treat path-denies as defense-in-depth only, not as a hard guarantee.

title: Agent skills: 8 canonical skills in .agents/skills/ + registration in AGENTS.md
content:
The canonical source for loadable task-specific skills is `.agents/skills/` (8 skills as of 2026-07-11): `add-chat-setting`, `add-database-migration`, `add-handler`, `add-llm-tool`, `read-project-docs`, `run-quality-gates`, `update-project-docs`, `write-regression-test`. `.codeassistant/skills/` is a symlink to `../.agents/skills/`. CodeAssistant and OpenCode both see the same skills. The authoritative skills list lives in AGENTS.md §"Existing instruction sources (do not duplicate, prefer linking)" — the bullet list under `.agents/skills/`.

When a new skill is added under `.agents/skills/`, it MUST also be registered as a bullet in that AGENTS.md skills list (this is the `update-project-docs` skill's rule). Entry format: `- [skill-name](.agents/skills/skill-name/SKILL.md) — <one-line description>`, condensed from the skill's frontmatter `description:` field (purpose + load-bearing invariant/rule, one line, no "Triggers:" list). Ordering convention: workflow skills grouped first (read-project-docs, update-project-docs, run-quality-gates, write-regression-test), then the `add-*` recipes grouped together (add-database-migration, add-handler, add-llm-tool, add-chat-setting).

title: Agents are auto-discovered, NOT listed in AGENTS.md (only skills are)
content:
Project convention confirmed 2026-07-11: opencode agent definitions (in `.opencode/agents/*.md`) are AUTO-DISCOVERED by the tooling and must NOT be registered/listed in AGENTS.md. Only SKILLS (in `.agents/skills/`) get an explicit entry in the AGENTS.md "Existing instruction sources" skills list.

When a session creates both a new skill AND a new agent, the skill must be added to the AGENTS.md skills list, but the agent must not. This distinction bit one session: a new `docs-writer` agent was created alongside two new skills, and the task had to explicitly warn "do NOT add the agent to AGENTS.md." The two new skills (`write-regression-test`, `add-llm-tool`) were correctly added; the agent was correctly omitted.

title: code-reviewer task recursion hazard resolved (self-spawn removed)
content:
RESOLVED. The code-reviewer agent's `permission.task` block at `.opencode/agents/code-reviewer.md` previously granted `"code-reviewer": allow` under a `"*": deny` default, while the prose said the task tool is "restricted to `code-analyst`." This was both a direct prose-vs-gate contradiction AND a recursion hazard: a code-reviewer could spawn another code-reviewer indefinitely.

Fix applied: removed `"code-reviewer": allow` from the task allowlist. The allowlist now grants only `"code-analyst": allow`, matching the prose. Verified the legitimate `"code-reviewer": allow` entries in `teamlead.md:98` and `software-developer.md:83` (which correctly delegate TO the reviewer) are untouched.

**Design principle (reusable for agent audits):** An agent's `permission.task` allowlist must not grant permission to spawn itself. Self-referential task permissions create unbounded recursion. Always cross-check that the allowlist is a subset of what the prose claims, in both directions.

title: make format lint bypass pattern: resolved agents and confirmed-legitimate agents
content:
The `make format lint` source-bypass pattern (an agent with restricted edit perms like `*.md`/`*.txt` only, but whose bash allowlist grants `make format lint`, which runs black+isort and rewrites `.py` files — bypassing the edit restriction) has been audited across all agent definitions. Status by agent (re-verified 2026-08-20):

**RESOLVED (fixed):**
- `code-reviewer.md` — `make format`/`make format lint` removed from bash allowlist; absent from the current file. Quality-gate entries (lines 118-124) are: EXACT-MATCH `"make lint"`, `"make test"`, `"make check-docs"` (lines 118-120), plus explicit `"make lint 2>&1"`, `"make test 2>&1"`, `"make check-docs 2>&1"` variants (lines 121-123, added 2026-08-07 — the earlier `"make check-docs*"` wildcard was replaced by these exact entries), and `"./venv/bin/pytest *"` wildcard (line 124).
- `docs-writer.md` — `"make format lint"` absent from bash allowlist. Current allowlist (lines 80-92) is all suffixed-wildcards: `"make lint*"`, `"make check-docs*"`, `"rg*"`, `"grep*"`, `"ls*"`, `"git diff*"`, `"git log*"`, `"git show*"`, `"git status*"`, `"git ls-files*"`, `"wc*"`. The docs-writer edits `.md`/`.txt` only and must NOT modify `.py` files. `make lint` (flake8 + isort --check-only + import check + pyright) is read-only and safe.

**CONFIRMED LEGITIMATE (agent edits code, so source formatting is appropriate):**
- `debugger.md` — `bash: allow` (full shell); edits code.
- `software-developer.md` — `bash: allow`; primary job is writing code.
- `teamlead.md` — has `bash: deny`, so cannot execute `make format lint` even though its prose mentions it (as a rule to propagate to specialists, not to run itself). Not a functional bypass.

**Reusable rule:** `make format lint` (which runs black + isort and REWRITES source per Makefile) is only appropriate for agents that are SUPPOSED to edit code. Review-only or docs-only agents must not have it in their bash allowlist; the permission gate must enforce the agent's identity, not just the prompt prose.

title: Gotcha: chat_settings.key column is a MySQL reserved word (unquoted everywhere)
content:
The `chat_settings` table has a column named `key` that is used UNQUOTED throughout the codebase — in the repository (`internal/database/repositories/chat_settings.py:161,186`), in migration_013 (lines 148-149, 719-720), and in migration_023 (lines 79, 99: `UPDATE chat_settings SET key = :newKey WHERE key = :oldKey`).

`KEY` is a reserved word in MySQL. These queries will fail with a syntax error when the MySQL provider is enabled, unless the column is identifier-quoted or renamed.

This is a PRE-EXISTING issue — every query against `chat_settings` in the codebase has this problem; it was not introduced by any specific change. The fix belongs at the schema level (column rename from `key` to something non-reserved like `setting_key` or `name`) and would require a migration + repository update + all dependent migrations updated. This should be addressed as part of enabling the PostgreSQL/MySQL providers, not piecemeal.

Identified during Gate 2 review of the ChatSettings consolidation (2026-07-11, code-reviewer/glm-5.2). The migration_023 under review followed the established pattern correctly; this is an observation for the future, not a defect in that migration.

Other MySQL reserved words potentially used as identifiers in this schema worth auditing when multi-DB goes live: `key`, `value`, `status`, `order`, `group`, `type`, `mode`, `user`, `condition`.

title: scripts/check_condensing.py created — calls condenseContext() for A/B testing
content:
A new debug/evaluation script `scripts/check_condensing.py` was created (2026-07-11). Unlike `scripts/reproduce_llm_dialog.py` (which does NOT call `condenseContext()` — see memory f3a11ff2), this script ACTUALLY calls `LLMService.getInstance().condenseContext()` on a real chat thread, making it suitable for A/B testing condensing prompt/model changes.

**Purpose**: Given `--chat-id` + `--message-id`, fetches the full thread, builds ModelMessages mirroring `getThreadByMessageForLLM` (base.py:712-911), runs condenseContext, and prints BEFORE/AFTER sections with token estimates and each condensed block delineated.

**Key design decisions**:
1. **`force=True`** is passed to `condenseContext`. Without it, `condenseContext` no-ops (returns original messages unchanged) when the thread fits within `maxTokens` (service.py:668-669). For evaluation purposes, `force=True` ensures condensing always runs regardless of thread size.
2. **No condense-cache reconstruction** — builds from raw ChatMessageDict rows, skipping the handler's cached-summary replay (base.py:786-821). This is intentional for fresh A/B testing.
3. **`cache=None`, `excludeMemoryIds=set()`** for toModelMessageList — no memory resolution needed for condensing evaluation.
4. **keepFirstN=1, keepLastN=1** (mirrors handler defaults base.py:783-784); **maxTokens = int(llmModel.contextSize * 0.5)** (mirrors base.py:849).

**Args**: `--config-dir` (repeatable, dest="configDirs"), `--env` (dest="envFile"), `--chat-id` (int), `--message-id` (str), `--dry-run` (dest="dryRun"), `--verbose`. `configs/00-defaults` always included implicitly.

**Config/settings keys read**: CHAT_MODEL, CONDENSING_MODEL, CONDENSING_PROMPT, CONDENSING_SYSTEM_PROMPT, CHAT_PROMPT, CHAT_PROMPT_SUFFIX, LLM_MESSAGE_FORMAT.

title: condenseContext force=True required to actually condense short threads
content:
`LLMService.condenseContext()` has an early-return no-op at `internal/services/llm/service.py:668-669`: if the current token count (`llmModel.getEstimateTokensCount`) is below `maxTokens`, it returns the original messages list unchanged WITHOUT calling the condensing LLM. 

This means any script/tool intended to evaluate condensing quality MUST pass `force=True` to `condenseContext()` — otherwise threads under the maxTokens threshold produce no condensing output, defeating the evaluation purpose.

The `force` parameter bypasses this early-return check. `scripts/check_condensing.py` passes `force=True` for exactly this reason.

Additionally, `condenseContext` internally adjusts `keepFirstN` by +1 if `messages[0].role == "system"` (it detects and preserves the system prompt). So if you pass `keepFirstN=1` with a system prompt at index 0, the internal head will be 2 messages (system + first), and the body (the part that gets condensed) is `messages[2:-keepLastN]`.

title: root_message_id is self-referential for root messages in production (NOT NULL)
content:
**CORRECTION/NUANCE to memory bee638c3** which states "root_message_id = NULL for root messages."

The production message-storage code at `internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:1082` shows:
```python
rootMessageId = message.messageId  # default: self-referential for non-reply messages
if message.isReply and replyId:
    parentMsg = await self.db.chatMessages.getChatMessageByMessageId(...)
    if parentMsg:
        rootMessageId = parentMsg["root_message_id"]
```

For non-reply messages (roots), `rootMessageId` is set to `message.messageId` — **self-referential, NOT NULL**. This means in modern production data, `getChatMessagesByRootId(chatId, rootId)` DOES include the root message itself (since its root_message_id matches the query).

The `if dbMessage["root_message_id"] is None:` branch at base.py:761 is legacy/defensive handling for older data where roots may have had NULL root_message_id. The `getMessageThread()` docstring at chat_messages.py:582-590 also references this None case defensively.

**Practical implication for scripts/tools**: When resolving a thread root from a given message ID, handle both cases:
```python
rootId = dbMessage["root_message_id"]
if rootId is None:
    rootId = dbMessage["message_id"]  # legacy/defensive fallback
```
This is what `scripts/check_condensing.py` does.

NOTE: Memory bee638c3 was based on TEST data where roots may have NULL root_message_id. Test fixtures and production data may differ on this point.

title: Script bootstrap ordering: injectLLMManager must run before any ChatSettingsValue.toModel()
content:
When writing standalone scripts that use `ChatSettingsValue.toModel()`, you MUST call `LLMService.getInstance().injectLLMManager(llmManager)` BEFORE any `.toModel()` call.

`ChatSettingsValue.toModel()` (internal/bot/models/chat_settings.py:590) calls `getLLMManager()` (the module-level lazy wrapper at chat_settings.py:22), which in turn calls `LLMService.getInstance().getLLMManager()`. If `injectLLMManager()` hasn't been called, `getLLMManager()` raises `RuntimeError("LLMManager not initialized, call llmService.getInstance().injectLLMManager(...)")` (internal/services/llm/service.py:1543).

**Correct bootstrap order for scripts** (see scripts/check_condensing.py:421-444):
1. `configManager = ConfigManager(configPath, configDirs, dotEnvFile)`
2. `bootstrapProxy(configManager)` from `scripts/_lib/bootstrap.py` — initialises the ProxyHelper singleton (and, at module import, aliases httpx→httpx2); must run before Database/LLMManager/any httpx client
3. `db = Database(configManager.getDatabaseConfig())`
4. `llmManager = LLMManager(configManager.getModelsConfig())`
5. `LLMService.getInstance().injectLLMManager(llmManager)`  ← MUST be before step 7
6. `CacheService.getInstance()` + `await cache.injectDatabase(db)`
7. NOW `chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.CHAT_MODEL].toModel()` will work

Production equivalent is main.py:64-105 (Database → ProxyService.initialize → LLMManager → injectLLMManager). Scripts that only call `.toStr()` (like reproduce_llm_dialog.py) don't need the inject ordering since `.toStr()` doesn't access the LLM manager.

title: Prefix-glob bash allow-lists match destructive command variants (cat*/find* bypass)
content:
A `.opencode/agents/*.md` bash allow-list pattern like `"cat*": allow` or `"find*": allow` — intended as read-only utilities — also matches DESTRUCTIVE command variants if opencode matches raw command strings against prefix globs (which the `"./venv/bin/pytest *"` and `"make lint*"` patterns in the same agents strongly imply):

- `cat > internal/foo.py` — shell redirection **overwrites/truncates** a source file
- `cat >> file` — appends to a file
- `find . -name '*.py' -delete` — **deletes** source files
- `find . -exec <anything> \;` — **arbitrary command execution** (including `git commit`, `rm -rf`, etc.)

These bypass the agent's `edit`/`write` deny entirely because the mutation happens via the shell command, not the edit/write tool.

**Discovered in:** Gate 2 code review of the docs-writer agent (`.opencode/agents/docs-writer.md` lines 87, 94) on 2026-07-11. The agent's prose promises it "edits only `*.md`/`*.txt`" and "may run `make lint` and read-only searches" — but `cat*` and `find*` punch through that guarantee.

**Pre-existing sibling:** code-reviewer.md has `"sed -n *": allow` — `sed -n 'w file'` writes a file even under `-n`. Same class, not introduced in that change set.

**Fix:** Narrow patterns so they cannot match redirection/exec forms — e.g. drop `find*` entirely (the agent already has `rg*`/`grep*` for search; `find` is redundant), and replace `cat*` with the `read` tool (which the agent already has). If narrowing isn't possible, verify opencode's command-matching semantics: if it tokenizes argv and forbids shell metacharacters (`>`, `>>`, `-exec`, `-delete`), these are moot; if it string-matches, they must be tightened.

**Contrast with memory 2cb79249:** That memory covers the "too restrictive" direction (piped commands fail to match). This finding covers the "too permissive" direction (destructive variants of nominally-read-only commands DO match). Both stem from the same root: prefix-glob matching of raw command strings is coarse in both directions.

title: Bash allowlist bypass: cat* and find* are NOT read-only (shell redirection/exec escapes edit/write scoping)
content:
When designing `bash:` permission allow-lists in `.opencode/agents/*.md` frontmatter, "read-only" commands like `cat` and `find` are **bypassable** and should be excluded if the agent is restricted to edit/write only specific file types:

- `cat > file` — overwrites arbitrary source files, bypassing `edit`/`write` scoping (e.g., `edit: { "*": deny, "*.md": allow, "*.txt": allow }`).
- `find . -name '*.py' -delete` — deletes arbitrary files.
- `find . -exec <anything>` — executes arbitrary commands, full escape.

**Remediation (applied 2026-07-11 to `.opencode/agents/docs-writer.md`):** Removed both `"cat*": allow` and `"find*": allow`. The agent already has the `read` tool (proper file reading), `rg*`/`grep*` (content search), and the `Glob` tool (pattern matching), making `cat`/`find` redundant.

**Remaining safe commands:** Commands like `ls > file` are technically redirectable but only emit filenames (not attacker-controlled content), so they are acceptable. The concern is specifically about commands that can write/delete/execute ARBITRARY content.

**Outstanding hardening item:** `.opencode/agents/code-reviewer.md:113` still has `"cat *": allow` (note the space — different pattern from `cat*`). Other agent files (`code-analyst.md`, `software-developer.md`) reference `cat`/`find` in prose. A consistent hardening pass across all agent definitions is recommended but was out of scope for the original task.

title: Production OutputFormat + system prompt construction in getThreadByMessageForLLM
content:
When building the ModelMessage list that production sends to the LLM, `BaseBotHandler` (internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py) does two things that scripts/tools must replicate for parity:

**1. OutputFormat mapping (base.py:744-749):** The output format for `toModelMessageList` is selected by `botProvider` via a match statement:
```python
outputFormat = OutputFormat.MARKDOWN
match self.botProvider:
    case BotProvider.TELEGRAM:
        outputFormat = OutputFormat.MARKDOWN_TG
    case BotProvider.MAX:
        outputFormat = OutputFormat.MARKDOWN_MAX
```
This matters because messages with `formatEntities` (markup column populated) render differently under MARKDOWN vs MARKDOWN_TG/MARKDOWN_MAX. Plain-text threads are unaffected, but markup-heavy threads diverge if the wrong format is used.

**2. System prompt construction (base.py:751-758):** The system message is prepended as:
```python
ModelMessage(
    role="system",
    content=chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.CHAT_PROMPT].toStr()
    + "\n"
    + chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.CHAT_PROMPT_SUFFIX].toStr(),
)
```
The two prompt values are joined with a single `"\n"` separator.

**Platform from config:** The botProvider is read via `configManager.getBotConfig().get("mode", BotProvider.TELEGRAM)` (main.py:103) — `getBotConfig()` returns `self.get("bot", {})`, and the `[bot]` section's `mode` key holds the platform string (telegram/max).

title: ChatSettingsValue.toModel() raises ValueError on unknown/empty model names
content:
`ChatSettingsValue.toModel()` (`internal/bot/models/chat_settings.py:580-596`) raises `ValueError` when the stored model name is unknown to the LLM manager or empty. The method calls `modelManager.getModelByName(...)` which returns None for unknown names, and the subsequent code raises `ValueError`.

Gotcha: any code calling `.toModel()` on a chat-settings value (e.g. `chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.CHAT_MODEL].toModel()` or `chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.CONDENSING_MODEL].toModel()`) must be prepared to catch `ValueError` if the model name could be missing/invalid. This is especially relevant in scripts/dev tools that resolve models from config — wrap `.toModel()` calls in try/except.

This was review finding #3 for `scripts/check_condensing.py`: the setup-phase `.toModel()` calls (and all config/DB setup) propagated exceptions uncaught, producing raw tracebacks and skipping DB cleanup.

title: check_condensing.py now matches production after 6 review fixes applied
content:
On 2026-07-11, all 6 Gate 1 code-review findings for `scripts/check_condensing.py` were fixed. This CORRECTS memory `5da014a8` (which claimed the script mirrors production) — that claim was FALSE before these fixes and is now TRUE after them. Also resolves review finding `fbce188d`.

**Fixes applied:**
1. **(IMPORTANT) System prompt now prepended:** `buildThreadModelMessages` accepts `chatSettings` and prepends `ModelMessage(role="system", content=CHAT_PROMPT + "\n" + CHAT_PROMPT_SUFFIX)`. BEFORE/AFTER token counts now include persona tokens (parity with production).
2. **outputFormat forwarded:** Platform read from config (`configManager.getBotConfig().get("mode")` → `BotProvider`) and mapped to `MARKDOWN_TG`/`MARKDOWN_MAX`/`MARKDOWN` (mirroring base.py:744-749). No new CLI flag — mirrors production automatically.
3. **Setup phase wrapped in try/except:** Config → DB → settings → model resolution → thread fetch → message build all wrapped. `db` pre-declared `Optional[Database] = None`; on exception prints to stderr, runs `traceback.print_exc()`, closes DB, returns exit code 1.
4. **Tier defaults folded into merge:** New `resolveChatTier()` helper mirrors `getChatTier` + fallback chain. Merge order now global → per-type → tier → DB. Tier-filtering of DB overrides (base.py:281-303) intentionally omitted (dev tool simplification, documented in docstring).
5. **Dead keptTail arithmetic simplified:** Replaced with direct `print(f"Kept as-is (tail): {_KEEP_LAST_N}")`.
6. **hasSystemPrompt branch verified correct:** Now live and correct after fix #1 — `effectiveKeepFirstN = _KEEP_FIRST_N + 1` when system prompt present, matching production's `keepFirstN += 1`.

Verification: `make format lint` clean (pyright 0 errors), `--help` renders, `import scripts.check_condensing` clean.

title: ChatTier.fromStr returns Optional[Self] — None on invalid string, never raises
content:
`ChatTier.fromStr(v: str)` at `internal/bot/models/chat_settings.py:144-157` returns `Optional[Self]`: it wraps `cls(v)` in `try/except ValueError: return None`. So a malformed or unrecognized tier string yields `None`, NOT an exception.

Production impact in `base.py`:
- `getChatTier` (`base.py:341-359`, returns `Optional[ChatTier]`) calls `ChatTier.fromStr(...)` at lines 354 and 357 and returns the result DIRECTLY, without an immediate null-check. So a malformed PAID_TIER or BASE_TIER string makes getChatTier return None.
- The downstream fallback chain (`base.py:262-266`) catches that None: if `chatTier is None and BASE_TIER in defaultSettings` → try fromStr again; if still None → `ChatTier.BANNED`.
- Net behavior: a malformed paid/base tier string silently resolves to the next tier in the fallback chain (ultimately BANNED) rather than erroring.

Confirmed during the `scripts/check_condensing.py` confirmation re-review (2026-07-11): the script's tier resolver uses defensive `paidTier = fromStr(...); if paidTier is not None: return paidTier` checks, which is MORE robust than production's direct-return pattern (it short-circuits correctly instead of returning None when the key is present but the value is malformed). Callers replicating tier logic should null-check the fromStr return before using it.

title: Chat settings resolution: tier-defaults layer and per-setting tier gating
content:
Production chat-settings resolution (`BaseBotHandler.getChatSettings` / context assembly in `internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py`, ~lines 255-308) is NOT a simple "defaults + DB overrides" merge. It has four layers and tier-gating:

**Layer 1 — defaults:** global + per-chat-type defaults (loaded in `HandlersManager.__init__`).

**Layer 2 — tier-defaults:** `tierSettings = cache.getDefaultChatSettings(f"tier-{chatTier}")` (`base.py:268`), keyed like `tier-paid`, `tier-base`, `tier-banned`. Loaded from `botConfig.get("tier-defaults", {})`. This is the non-obvious middle layer — scripts that omit it diverge from production. The original `check_condensing.py` bug (Gate 1 finding #4) was precisely this omission.

**Layer 3 — DB per-chat overrides, tier-GATED:** iterating `chatSettings.items()` (`base.py:281-303`), each override is conditionally included:
- Each settings page has a `minTier()` (`base.py:282`). If `not chatTier.isBetterOrEqualThan(settingTier)` AND the setting was not set by a bot owner → the override is DROPPED (`base.py:289-292`).
- MODEL / IMAGE_MODEL settings get EXTRA gating: the model's own tier (`ChatTier.fromStr(modelInfo.get("tier", ""))`) is checked, and if it exceeds the chat's tier, the override is dropped (`base.py:293-301`).

**Tier resolution** (`base.py:259-266` + `getChatTier` at `341-359`): PAID_TIER checked first (active only if `PAID_TIER_UNTILL_TS >= time.time()`), then BASE_TIER from DB settings, then BASE_TIER from defaults, finally `ChatTier.BANNED`.

Scripts/tools replicating the resolution (e.g. `scripts/check_condensing.py`) must: load global+per-type defaults, load tier-defaults (`tier-{chatTier}`), then merge DB overrides. The tier-gating of per-chat overrides can usually be approximated as a flat `dict.update()` for dry-run purposes, but the tier layer must not be skipped.

title: Agent files enumerate permitted commands in multiple sites — update all together
content:
When adding a new permitted command (e.g., `make check-docs`) to an opencode agent definition (`.opencode/agents/*.md`), the file typically has MULTIPLE sites that enumerate "permitted commands" — all must be updated together or the agent may second-guess whether the command is truly allowed:

1. **The `bash:` permission allow-list** in the YAML frontmatter (e.g., `"make check-docs*": allow`).
2. **"Hard Constraint" / "Operating Principles" prose sections** that enumerate "permitted read-only gates" or "explicitly permitted" commands — e.g., code-reviewer.md has at least two such spots: one in the Hard Constraint section ("Read-only verification commands — `make lint`, `make test`, `./venv/bin/pytest` — are explicitly permitted") and one in an allowed-usage enumeration.
3. **Methodology / verification checklist sections** that tell the agent which commands to run and when.

Concrete example: when propagating `make check-docs` to `.opencode/agents/code-reviewer.md` (2026-07-11), the developer added it to the bash allowlist AND the review methodology (step 3 quality gates), then realized the Hard Constraint prose still listed only lint/test/pytest as permitted. Without updating the prose, an agent reading the Hard Constraint might refuse to run check-docs because it "wasn't in the allowed list." So the developer went beyond the two-requested-changes scope and added check-docs to the Hard Constraint enumerations too — this was the right call for internal consistency.

Style note: bash allow-list entries can be exact-match (`"make lint": allow`) or wildcard (`"make lint*": allow`). The two agent files differ in convention — docs-writer.md uses wildcards, code-reviewer.md uses exact matches. When adding a new read-only command, the wildcard form (`"make check-docs*": allow`) is safer since it allows arguments (e.g., `make check-docs V=1`).

title: CORRECTION: Piped bash commands ARE allowed in opencode when every segment matches an allowlist pattern
content:
CORRECTION of deleted memory 2cb79249 (which incorrectly claimed piped commands fall through to deny). That memory was "inferred from pattern semantics, not verified." This is the empirically verified behavior:

**Empirical evidence (2026-07-11, in a live code-reviewer session):**
1. `ls .agents/skills | wc -l` → **ALLOWED** (returned 8). The session's allowlist had `"ls *": allow` and `"wc *": allow`.
2. `make lint 2>&1 | tail -20` → **DENIED**. The session had `"make lint": allow` (exact, no wildcard). The `2>&1` made the first segment not match the exact pattern.
3. Bare `make lint` → **ALLOWED** (exact match works for the bare command).

**Conclusion:** opencode does NOT reject piped commands wholesale. It appears to split the command on pipe `|` and evaluate each segment independently against the allowlist. If EVERY segment matches an allow pattern (considering wildcard semantics), the entire piped command is permitted. If ANY segment fails to match, the whole command is denied via the catch-all `"*": deny`.

**Key interaction with exact-match rule (memory eefc752f):** Patterns without `*` are exact-match. So `"make lint"` matches only bare `make lint`, not `make lint 2>&1`. Patterns WITH `*` are prefix/glob match. So `"ls *"` matches `ls <anything>`, and a pipe segment `ls .agents/skills` matches it.

**Impact on docs-writer.md:** docs-writer has `"ls*": allow`, `"grep*": allow`, `"wc*": allow`. So `ls … | grep … | wc -l` IS permitted (all segments match wildcard patterns). The claim at docs-writer.md:171 that this "falls through to *: deny" is factually WRONG. The guidance to use Glob/Grep tools is still sound advice (structured results are more reliable), but the stated permission-system reason is incorrect.

title: Agent definition changes (.opencode/agents/*.md) only take effect in a new session
content:
Changes to `.opencode/agents/*.md` files (frontmatter permissions, prompt text, allowlists) are loaded at session start and do NOT apply to an already-running session.

**Evidence (2026-07-11):** A code-reviewer agent was launched, then `code-reviewer.md` was committed with a new `"make check-docs*": allow` entry in the bash allowlist. When the running code-reviewer tried to execute `make check-docs`, it was DENIED — the session was still using the pre-commit permission set (which had `make format`/`make format lint` but no `make check-docs*`). The committed changes only take effect when a new agent session is started.

**Practical implication:** When iterating on agent definitions (permissions, allowlists, prompts), you must start a new session to test the changes. A running agent cannot validate its own updated definition. This is particularly important for code-reviewer/debugger agents reviewing their own config changes — they can read the committed file but cannot exercise its new permissions.

title: Config section [search-history] vs class ChatSearchHandler naming mismatch
content:
The chat-history-search feature has an inconsistent three-way naming that causes real confusion:

- **Config section:** `[search-history]` in `configs/00-defaults/search-history.toml` (key `enabled`, plus `[search-history.embeddings]` and `[search-history.defaults]`).
- **Accessor:** `configManager.getSearchHistoryConfig()` (note: "SearchHistory", not "ChatSearch").
- **Handler class:** `ChatSearchHandler` in `internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py`.
- **Conditional registration gate:** `manager.py:540` — `if configManager.getSearchHistoryConfig().get("enabled", False):` wraps the `ChatSearchHandler` instantiation.

The config key is `[search-history]`, NOT `[chat-search]`. The handler class is `ChatSearchHandler`, but the config section and accessor use "search-history" naming. People (including the user) informally write `[chat-search]` — that config section does NOT exist.

When documenting or referencing the enable gate, use `[search-history].enabled` to match the code (source of truth). Verified in configs/00-defaults/search-history.toml:4 and manager.py:540 on 2026-07-11.

title: Zero-tolerance broken-link policy: no baseline caveats in agent-facing docs
content:
**Decision (2026-07-11, user directive; re-verified in force 2026-08-20):** Agent-facing instructional docs must present `make check-docs` as a clean pass/fail gate with ZERO caveats about pre-existing broken links. No mention of "~375 pre-existing", no "known drift", no "baseline", no "focus on new breakages." If `make check-docs` fails, agents must report ALL broken links — whether from their own edits or pre-existing.

**Rationale:** Normalizing a broken baseline conditions agents to tolerate broken output, and the count itself becomes stale drift once links are fixed. The goal is zero broken links.

**Scope:** Applies to `.opencode/agents/*.md`, `.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md`, `AGENTS.md`; also historical-exempt records (`docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md`, `.opencode/memory.jsonl`) — factual records by date, not standing instructions.

**Transition COMPLETE — the goal state was reached 2026-07-11:** all 376 broken links were fixed and the `xfail(strict=True)` marker on `tests/scripts/test_check_docs.py::test_noBrokenLinks_inRealRepo` was REMOVED (same day, per docs/llm/memories/doc-link-fix-campaign.md §"xfail marker lifecycle"). The test is now a plain assert (`exitCode == 0`, line 304) that hard-enforces zero in `make test` and CI. The earlier scope exemption for the test file (needed while the xfail transition mechanism was live) is obsolete — no exemption is needed or granted now.

**Verified caveat-free sites (current line numbers):** `.opencode/agents/docs-writer.md:172` (Method step 4) + `:205` (checklist: "no broken markdown links") + allowlist `:83`; `.opencode/agents/code-reviewer.md:174` (review methodology step 3) + allowlist `:120,:123` + hard-constraint prose `:140,:143`; `.agents/skills/update-project-docs/SKILL.md:180`. The `make check-docs` instruction itself is preserved everywhere — only normalizing caveats are forbidden.

**Supersedes:** prior memory `b2d67c93` which recommended "focus on NEW breakages, compare against known baseline" — that approach is explicitly rejected.

title: check_docs.py non-obvious behaviors: archive source/target asymmetry, no :line verification, template placeholders
content:
Two non-obvious behaviors of `scripts/check_docs.py` (the `make check-docs` checker) that are NOT documented in doc-link-fix-campaign.md and still hold as of 2026-07-14:

**1. docs/archive/ source/TARGET asymmetry.** `docs/archive/` is excluded from scanning as a SOURCE (its own outbound links are never checked — it's a frozen historical snapshot, pruned via `_isExcludedDir` during `os.walk`), but it is **NOT excluded as a TARGET**. Links pointing INTO `docs/archive/` from other files are still validated normally — `_resolveTarget` (scripts/check_docs.py lines 297-334) only checks `resolved.exists()` with no excluded-target logic. This is intentional and load-bearing: `lib/geocode_maps/README.md:246` links to `/docs/archive/design/geocode-maps-client-design-v1.md` (verified present) and that link must resolve. Do NOT add `docs/archive/` to any 'skip targets' list.

**2. Only file existence is checked, NOT :line accuracy.** The tool strips `:lineNumber` and `:start-end` suffixes (regex `:[0-9]+(?:[-,][0-9]+)*$` at scripts/check_docs.py line 329) before checking `resolved.exists()` (line 380). It never opens the target file to verify the line number points at meaningful content. Consequence: a link like `[](internal/config/manager.py:59)` passes check-docs even if line 59 has drifted to unrelated content after a refactor. When batch-repointing broken links to moved files, stale `:line` anchors go UNDETECTED — this is why doc-link-fix-campaign.md advises DROPping stale `:line` suffixes when repointing to moved files.

(A former third behavior — docs/templates/ placeholder links — is RESOLVED: docs/templates/ is excluded via `_EXCLUDED_PATH_PREFIXES`; documented in doc-link-fix-campaign.md.)

content:
