title: Parallel agents on shared working tree produce unreliable global-state observations
content:
When two (or more) agents work concurrently on the same git working tree, each agent sees the OTHER agent's intermediate edits as they happen. This makes any observation of GLOBAL/shared state — e.g., "how many broken links total in the repo" — unreliable from either agent's perspective, because the count reflects a partially-edited tree (some links fixed by agent A, some by agent B, some not yet started).

**Encountered during:** the 2026-07-11 doc-link-fix campaign. Two parallel agents fixed ~376 broken markdown links. Each agent's TOTAL broken count was unreliable because they saw each other's intermediate working tree state. A third agent had to do a clean SERIAL verification (`make check-docs` run once, alone) after both finished to get the authoritative count (0 broken).

**Lesson:** After parallel agents finish editing overlapping areas of the working tree, always run a fresh serial verification of any shared/global metric before trusting it. Do NOT trust either parallel agent's count of global state.

title: condenseContext(returnCoverage=True) silently drops failed-batch messages — coverage indices don't span full range
content:
**Non-obvious gotcha (originally confirmed 2026-07-11; API references updated 2026-07-14 after the `returnCoverage` / index-range simplification).** `LLMService.condenseContext()` now ALWAYS returns `Tuple[Sequence[ModelMessage], Dict[int, CondensingDict]]` — there is NO `returnCoverage` kwarg anymore (removed 2026-07-13). It can silently DROP messages from its output. Dropped messages appear in NO coverage entry's `messageIds` list; the dict keys (indices into `newBody`) remain contiguous 0..N-1, but some original body messages are simply unrepresented.

**Two drop paths in `internal/services/llm/service.py` (condenseContext body-summarization loop):**
1. **Oversized single message** (~line 831-834): if a batch of `currentBatchLen == 1` still exceeds `summaryMaxTokens`, `startPos += 1; continue` — that single message is skipped, no coverage entry, no `generateText` call.
2. **Batch exception** (~line 846-852): on LLM call failure, `startPos += currentBatchLen; continue` — entire batch dropped, no coverage entry.

**Consequence for callers:** `condensedRet = retHead + newBody + retTail`, but `newBody` may represent FEWER original messages than the body held. Any caller that assumes every original body message appears in exactly one coverage entry's `messageIds` will be wrong — dropped messages are absent from all entries with NO explicit skip marker. The dict keys are always contiguous (0..len(newBody)-1), so key-contiguity is NOT a signal of completeness.

**Safe approach:** derive head/tail lengths from `len(condensedRet)` structure (`retHeadLen = len(condensedRet) - len(coverage) - keepLastN`) rather than assuming coverage covers the full body. To find which original messages were dropped, diff the union of all `coverage[k]["messageIds"]` against the original body message IDs.

**Note on obsolete fields:** the pre-2026-07-13 design used a `returnCoverage: bool` kwarg, a `CondenseBatchCoverage` TypedDict with `coveredFromIndex`/`coveredToIndex` fields, and caller-side `indexToEntry`/`indexToEntry2` parallel lists. ALL of these were deleted in the 2026-07-13 simplification and replaced by `ModelMessage.source`-based coverage computed inside `condenseContext` via `generateCondensingDict` (see ADR-019 in `docs/llm/architecture.md` and `docs/llm/memories/condensed-context-retrieval.md`).

title: Testing condensing path: _condensingChatSettings() helper + ChatSettingsValue.toModel patch pattern
content:
To test the condensing branch of `handleRandomMessage` (Phase 3b), a new test helper pattern was introduced in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_llm_messages.py`:

**`_condensingChatSettings()`** — extends the existing `_fullChatSettings()` with the 4 condensing-branch keys that `_fullChatSettings()` deliberately omits (CHAT_MODEL, CONDENSING_MODEL, CONDENSING_PROMPT, CONDENSING_SYSTEM_PROMPT). The model-typed values use real `ChatSettingsValue("dummy-model")` instances, but `ChatSettingsValue.toModel` is patched at class level to return `Mock()` — this avoids hitting the real LLM manager (`getLLMManager().getModel()` raises ValueError for unregistered model names).

**Integration test patching stack** (all needed simultaneously):
```python
with patch.object(EnsuredMessage, "fromDBChatMessage", AsyncMock(return_value=lightweightEM)), \
     patch.object(EnsuredMessage, "toModelMessageList", AsyncMock(return_value=[ctxModelMsg])), \
     patch.object(ChatSettingsValue, "toModel", return_value=Mock()), \
     patch("random.random", return_value=0.0):
    result = await liveHandler.handleRandomMessage(em, Mock())
```

**`_makeContextRow(messageId, username, ts) -> ChatMessageDict`** — builds minimal but complete ChatMessageDict rows for the context walk. Must include `message_id`, `username`, `date` (as datetime, not float) because `buildCondensingFields` reads all three. Rows are stored in the parallel `contextRows` list and eventually passed to `buildRandomContextDict`.

**`_lightweightContextEM()`** — returns a bare `EnsuredMessage` with empty metadata (no `randomContext`, no memories). Used as the `fromDBChatMessage` return value so the context-building loop doesn't break early (the break condition checks `eMsg.metadata.get("randomContext") is not None`).

**Key gotcha**: patching `EnsuredMessage.toModelMessageList` at class level affects BOTH the context messages (in the walk loop) AND the current message (appended after condensing). This is acceptable because the test only cares about the condense path and persisted metadata, not the final `_sendLLMChatMessage` output.

**Verification status**: This pattern is UNVERIFIED — `make test` was not run. The integration tests may need debugging.

title: Test gotcha: mock getChatMessagesSince with newest-first rows or deque double-reverses
content:
When writing integration tests that mock `getChatMessagesSince` for the `handleRandomMessage` context-building walk, you MUST provide rows in **newest-first** order to match production's `ORDER BY c.date DESC, c.message_id DESC`. The natural/intuitive way to build test rows is oldest-first (ascending timestamps), but feeding oldest-first rows to the mock causes a **double-reversal bug**: the deque's `extendleft(...)` reverses them AGAIN to newest-first instead of the expected oldest-first.

## The fix
In the test helper `_wireCondensePath` (`tests/bot/common/handlers/test_llm_messages.py`), reverse the rows before handing them to the mock:
```python
handler.db.chatMessages.getChatMessagesSince = AsyncMock(return_value=list(reversed(rows)))
```
The `rows` param is documented as chronological (oldest-first) for test-author convenience; the helper reverses to match production DB order.

## Why this matters
- `sourceRows` (the post-deque list) must be oldest-first for `buildCondensingFields` to yield `messageIds` in ascending order.
- `tillMessageId = messageIds[-1]` (newest) and `tillTS = dateRange["to"]` (max timestamp) are consistent ONLY when sourceRows is oldest-first.
- The fallback branch uses `sourceRows[0]` as the "oldest row" — correct only if oldest-first.

## ContextRows deque alignment (verified correct)
The production code uses two parallel deques:
- `contextMessages.extendleft(reversed(emittedMessages))` — preserves order within batch, reverses across batches.
- `contextRows.extendleft([storedMsg] * n)` — NO `reversed()`, but doesn't need it because all entries within a batch are identical. Across batches, both deques reverse identically, so 1:1 alignment holds.

title: P3b review: integration tests never exercise multi-emit contextRows tagging — alignment only verified for single-emit
content:
**Finding from 2026-07-11 code review (test quality gap).** The Phase 3b integration tests (`TestHandleRandomMessageCondensing` in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_llm_messages.py`) patch `EnsuredMessage.toModelMessageList` to return a fixed `[ctxMsg]` — exactly ONE ModelMessage per row. This means the production line `contextRows.extendleft([storedMsg] * len(emittedMessages))` (llm_messages.py:983) is only ever exercised with `len(emittedMessages) == 1`, where deque alignment is trivial.

The multi-emit alignment correctness was verified ONLY by the simulation test `testAlignmentWithMultiEmitRows` (test_message_metadata.py:551-588), which hand-builds `indexToEntry` and never calls the production `contextRows.extendleft(...)` code. If the production tagging had a reversal bug, no integration test would catch it.

**Production code IS correct** (traced algebraically): because every tag in `[storedMsg] * n` is identical, `extendleft`'s element-reversal is observationally irrelevant, and the count prepended matches `contextMessages.extendleft(reversed(emittedMessages))` exactly. Both sides prepend N elements to the left, maintaining 1:1 positional correspondence even for multi-emit rows.

**Recommended fix:** Add one integration test where `toModelMessageList` is patched with a `side_effect` that returns `[ctxMsg, extraMsg]` (2+ messages) for specific rows, drive the real walk, and assert persisted `messageIds` come out deduped and in source order. This would also exercise the `messageCount` overcount defect.

**This qualifies the prior memory (id: 1bba05eb) which stated "1:1 alignment verified correct by integration tests" — that verification only covered single-emit, not multi-emit.**

title: Phase 4 implemented: renderCondensedSummary — JSON renderer for condensed summaries
content:
Phase 4 of condensed-context-retrieval: the `renderCondensedSummary(data: CondensingDict) -> str` function in `internal/bot/models/message_metadata.py` (line 165) renders condensed summaries as JSON, resolving the asymmetry where real user messages were JSON but summaries were raw text. (Signature corrected 2026-08-21: accepts ONLY CondensingDict, not Union[CondensingDict, str].)

**Output JSON shape** (keys sorted by jsonDumps):
```json
{"type": "condensed", "coveredMessageIds": [...], "participants": [...], "dateRange": {"from": "<ISO>", "to": "<ISO>"}, "messageCount": N, "summary": "<text>"}
```

**Implementation details (current):**
- `CondensedSummaryKind(StrEnum)` with single member `CONDENSED = "condensed"` — deliberately separate from `MessageType`. Condensed is a render-only construct, structurally disjoint from real user messages.
- Falsy-drop mirrors `formatForLLM` (`if v`) for coveredMessageIds/participants/dateRange/messageCount — empty/0/absent values OMITTED. **`summary` is EXEMPT**: it is hoisted out of the comprehension and assigned unconditionally (`ret["summary"] = data["text"]`, lines 230-234), so `type` and `summary` are always present even when text is `""` (see memory aaf1d4fb).
- `coveredMessageIds`: each MessageId serialized via `.asMessageId()` (int Telegram, str Max).
- `dateRange`: unix floats converted to ISO via `datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(ts, timezone.utc).isoformat()`. Absent → key omitted.
- Legacy `str` rows are NOT handled by the renderer anymore — the CALLER pre-wraps them into `CondensingDict(text=...)` before calling (sole caller: `EnsuredMessage.formatForLLM`, ensured_message.py ~1231).
- Legacy 3-field `CondensingDict` (text/tillMessageId/tillTS only): renders summary-only since new metadata fields are absent.
- Serialised via `utils.jsonDumps(ret, compact=False)`.

Both injection sites emit JSON (Path A: `internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py` ~864-875 uses toModelMessageList + extendleft; Path B in llm_messages.py).

title: FORCE_SQL_TIMEZONE = UTC — all DB-loaded datetimes forced to UTC on read
content:
`internal/database/utils.py` line 23: `FORCE_SQL_TIMEZONE: Optional[datetime.tzinfo] = datetime.timezone.utc`

This is a MODULE-LEVEL CONSTANT that affects the DESERIALIZATION (read) path in `sqlToCustomType`. When a `datetime.datetime` is loaded from the DB and has no tzinfo (naive datetime), it is automatically assigned UTC via `data.replace(tzinfo=FORCE_SQL_TIMEZONE)` (utils.py:122-123). When it has tzinfo, it's converted to UTC (utils.py:157, 178).

**Consequence:** ALL datetimes loaded from the DB via the provider layer are tz-aware UTC. So `self.date.isoformat()` on `EnsuredMessage` (where `self.date` comes from `fromDBChatMessage` → `sqlToCustomType`) produces `+00:00` offset. This means:
- Real user messages' `date` field in `formatForLLM` JSON renders as `+00:00`.
- `renderCondensedSummary`'s `dateRange` (which also forces UTC via `datetime.timezone.utc`) renders as `+00:00`.
- Both are CONSISTENT — no mixed timezone offsets in LLM context.

This resolved the concern raised in `docs/plans/condensed-context-retrieval-plan-v1.md` §11 #4 about timezone inconsistency between real messages and condensed summaries.

Note: this is distinct from the WRITE-path convention `dbUtils.getCurrentTimestamp()` (which also returns UTC). `FORCE_SQL_TIMEZONE` covers the READ path — ensuring loaded datetimes are always tz-aware UTC regardless of how they were stored.

title: renderCondensedSummary FIX: summary hoisted out of falsy-drop (always present)
content:
Code-review fix (2026-07-12) to `renderCondensedSummary` in `internal/bot/models/message_metadata.py`, later simplified (verified 2026-08-21).

**Fix (STILL IN PLACE, lines 219-234):** In the dict-path, `summary` is hoisted out of the falsy-drop comprehension and assigned unconditionally:
```python
ret: Dict[str, Any] = {k: v for k, v in {"type": ..., "coveredMessageIds": ..., "participants": ..., "dateRange": ..., "messageCount": ...}.items() if v}
ret["summary"] = data["text"]   # always present — honors the contract
```
`type` and `summary` are ALWAYS present in the output; all other fields remain subject to the `if v` falsy-drop. Docstring states the minimal shape is `{"type":"condensed","summary":"..."}` (a summary with no summary text is meaningless).

**Simplification since the fix:** the renderer signature is now `renderCondensedSummary(data: CondensingDict) -> str` — the legacy `str` input path was REMOVED entirely. Callers holding a legacy str row (old `randomContext` pre-feature) must pre-wrap it into `CondensingDict(text=...)` themselves; the sole caller (`EnsuredMessage.formatForLLM`, ensured_message.py ~1231) does exactly that.

**Regression test:** `TestRenderCondensedSummary.testEmptyTextSummaryKeyStillPresent` (tests/bot/models/test_message_metadata.py:199) — passes `text=""` and asserts `"summary" in parsed` and `parsed["summary"] == ""`.

**General gotcha:** when using a `{k: v for k, v in d.items() if v}` falsy-drop comprehension, fields that must ALWAYS be present per a design contract must be hoisted out and assigned unconditionally, not included in the comprehension.

title: Testing convention: inspect.getsource() to strengthen wiring/injection-site tests
content:
Convention established (2026-07-12, Phase 4 code review) for strengthening wiring tests where full integration testing is impractical due to heavy mocking requirements (DB/cache/LLM service/chat settings).

**Problem:** A wiring test that only asserts import identity (`module.func is func`) would NOT catch a regression where the injection site reverts to calling the wrong function or accessing the wrong field. For example, `testRendererImportedInBaseModule` asserted `base.renderCondensedSummary is renderCondensedSummary` — but if `getThreadByMessageForLLM` silently reverted to `content=condensedMessage["text"]`, the import-identity check would still pass.

**Solution — source inspection:** Add a source-inspection assertion alongside the import-identity check:
```python
import inspect   # module-top import per project rules

# in the test:
src = inspect.getsource(BaseBotHandler.getThreadByMessageForLLM)
assert "renderCondensedSummary(condensedMessage)" in src
```

This proves the injection site actually CALLS the renderer with the expected argument shape. `inspect.getsource()` returns the source of a specific method, so the string assertion is scoped to that method's body only.

**When to use:** When a wiring test can't do full integration (the target method requires too much mocking), pair the import-identity assertion with a `inspect.getsource()` + string-in-source assertion. Both are cheap and complementary — import identity catches re-exports, source inspection catches call-site regressions.

**Where applied:** `tests/bot/models/test_message_metadata.py` → `TestPathAWiring.testRendererImportedInBaseModule`, verifying `BaseBotHandler.getThreadByMessageForLLM` (base.py:868) calls `renderCondensedSummary(condensedMessage)`.

**Note:** This addresses the testing limitation noted in the earlier Phase 4 memory (724792b7): "used lightweight import-wiring verification instead."

title: Test suite root cause: ~65-68% of wall-clock is real time.sleep/asyncio.sleep blocking
content:
**Historical profiling record (2026-07-12). STATUS: the optimization is COMPLETE — see memory `6f58cec7` for the implemented result (107s → 38s). This entry is kept only as the root-cause baseline. Line refs refreshed 2026-08-20.**

Profiling the full test suite (3202 tests, ~107s wall-clock) revealed that approximately 65-68% of measured execution time was consumed by REAL wall-clock `time.sleep`/`asyncio.sleep` calls, NOT by computation, DB setup, or I/O.

**The dominant slow subsystems (all sleep-bound, all since fixed):**
1. `tests/lib/utils/ttl_dict_test.py` — direct `time.sleep(2)` calls to test TTLDict expiration. FIXED: in-module `fakeClock()` CM (memory `350183c0`).
2. `tests/lib/rate_limiter/test_sliding_window.py` — tests call `applyLimit()` which internally does `await asyncio.sleep(waitTime)` at `lib/rate_limiter/sliding_window.py:208` (re-verified 2026-08-20). FIXED: `installFakeClock` helper (memory `14c7e34c`).
3. `tests/lib/rate_limiter/test_integration.py` — same `applyLimit` blocking pattern. FIXED.
4. `tests/lib/cache/test_integration.py` + `test_dict_cache.py` — direct `asyncio.sleep` for TTL expiration. FIXED: `fakeClockContext` CM + `fakeClock` fixture (memory `836a0605`).
5. `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_chat_search.py::test_cron_self_reset_does_not_fire_on_full_batch` — production `asyncio.sleep(BACKFILL_INTER_MESSAGE_DELAY_SECS=0.1)` at `internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py:513` (re-verified 2026-08-20; was line 450 when first recorded — the constants have since been extracted to `internal/bot/constants.py`, lines 267/275) fires per message in a backfill batch (`BACKFILL_DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE=50`). FIXED: autouse class-scoped `_noOpBackfillPacingSleep` fixture patching it to an `AsyncMock()` no-op (test_chat_search.py:1109).

**Key architectural insight (still valid):** `TTLDict` and `SlidingWindowRateLimiter` read `time.time()` directly and call `time.sleep`/`asyncio.sleep` directly (module-attribute lookup), so patching the module attributes reaches production without touching production code.

title: Pytest markers are mis-targeted — genuinely slow tests carry no marker
content:
The project defines 6 custom pytest markers (`slow`, `performance`, `benchmark`, `memory`, `stress`, `profile`) in pyproject.toml, but NONE are auto-skipped and the marker system delivers ~0% time savings today (verified 2026-07-12).

**Problem:** The markers are on the wrong tests.
- `slow` = 15 tests, ALL in `tests/lib/sandbox/backends/test_docker.py` (11 Docker integration) + `tests/lib/bayes_filter/test_bayes_filter.py` performance class (4) + 1 sandbox bootstrap.
- `performance`, `benchmark`, `memory`, `stress`, `profile` = **0 tests each** (defined but completely unused).

The genuinely slow tests (rate_limiter, ttl_dict, cache — which account for ~65% of suite time) carry **NO marker at all**. Deselecting all markers (`-m "not slow and not performance and not benchmark and not stress and not memory and not profile"`) takes 108.53s vs 107.36s full run — i.e., zero improvement, within noise.

**Implication:** `make test` cannot be selectively trimmed via markers without either (a) re-marking the genuinely slow tests, or (b) fixing the root cause (see the sleep-bound profiling memory). If a fast local lane is desired, the slow tests need to be marked first.

title: Inspecting registered LLM tool schemas in tests — use real LLMService singleton, not a Mock
content:
To test that an LLM tool is registered AND that its emitted JSON schema is correct (e.g. asserting `extra={"items": {"type": "string"}}` is present on an ARRAY param), you CANNOT use the common test-fixture pattern of `h.llmService = Mock()` — replacing llmService with a Mock discards all `registerTool(...)` calls made during `ChatSearchHandler.__init__`, leaving no recorded invocations and no `toolsHandlers` dict to inspect.

Correct technique (used by `TestGetMessagesByIdsLLMTool` registration/schema tests in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_chat_search.py`):

1. Construct the handler WITHOUT replacing `llmService`. The base class `__init__` sets `self.llmService = LLMService.getInstance()`, which runs the real `registerTool(...)` calls and populates `self.llmService.toolsHandlers`.
2. The `resetLlmServiceSingleton` autouse fixture in `tests/conftest.py` resets `LLMService._instance = None` before each test, so the singleton is fresh per test.
3. Inspect via:
   - `handler.llmService.toolsHandlers[ToolName.GET_MESSAGES_BY_IDS]` → the `LLMToolFunction` (or `None` if not registered).
   - `.parameters[N]` → `LLMFunctionParameter` objects, each with `.extra` (the dict carrying schema extras like `{"items": {"type": "string"}}`) and `.toJson()` (full parameter JSON).
4. For functional tests (gating, fetch, formatting), you CAN replace `h.llmService = Mock()` — that's fine because those tests don't need to inspect registration.

Note: `LLMToolFunction` holds `.parameters` (a sequence of `LLMFunctionParameter`). `LLMFunctionParameter` is defined in `lib/ai/models.py` and has `.name`, `.description`, `.type`, `.required`, `.extra`, and `.toJson()`.

For deliberately-bad-input tests that violate the declared param type (e.g. passing `[None, "", 100]` to a `List[str]` param), wrap the value in `cast(Any, ...)` to satisfy pyright — this is the sanctioned `Any` use (matching the tool-handler `**kwargs: Any` pattern).

title: _formatMessageDict works against Mock db when media fields are None
content:
**Test-design gotcha for `_formatMessageDict` in `ChatSearchHandler` (internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py).**

The helper `_formatMessageDict(msg)` internally calls `EnsuredMessage.fromDBChatMessage(msg, self.db)` then `eMessage.formatForLLM(self.db, ...)`. These only touch `self.db` when the row has media content (`media_id` or `media_group_id` is non-None). If both are `None`, the formatter runs entirely from in-row data without any DB calls.

**Practical implication for tests:** you can set `h.db = Mock()` (a plain Mock, not a real Database) and still exercise the REAL `_formatMessageDict` end-to-end — as long as your test rows have `media_id=None` and `media_group_id=None`. The formatter will produce a real dict with keys like `messageId` (int), `text`, `date`, etc. This means happy-path tests for `_llmToolGetThread`, `_llmToolSearchMessages`, and `_llmToolGetMessagesByIds` genuinely exercise the formatter (not a mocked-away invariant) without needing a real Database or complex DB mocking.

This is documented in the docstring of `TestFormatMessageDict` (tests/bot/common/handlers/test_chat_search.py ~line 2691): "the test message dicts have `media_group_id=None` and `media_id=None` so no DB methods are actually awaited."

**To test media-bearing rows:** you must provide real (or carefully mocked) DB responses for the media-fetch methods that `fromDBChatMessage`/`formatForLLM` will call. A plain `Mock()` db will return truthy MagicMock objects which may cause type errors downstream.

Verified during the Phase 5 `get_messages_by_ids` code review (2026-07-12). The `_makeRow` test helper produces rows with `media_id=None`/`media_group_id=None`, and tests like `test_allFound` assert on real formatter output (`[m["messageId"] for m in result["messages"]] == [100, 101, 102]`).

title: pytest cannot inject fixture return values into unittest.TestCase methods
content:
**Empirically verified on pytest 9.1.1 (2026-07-12):** pytest fixture parameter injection does NOT work with `unittest.TestCase` test methods. If a `unittest.TestCase.test_*` method declares a fixture parameter, the parameter is silently IGNORED and the method is called with zero arguments → `TypeError: test_foo() missing N required positional arguments`.

This is a hard, documented pytest limitation, NOT a bug. `unittest.TestCase` subclasses can only consume fixtures via:
- `autouse=True` fixtures (the fixture's setup/teardown runs, but the return value CANNOT be obtained via parameter).
- Standard unittest setUp/tearDown.

**Impact on Gromozeka test work:** Several test files that are candidates for fake-clock speedups are `unittest.TestCase`-based (not plain pytest classes), notably `tests/lib/utils/ttl_dict_test.py`. When adding a controllable fake clock to such files, do NOT use a pytest fixture as a test-method parameter. Instead use one of:
1. A **context manager** (`@contextmanager` + `unittest.mock.patch`) that tests wrap their body in: `with fakeClock(): ...` — the proven, clean approach.
2. An **autouse fixture** that patches globally for the whole module (works but applies to ALL tests, including ones that don't need it).

When the task spec asks for a "pytest fixture" but the target file is `unittest.TestCase`, adapt to a context manager — it is the faithful, per-test-scoped equivalent.

**Verification method used:** Created a temp `unittest.TestCase` test with a fixture param, ran it, observed the TypeError.

title: Fake-clock context manager pattern eliminates time.sleep in TTLDict tests (25.19s → 0.58s)
content:
**Updated 2026-07-14 (lambda form replaced with named nested functions per memory `6b2d035f`).** Implemented in `tests/lib/utils/ttl_dict_test.py` — first concrete application of the test-suite speedup plan. Working pattern to replicate for the remaining slow files.

**How production reads time (determines patch target):** `lib/utils/ttl_dict.py` does `import time` at module top, then calls `time.time()` at 5 sites (`__init__` line 74 for `lastGC`, `gc` line 131, `set` line 179, `setdefault` line 284, `update` line 315). It NEVER calls `time.sleep` internally. Because production holds a module reference (`import time`) and does attribute lookup at call time (`time.time()`), patching `time.time` on the `time` module object reaches production: `mock.patch("time.time", ...)`.

**Current working pattern (named nested functions, context manager — NOT a pytest fixture, see separate memory on unittest.TestCase limitation):**

```python
from contextlib import contextmanager
from typing import Iterator, List
from unittest import mock

@contextmanager
def fakeClock() -> Iterator[List[float]]:
    now: List[float] = [time.time()]  # seed BEFORE patching
    def fakeTime() -> float:
        return now[0]
    def fakeSleep(seconds: float) -> None:
        now[0] += seconds
    with (
        mock.patch("time.time", fakeTime),
        mock.patch("time.sleep", fakeSleep),
    ):
        yield now
```

**Key design decisions that made this work:**
1. Existing `time.sleep(N)` calls in tests are KEPT as-is — under the patch they advance the fake clock instead of blocking. This means assertions stay byte-for-byte identical; only indentation changes (wrapping each sleeping test body in `with fakeClock():`).
2. Seed value is captured with REAL `time.time()` before the `mock.patch` context is entered (line 36 of `ttl_dict_test.py`), so each test gets a fresh, sane epoch. (Note: this is the lone outlier — rate_limiter and cache both seed at 0.0 now; see memory `f2ccce43`.)
3. Only tests that actually call `time.sleep` are wrapped — the thread-safety tests (`test_concurrent...`) stay on real time.

title: Cache test files converted to fake clock (5.81s → 0.96s); DictCache reads time.time() directly
content:
**Implemented 2026-07-12; site count corrected 2026-08-20 (2 sites, not 3).** The cache slice of the test-suite speedup plan, applying the proven fake-clock pattern (see TTLDict memory `350183c0`, `tests/lib/utils/ttl_dict_test.py`).

It does **NOT** use `lib/utils/ttl_dict.py`, `time.monotonic()`, or `time.perf_counter()` (verified). So the patch target is the global `time.time` / `time.sleep` (same module-attribute-lookup pattern as TTLDict). Patching `time.time` on the `time` module object reaches production.

**Shared fixture location:** `tests/lib/cache/conftest.py` — exports BOTH:
- `fakeClockContext()` — a `@contextmanager` yielding a mutable `[now]` list seeded at **0.0**; patches `time.time`/`time.sleep` via `patch("time.time", new=fakeTime)` with named closures (NOT lambdas — see memory `6b2d035f`).
- `fakeClock` — pytest fixture wrapping `fakeClockContext()` (generator fixture, `yield now`).

The fixture is OPT-IN (not autouse — see memory `a76198be`: an autouse fake clock freezes `time.time()` and breaks assertions like `result["timestamp"] != result["timestamp"]`). Verified: no `autouse` anywhere in `tests/lib/cache/conftest.py`.

**Importing the context manager from conftest works:** `tests/lib/cache/test_integration.py` is `unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase`-based (cannot take pytest fixture args). It imports the CM via `from tests.lib.cache.conftest import fakeClockContext` (line 32, verified). This resolves because `tests/`, `tests/lib/`, `tests/lib/cache/` all have `__init__.py` (verified — proper package chain, rootdir in sys.path). `test_dict_cache.py` is plain pytest classes → uses the `fakeClock` fixture as a method parameter (verified: `test_ttl_expiration`, `test_custom_ttl_per_get`, `test_lru_eviction`, `test_cleanup_performance` all take `fakeClock: List[float]`).

title: Autouse fake clock breaks time.time()-based timestamp-difference assertions
content:
**Discovered 2026-07-12 during cache test speedup; test path corrected 2026-07-14.** Making the `fakeClock` fixture `autouse=True` (so every test in `tests/lib/cache/` gets it automatically) is WRONG and breaks tests that are NOT timing tests.

**Concrete failure (verified test path):** `tests/lib/cache/test_integration.py::TestCacheReplacementScenarios::test_cache_behavior_transparency` (line 507, assertion at line 574) asserts:
```python
result3 = await process_data_with_cache("456", null_cache)
result4 = await process_data_with_cache("456", null_cache)
assert result3["timestamp"] != result4["timestamp"]  # timestamps should differ
```
where `process_data_with_cache` sets `"timestamp": time.time()`. With a frozen fake clock, both calls return the SAME `time.time()` → `result3["timestamp"] == result4["timestamp"]` → assertion FAILS. (Earlier version of this memory mis-attributed the assertion to `TestCacheRealWorldPatterns::test_caching_api_responses`; that test does NOT contain this assertion.)

**General lesson:** ANY assertion that compares two `time.time()`-derived values for inequality (timestamps, ordering keys, dedup checks) will break under a fake clock that isn't advanced between the calls. Performance assertions that measure elapsed time (`elapsed = time.time() - start`) also become 0 — which may or may not break the assertion (an `assert elapsed < 5.0` still passes; an `assert elapsed > threshold` fails).

**Rule:** The fake clock MUST be opt-in per test (fixture param or explicit `with fakeClockContext():`), NEVER autouse. Apply it ONLY to tests that verify TTL/expiry. Tests that verify timestamp distinctness, ordering, or real-work-cost must stay on real `time.time()`. This is verified in the current `tests/lib/cache/conftest.py` (the `fakeClock` fixture is NOT autouse) and `tests/lib/utils/ttl_dict_test.py` (only sleeping tests wrap themselves in `with fakeClock():`).

title: asyncio.sleep mocking in handler tests: pattern, resolved files, infinite-loop gotcha
content:
Handler/cron tests that exercise production `asyncio.sleep` pacing delays must patch the sleep to avoid real wall-clock blocking. Two Gromozeka test files were fixed on 2026-07-12 (ses implementing the test-speedup plan).

## Correct pattern (two idioms, both used in-repo)

**Per-test context manager** (original precedent, `test_user_memories_memory_regen.py:676`):
```python
with patch(
    "internal.bot.common.handlers.user_memories.asyncio.sleep",
    new=AsyncMock(),
) as sleepMock:
    await _runRegen(handler)
```

**Class-scoped autouse fixture** (PREFERRED when multiple tests in a class need the no-op — used in the 2026-07-12 fix; idiomatic: 9 existing `autouse=True` fixtures across the test tree):
```python
@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def _noOpBackfillPacingSleep(self) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
    """No-op the backfill inter-message pacing sleep. ..."""
    with patch(
        "internal.bot.common.handlers.chat_search.asyncio.sleep",
        new=AsyncMock(),
    ):
        yield
```
Requires `from typing import Generator` and `from unittest.mock import AsyncMock, patch`.

## RESOLVED (2026-07-12) — chat_search + resender
- `test_chat_search.py::TestDtCronJob` — added `_noOpBackfillPacingSleep` autouse fixture. `test_cron_self_reset_does_not_fire_on_full_batch` went 5.05s → <0.005s. Covers all 3 loop-hitting tests; harmless no-op for the 6 gate-skip tests that never reach the loop.
- `test_resender.py::TestResendCronJobForwarding` — added `_noOpSendPacingSleep` autouse fixture. 8 forward tests went 0.25-0.45s each → <0.005s. No-ops lines 474 (`asyncio.sleep(0.1)`, between forward targets) and 476 (`asyncio.sleep(messageSendDelay)`, exp-backoff between sends, init 0.25).

## CRITICAL GOTCHA: resender line 389 is a timing-CONDITION sleep — NEVER blanket-no-op
`resender.py:389` does `await asyncio.sleep(job.mediaGroupDelaySecs - age)` inside a `while age < job.mediaGroupDelaySecs:` loop where `age = utils.getAgeInSecs(lastUpdated)` is recomputed from real time after each sleep. If you no-op ALL `asyncio.sleep` in resender, `age` never advances (lastUpdated is fixed) and the loop SPINS FOREVER (infinite loop / hang). This is why the resender patch is scoped to `TestResendCronJobForwarding` ONLY (where `mediaGroupId=None` makes the media-group gate always false, so line 389 is unreachable) — never apply it module-wide. The fixture docstring documents this constraint.

General rule: distinguish PACING sleeps (rate-limit avoidance between iterations — safe to no-op) from TIMING-CONDITION sleeps (waiting for a real-time condition to become true inside a loop — no-op'ing causes infinite loops). The rate_limiter/TTL/cache test files use timing-ASSERTION sleeps (verifying expiry) and are owned by a separate workstream (fake-clock injection, not no-op patching).

## AUDIT RESULTS (2026-07-12) — these need NO action
- `weather.py:634`, `yandex_search.py:634` — `asyncio.sleep(0.5)` pacing between multi-message sends. NO test files exist for these handlers at all.
- `spam.py:1143` — `asyncio.sleep(0.5)` in the `spam_stats` command path. The only test (`test_spam_microopt.py`) tests `_getUserInfoFreshIfMessagesLessThan` via `__new__`; never touches the sleep path.
- `summarization.py:204/333` — blocking `time.sleep(0.5)` (not asyncio). No test file exists.
All confirmed absent from `--durations=15` (under 0.06s).

title: Rate limiter fake clock IMPLEMENTED — max-deadline concurrent overlap design
content:
**Implemented 2026-07-12 in `tests/lib/rate_limiter/conftest.py`; snippet corrected 2026-08-20 — the `asyncio.sleep` patch is now SCOPED to the production module, not global (narrowing documented in memories `bcef2a10` / `f2ccce43`).** Eliminated real time-blocking from the 3 rate_limiter test files: combined wall-clock 36.56s → 0.67s (70 tests, count unchanged). This is the asyncio.sleep variant of the fake-clock pattern (cf. TTLDict memory `350183c0`, which only patched time.time/time.sleep).

**Production patch targets (`lib/rate_limiter/sliding_window.py`, line refs re-verified 2026-08-20):** `import time` → `time.time()` at lines 193/211/246 (NOT `time.monotonic()` — verified no monotonic/perf_counter in the file). `import asyncio` → `await asyncio.sleep(waitTime)` at line 208 (attribute access on the asyncio module object, NOT `from asyncio import sleep`). `manager.py` reads no clock — delegates to limiter.

**The conftest helper (NOT a pytest fixture, NOT a context manager) — current form (verified against source):**
```python
def installFakeClock(testCase: unittest.TestCase) -> List[float]:
    realAsyncSleep = asyncio.sleep
    now: List[float] = [0.0]
    def fakeTime() -> float: return now[0]
    def fakeTimeSleep(seconds: float) -> None: now[0] += seconds
    async def fakeAsyncSleep(seconds: float) -> None:
        deadline = now[0] + seconds
        await realAsyncSleep(0)          # keep cooperative scheduling alive under gather
        now[0] = max(now[0], deadline)   # concurrent sleeps overlap, not stack
    patchers = (
        patch("time.time", fakeTime),
        patch("time.sleep", fakeTimeSleep),
        patch("lib.rate_limiter.sliding_window.asyncio.sleep", fakeAsyncSleep),  # SCOPED, not "asyncio.sleep"
    )
    for patcher in patchers:
        patcher.start()
        testCase.addCleanup(patcher.stop)
    return now
```
NOTE: the third patcher targets `lib.rate_limiter.sliding_window.asyncio.sleep`. Since production uses `import asyncio` + attribute access, this is mechanically identical to a global patch for PRODUCTION call sites — the narrowing only affects test-body `await asyncio.sleep` calls (they become real sleeps and do NOT advance `now[0]`). Tests advance the clock via `self.clockNow[0] += N`, never via test-body asyncio.sleep.

Called as `self.clockNow = installFakeClock(self)` in the asyncSetUp of 4 classes (file:line re-verified 2026-08-20): `TestSlidingWindowRateLimiter` (`tests/lib/rate_limiter/test_sliding_window.py:115`), `TestRateLimiterIntegration` and `TestRateLimiterRealWorldScenarios` (`test_integration.py:51` and `:602`), `TestRateLimiterManager` (`test_manager.py:188`).

**3 KEY DESIGN DECISIONS (differ from TTLDict pattern — all load-bearing, all documented in the conftest docstrings):**
1. **Max-deadline update** (`now[0] = max(now[0], deadline)`): concurrent `asyncio.sleep` calls overlap like real wall-clock instead of stacking additively. Known limitation for mixed concurrent+sequential patterns — see memory `9387935a` (no current test hits it).
2. **Seed at 0.0** (not real epoch): keeps window comparisons like `currentTime - reqTime < windowSeconds` free of float-precision drift at exact window boundaries.
3. **`await realAsyncSleep(0)` yield**: keeps cooperative scheduling healthy under `asyncio.gather` — all gathered coroutines compute their deadline against the pre-update clock before any advances it.

title: asyncio.get_event_loop().time() returns monotonic clock — NOT patched by time.time
content:
**Confirmed 2026-07-14 (file path corrected).** `asyncio.get_event_loop().time()` returns `time.monotonic()` (via the event loop's `time()` method), NOT `time.time()`. When using a fake-clock pattern that patches `time.time`, any elapsed measurement via `loop.time()` / `asyncio.get_event_loop().time()` will read the REAL monotonic clock and see ~0 elapsed (if production sleeps are patched to be instant), causing `assertGreaterEqual(elapsed, N)` assertions to FAIL.

**Current call site (verified):** `tests/lib/yandex_search/test_integration.py` lines 371 and 377 — `startTime = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()` and `endTime = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()`. (Earlier version of this memory mis-attributed the call site to `tests/lib/rate_limiter/test_manager.py::testRealLimitersIntegration`; that file does NOT call `get_event_loop().time()` — it measures elapsed with `time.time()` and uses `installFakeClock`.)

**Symptom:** production `asyncio.sleep` is patched (instant), but the test measures elapsed with `asyncio.get_event_loop().time()` — elapsed ≈ 0 → assertion fails.

**Fix (test-side):** change the elapsed measurement from `asyncio.get_event_loop().time()` to `time.time()` so the patched fake clock governs it. Do NOT patch `time.monotonic` — that would break the event loop's internal scheduling (`call_later` etc. use the loop's monotonic clock via the selector).

**General rule for fake-clock test refactors:** audit ALL time-reading mechanisms in the test (and production it exercises): `time.time()`, `time.monotonic()`, `time.perf_counter()`, `asyncio.get_event_loop().time()`, `datetime.now()`. Each needs its own patch target. Patching `time.time` alone is insufficient if any other clock is read.

title: testCleanupAfterWaiting flakiness RESOLVED by fake clock (was timing-dependent)
content:
`tests/lib/rate_limiter/test_sliding_window.py::TestSlidingWindowRateLimiter::testCleanupAfterWaiting` was a known PRE-EXISTING flaky test (timing-dependent, relied on real wall-clock expiry, could intermittently fail).

**RESOLVED 2026-07-12:** The fake clock (`installFakeClock` in `tests/lib/rate_limiter/conftest.py`, installed class-wide in `asyncSetUp`) now governs this test. Time advances deterministically via patched `asyncio.sleep`/`time.time`, so the window-expiry behavior is no longer subject to real-clock jitter. The test is now deterministic and passes reliably.

If it fails in the future, treat it as a real regression (investigate), NOT as the old known-flaky noise. The flakiness root cause (real wall-clock timing dependency) has been eliminated.

title: Fake-clock helper: prefer named nested functions over __setitem__ lambda (readability + type hints)
content:
**Convention — confirmed applied across all three fake-clock sites (verified 2026-07-14).** The original review flagged `tests/lib/utils/ttl_dict_test.py` for using a `lambda seconds: now.__setitem__(0, now[0] + seconds)` to mutate the clock cell inside `mock.patch("time.sleep", ...)`. Lambdas (a) are obscure at a glance because of the `__setitem__` dunder and (b) cannot carry parameter type annotations, which sits awkwardly with the AGENTS.md hard rule "Type hints required on all function/method params and returns."

**All three fake-clock helpers now use named nested functions** (the recommended form):
- `tests/lib/utils/ttl_dict_test.py::fakeClock()` — `def fakeTime() -> float:` / `def fakeSleep(seconds: float) -> None:`
- `tests/lib/cache/conftest.py::fakeClockContext()` — `def fakeTime() -> float:` / `def fakeSleep(seconds: float) -> None:`
- `tests/lib/rate_limiter/conftest.py::installFakeClock(...)` — `def fakeTime() -> float:` / `def fakeTimeSleep(seconds: float) -> None:` / `async def fakeAsyncSleep(seconds: float) -> None:`

**Template for new fake-clock sites:**
```python
now: List[float] = [0.0]

def fakeTime() -> float:
    return now[0]

def fakeSleep(seconds: float) -> None:
    now[0] += seconds
```
Do NOT copy the historical `__setitem__` lambda form when adding a new fake-clock site — use named nested functions.

title: Docstring Yields: acceptable for @contextmanager generators despite AGENTS.md "Returns:" rule
content:
**Confirmed during code review 2026-07-12.**

AGENTS.md's hard rule says: "Docstrings required on every module/class/method/function/field, with `Args:` and `Returns:` describing all params and return type."

For a `@contextmanager`-decorated generator function (or any generator), using the `Yields:` Google-style section instead of `Returns:` is **defensible and arguably more correct** — it matches the `Iterator[...]` return annotation and documents the generator's yield contract. Reviewer deemed it acceptable; no change required.

**Practical guidance for future agents:**
- If a function is a generator / decorated with `@contextmanager`, `Yields:` is the appropriate section name. Do NOT flag its absence of `Returns:` as a blocker.
- `Args:` can be omitted when the function takes no parameters (defensible).
- This is consistent with the existing memory about `__aenter__`/`__aexit__` requiring explicit `Returns:` — that applies to standard protocol methods, not to `@contextmanager` generators.
- The literal `Returns:` rule in AGENTS.md is intended for ordinary functions/methods that return a value; `Yields:` is the generator equivalent.

title: Bugfix: get_messages_by_ids — format-failed rows were mislabeled as notFound
content:
**Bug (fixed 2026-07-12, Gate-2 review).** In `ChatSearchHandler._llmToolGetMessagesByIds` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py`, the per-row loop over `asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` results), a row that EXISTS in the DB but for which `_formatMessageDict` raises was wrongly reported in the tool's `notFound` list.

**Root cause:** The loop checked `isinstance(ret, Exception)` and `continue`d BEFORE adding that row's `message_id` to `foundStrs`. Since `notFound = requestedIds − foundStrs`, a DB-resolved-but-unformattable row was computed as missing and appended to `notFound`.

**Why it matters:** The tool contract says `notFound` = "IDs that did not resolve." A format failure is NOT a resolution failure. Reporting a real message as missing misleads the LLM (it concludes the message doesn't exist and may abandon a retrieval).

**Fix / invariant:** A DB-resolved row's id is ALWAYS recorded in `foundStrs` regardless of whether formatting succeeded. The loop now computes `idStr` and adds it to `foundStrs` BEFORE the `isinstance(ret, Exception)` check. On format failure it logs `logger.warning("...failed to format row %s: %s", idStr, ret)` (now including the id) and `continue`s (the unformattable row is dropped from `messages` but never appears in `notFound`).

**Regression test:** `TestGetMessagesByIdsLLMTool::test_formatFailure_notReportedAsNotFound` in `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_chat_search.py` — patches `_formatMessageDict` to raise for one row of a 3-row batch, asserts that id stays out of `notFound`, the row is dropped from `messages` (count 2), and `done` is True. Verified it FAILS before the fix and PASSES after.

**General lesson:** Any LLM tool that distinguishes "resolved" vs "not resolved" must record resolution success BEFORE checking downstream-processing (formatting) failures. Keep the two failure modes in separate buckets.

title: Gotcha: message IDs appear as ints in summaries but LLM tool schema wants strings
content:
Gotcha (condensed-context-retrieval feature, re-verified 2026-08-20). In condensed summaries, `coveredMessageIds` serialize as JSON via `mid.asMessageId()` (renderCondensedSummary, message_metadata.py:209) — INT form for Telegram, matching real Telegram messages. The `get_messages_by_ids` tool wants string IDs, but the emitted schema is a plain ARRAY with NO item-type enforcement (`extra={"items": {"type": "string"}}` is commented out at chat_search.py:363). So the LLM sees message IDs as numbers in a summary while the parameter description asks for strings ('List of message ID strings to retrieve (e.g. ["100", "101"])' — chat_search.py:360). This friction applies to ANY LLM tool that accepts message IDs alongside condensed summaries.

NOTE: the mitigation recorded on 2026-07-12 (tool description ending with 'Pass the IDs as strings, even if they appear as numbers in a summary.') has been REMOVED — the current tool description (chat_search.py:350-356) ends with 'Messages are scoped to the current chat.' and carries no int/str clarification. The only surviving hint is the parameter-description example.

Runtime is safe: `_llmToolGetMessagesByIds` does `str(mid).strip()` + `MessageId(midStr)` coercion on all incoming ids (chat_search.py:985-999), and `foundStrs` is str-normalized (`.asStr()`) so int Telegram ids and str Max ids both match. The friction is purely LLM-comprehension, not a crash.

When adding a new message-id-accepting LLM tool: declare the param as `string` type (or keep the array items override actually enabled), str-coerce on intake, and consider a clarifying description clause about the int/str appearance mismatch.

title: int(0.1)=0 makes cache TTL tests pass for the wrong reason (test_cleanup_performance, test_custom_ttl_per_get)
content:
**Found 2026-07-12 during code review of the cache fake-clock conversion.** Pre-existing latent bug, NOT introduced by the fake-clock change (confirmed present in `HEAD~1` "Dedoodie the code"). Still unfixed.

**Root cause:** `DictCache.defaultTtl` and the per-`get` `ttl` param are typed `int` in `lib/cache/dict_cache.py` (~L63). Several cache tests pass fractional values through `int(...)`:
- `tests/lib/cache/test_dict_cache.py:~674` (`test_cleanup_performance`): `defaultTtl=int(0.1)` → `0`
- `tests/lib/cache/test_dict_cache.py:~248` (`test_custom_ttl_per_get`): `ttl=int(0.1)` → `0`

**Effect:** Per `DictCache._isExpired` (`dict_cache.py:~103-104`), `ttl == 0` means "always expired" (returns True). So:
- `test_cleanup_performance`: it loops `set` 100 keys intending to fill the cache then clean up "many expired entries". But with `defaultTtl=0`, each `set` calls `_cleanupExpired()` BEFORE adding, which removes ALL prior entries (they're all "expired" at ttl=0). The cache therefore NEVER holds 100 entries — it evicts one-by-one during each `set`. The final `assert stats["entries"] == 0` passes, but for the wrong reason (entries were never accumulated, not "cleaned up in bulk"). The "cleanup performance with many expired entries" intent is NOT exercised.
- `test_custom_ttl_per_get`: the custom-TTL branch (`ttl=int(0.1)`=0) tests "ttl=0 → immediate expiration", NOT "0.2s elapsed > 0.1s TTL" as the comments claim. The `fakeClock[0] += 0.2` advance is only meaningful for the default-TTL(10s) assertion in the same test, not for the custom-TTL assertion. Comments ("over custom 0.1s") are misleading.

**Faithful preservation:** The fake-clock conversion correctly preserved this pre-existing behavior — it did NOT introduce or worsen it. This is why the review cleared the conversion but flagged this as a follow-up.

**Suggested fix (separate pass, touches production typing):** Widen `DictCache.defaultTtl` / `ttl` from `int` to `float` (production `dict_cache.py`), then use a real fractional TTL in these tests (e.g. `defaultTtl=0.1` and advance clock past it, or `defaultTtl=1` + advance by 2). This is a production-side decision (architect/software-developer), not a test-only tweak — `_isExpired` math and the `ttl==0` sentinel must be re-checked.

**Lesson:** `int(fractionalValue)` silently truncates toward zero; combined with a `0` sentinel meaning "always expired", this produces tests that look correct but assert nothing. Audit any test using `int(<fraction>)` against a TTL param.

title: Fake-clock test conversions: 3 gotchas (tautological perf assertions, exact-boundary >=, real-time loops)
content:
**Surfaced 2026-07-12 during a code-review cleanup pass over the fake-clock test conversions.** These are transferable traps that will recur in any future `time.sleep`/`asyncio.sleep` → fake-clock test conversion. All three were fixed in `tests/` only; no production code touched.

## Gotcha A — Timing/performance assertions become TAUTOLOGICAL under a fake clock
When a test asserts a speed benefit (e.g. "cached call is faster": `assert second_time < first_time / 2` in `tests/lib/cache/test_integration.py::test_caching_computed_results_with_ttl`), converting to a fake clock often makes it tautological. The fake clock only advances when production code calls `time.sleep`/`asyncio.sleep`. The "fast" path (cache hit, already-computed result) performs NO sleep/computation, so its measured elapsed is always **0** → `0 < first_time / 2` can never fail. It no longer measures the intended benefit.
**Fix:** DELETE the tautological timing assertion. Rely on correctness assertions (value equality `cached_result == result1`, TTL-expiry-returns-None) to verify caching. Reword any docstring/comment that claims the call "is faster" / "benefits from caching".
**Corollary (lint):** deleting such an assertion leaves the timing scaffolding variables (`start_time`, `first_time`, `second_time`) that ONLY fed it as dead locals → flake8 **F841** (assigned-but-unused) fails `make lint`. Prune them too. (Pyflakes flags unused locals but NOT unused function args — see memory `547d71cd`.)

## Gotcha B — Fake clock yields EXACT boundary values; use `>=` (assertGreaterEqual), not a nudge
A fake clock produces exact boundary values (e.g. concurrent overlap models as exactly 2.0s, NOT 2.0 + scheduling overshoot). A strict lower-bound assertion `assertGreater(total_elapsed, 2.0)` that real wall-clock satisfies via overshoot will **FAIL** at exactly 2.0.
**Fix:** use the non-strict form `assertGreaterEqual(total_elapsed, 2.0)`. This matches existing sibling assertions in the same suite which already use the non-strict form (`>= 1.0`, `>= 0.8`, `>= 1.5`). Do NOT change the assertion VALUE (2.0).
**This SUPERSEDES the earlier "nudge" approach.** The rate-limiter fake-clock implementation (memory `14c7e34c`) originally bridged the [1.99, 2.0] band with `self.clockNow[0] += 0.01` immediately before the elapsed measurement, in `testConcurrentUsageAcrossMultipleQueues` and `testHighConcurrencyScenario` (`tests/lib/rate_limiter/test_integration.py`). That nudge introduced a ~0.5% boundary blind spot and a mutation-after-measurement smell. The nudge line (+ its rationale comment) was **REMOVED** and both assertions switched to `assertGreaterEqual` in this cleanup. Future fake-clock conversions: prefer `>=`, never re-introduce a clock-mutation nudge.

## Gotcha C — No-op'ing asyncio.sleep breaks production loops that self-advance via real time
When a test class no-ops `asyncio.sleep` for speed, any production code path reachable from that class that advances its OWN loop-control variable via real `asyncio.sleep`/`time.time` polling will **INFINITE-LOOP** under the no-op.
**Concrete case:** `tests/bot/common/handlers/test_resender.py::TestResendCronJobForwarding` has an autouse `_noOpSendPacingSleep` fixture that no-ops asyncio.sleep for the whole class. Safe today because all test messages have `mediaGroupId=None`, so the production media-group wait loop is unreachable. But the production loop at `internal/bot/common/handlers/resender.py:383-389` — `while age < job.mediaGroupDelaySecs: ... await asyncio.sleep(job.mediaGroupDelaySecs - age)` where `age` advances via real time — WOULD infinite-loop if a media-group forwarding test were added to THIS class.
**Fix applied:** added a class-level comment above `class TestResendCronJobForwarding:` stating media-group forwarding tests MUST go in a separate class.
**General rule:** before no-op'ing `asyncio.sleep` in a test class, audit all production paths reachable from that class for loops whose progress/termination depends on real sleep or real clock advancing. If any exist, those tests need a separate class whose fake sleep actually advances the progress variable (or no fake at all).

title: getChatMessagesByMessageIds does NOT dedup input ids — IN clause collapses at DB level
content:
GOTCHA (verified 2026-07-14): `ChatMessagesRepository.getChatMessagesByMessageIds(chatId, messageIds, *, dataSource=None)` does NOT dedup the input id list. The docstring states: "Dedup of input ids is the caller's responsibility (this method does not dedup; duplicate ids produce one row)."

Because the query uses `IN (:id0, :id1, ...)` expansion (now auto-chunked into batches of `MAX_SQL_VARIABLES`), the DB naturally returns one row per unique id even if a duplicate appears in the IN list. So passing `[id1, id1, id2]` returns `[row1, row2]` (2 rows), NOT `[row1, row1, row2]` (3 rows). The repo method does no post-processing to dedup — it only re-sorts the unioned chunks by date ascending.

CORRECTION to the prior version of this memory: the `get_messages_by_ids` LLM tool handler (the primary caller, `_llmToolGetMessagesByIds` in `internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py` ~line 827) DOES dedup before calling. Its input-normalisation loop (~lines 884-897) builds a `seen: set[str]`, skips blanks/None and already-seen ids (preserving first-seen order), coerces to str, and clamps to `MAX_GET_MESSAGES_BATCH` (=32, `internal/bot/constants.py`). Its docstring explicitly states "Items are de-duplicated". So the condensed-context-retrieval plan's "tool handler dedups before calling" requirement WAS implemented — the prior claim that it was not implemented is outdated/wrong.

End-to-end batch behavior today: the handler dedups+clamps, then the repo's IN clause collapses any remaining duplicates at the DB level as a defense-in-depth safety net.

File: `internal/database/repositories/chat_messages.py` (method now at line 329). Test coverage: `TestGetChatMessagesByMessageIds.test_duplicateInputIds` in `tests/database/repositories/test_chat_messages.py` (line 327).

title: fakeAsyncSleep max-deadline limitation: incorrect for mixed concurrent+sequential sleep patterns
content:
**New analysis from Gate 2 whole-work code review (2026-07-12).** Extends the max-deadline design documentation in memories `14c7e34c` and `6dc98dc2`, which prove correctness for same-instant concurrent sleeps.

**The max-deadline `fakeAsyncSleep` in `tests/lib/rate_limiter/conftest.py` is CORRECT for:**
- Same-instant concurrent sleeps (the `realAsyncSleep(0)` yield lets all gathered coroutines compute their deadline against the pre-update clock before any advances it — verified by trace). Two tasks both sleeping 1s at fake-time 0 → both compute deadline=1, final clock=1. ✓
- Sequential sleeps within one coroutine (deadline = now + seconds, each advances the clock additively). Two sleeps of 1s → clock goes 1 then 2. ✓

**BUT INCORRECT for mixed patterns:**
One coroutine sleeping 3s concurrently with another doing two sequential 1s sleeps:
- Task1: deadline=0+3=3, yields, resumes → now=max(0,3)=3.
- Task2: first sleep deadline=0+1=1, yields, resumes → now=max(3,1)=3. Second sleep deadline=3+1=4, yields, resumes → now=max(3,4)=4.
- Fake clock total: **4.0s**. Real wall-clock would be **3.0s** (task2's sleeps overlap with task1's, completing by t=2; gather waits for task1 at t=3).

**Root cause:** When Task1 advances the clock to 3 before Task2 resumes, Task2's second sleep starts from 3 instead of from 1 (its real wall-clock wake time). The `realAsyncSleep(0)` yield preserves overlap only within a single batch of sleeps started at the same fake-time instant; a sleep started AFTER another coroutine has already advanced the clock computes its deadline relative to the already-advanced time.

**Practical impact:** NONE for current tests — all rate_limiter test patterns are either pure-concurrent (all same duration) or pure-sequential. The fake clock gives correct results for these. The limitation only surfaces for the mixed pattern, which no current test exercises.

**Guidance for future test authors:** if you add a rate_limiter test with a mixed concurrent+sequential sleep pattern, do NOT trust the `installFakeClock` elapsed measurement. Either restructure the test to avoid the pattern, or use `time.perf_counter()` for the wall-clock assertion and only use the fake clock for expiry-logic control.

title: Fake-clock pattern divergence across 4 test suites is JUSTIFIED — consolidation recommendation
content:
**Updated 2026-07-14.** Architectural assessment of the fake-clock test-speedup conversion across the slow test suites. Memory `f2ccce43` supersedes the prior cache-seed-value claim; this entry keeps the architectural justification.

**Current state (4 shapes, each justified by what the production code under test does):**
1. **ttl_dict** (`tests/lib/utils/ttl_dict_test.py`): in-module `fakeClock()` context manager. Patches `time.time`/`time.sleep` only. Seeds at **real epoch** (`[time.time()]`, line 36) — the lone outlier on seed value. **Justified:** `lib/utils/ttl_dict.py` reads `time.time()` only — no `asyncio.sleep` in production.
2. **rate_limiter** (`tests/lib/rate_limiter/conftest.py`, helper `installFakeClock`): patches `time.time`/`time.sleep` GLOBALLY plus `asyncio.sleep` scoped to `lib.rate_limiter.sliding_window` (the narrow blast radius narrows test-body sleeps, not production — see memory `bcef2a10`). Max-deadline overlap semantics. Seeds at **0.0**. **Justified:** `lib/rate_limiter/sliding_window.py` blocks via `await asyncio.sleep(waitTime)` at line 208 AND reads `time.time()` at lines 193/211/246 — needs all three patched.
3. **cache** (`tests/lib/cache/conftest.py`, CM `fakeClockContext` + pytest fixture `fakeClock`): patches `time.time`/`time.sleep` only. Seeds at **0.0** (changed from real epoch for parity with rate_limiter — readable TTL deltas). **Justified:** `lib/cache/dict_cache.py` reads `time.time()` at lines 107 and 210 — no `asyncio.sleep` in production.
4. **handlers** (`tests/bot/common/handlers/test_chat_search.py`, `test_resender.py`): class-scoped autouse fixtures no-op'ing `asyncio.sleep` to `AsyncMock()`. **Justified:** production paces via `asyncio.sleep` (inter-message delays), NOT timing assertions — sleeps are pacing, not behavior under test.

**Seed-value divergence is now PARTIALLY collapsed:** cache aligned to 0.0 alongside rate_limiter; only ttl_dict retains real-epoch seeding (harmless — its expiry comparisons aren't boundary-sensitive). The patch-surface divergence (time-only vs time+asyncio.sleep) REMAINS and is correct: it matches what each production module actually does.

**Still valid rule:** Match the patch surface to what the production code actually does. When the production class blocks via `asyncio.sleep`, patch it. When it only reads `time.time()`, patch just `time.time`/`time.sleep`. Don't consolidate the helpers into one universal fixture that patches everything — over-patching breaks test-body `await asyncio.sleep(N)` calls (they become real sleeps that block AND don't advance `now[0]`).

title: test_cleanup_performance tautological assertion — FIXED with perf_counter
content:
**Fixed 2026-07-12** (was previously tracked as unfixed, status: unfixed, from the Gate 2 code review).

**Location:** `tests/lib/cache/test_dict_cache.py` — `TestDictCachePerformance::test_cleanup_performance` (NOT `TestDictCacheTTL` as previously recorded; the class is `TestDictCachePerformance`). Takes the `fakeClock` fixture.

**Original problem:** The test measured cleanup speed with before/after `time.time()` reads around `cache.getStats()` (which triggers cleanup). The `fakeClock` fixture patches `time.time`, and between the two reads only synchronous cleanup runs (no fake-clock advance), so `cleanup_time` was ALWAYS `0.0` → `assert cleanup_time < 1.0` could never fail. The performance coverage was silently dead.

**Fix applied:** Switched the two timing reads from `time.time()` to `time.perf_counter()`. `perf_counter` is NOT patched by the fakeClock fixture (which only patches `time.time`/`time.sleep`), so it returns real wall-clock elapsed time even under the fake clock. The fake-clock advancement (`fakeClock[0] += 0.2`) that drives expiry logic was left intact — only the *measurement* switched clocks.

**Verification:** Confirmed falsifiability with a script under the patched clock — `time.time()` delta = `0.0` (frozen), `time.perf_counter()` delta = real positive value (~0.0002s). Test passes; whole `tests/lib/cache/` subdir green (53 passed); `make format lint` clean.

**Out of scope (left as-is, still unfixed):** The `defaultTtl=int(0.1)` value in this test equals `0` (int truncation) — a separate pre-existing issue tracked in memory `855ac71f`.

**Transferable rule (also in memory `942fff71` Gotcha A):** When a fake-clock test needs to measure REAL performance while controlling fake time for expiry logic, use `time.perf_counter()` for the perf measurement. `time.time()`/`time.sleep` are patched; `perf_counter` is not. They are independent clocks.

title: LLM tool convention: every chat-data tool must have ALLOW_TOOLS_COMMANDS gate (Gate 2)
content:
SUPERSEDES the old claim that chat-data LLM tools check ALLOW_TOOLS_COMMANDS as "Gate 2". Verified 2026-08-20: NO LLM tool in `internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py` checks `ALLOW_TOOLS_COMMANDS` anymore. That setting now gates only slash commands of `CommandCategory.TOOLS` at the handler-manager level (`internal/bot/common/handlers/manager.py:1014`, `canProcess = chatSettings[ChatSettingsKey.ALLOW_TOOLS_COMMANDS].toBool() or isBotOwner`).

Current LLM-tool gating architecture (three layers):

1. **Registration gate** (handler `__init__`): a tool registers only when its feature config flag is on (e.g. `[search-history].enabled` for ChatSearchHandler tools, `[user-memory]` for memory tools, `[sandbox].enabled` for sandbox tools).

2. **Chat-time gate — the single per-chat LLM-tool toggle is `USE_TOOLS`**, applied in `LLMMessageHandler._sendLLMChatMessage` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/llm_messages.py` ~line 282): when true, it builds a useTools dict `{TOOLS_DEFAULT_DICT_KEY: True, ToolName.DELETE_MEMORY: False}` and conditionally disables sandbox tools (`ALLOW_SANDBOX=false`) and memory tools (`MEMORY_ENABLED=false`). This is the D3 rule documented in `.agents/skills/add-llm-tool/SKILL.md` Site 4. Do NOT widen the `if useTools:` guard — pinned by `TestD3DeleteMemoryGating`.

3. **In-handler defensive gates** (per tool, current state):
   - `_llmToolSearchMessages` (chat_search.py:578): Gate 1 chat context → Gate 2 settings load (try/except, never-raise on settings failure) + `EMBEDDINGS_ENABLED` check applied to SEMANTIC queries only (substring/filter-only mode deliberately skips it) → Gate 2b rate-limit → input clamps (limit 1..100).
   - `_llmToolListUsers` (chat_search.py:772): Gate 1 chat context only — no settings gate.
   - `_llmToolGetThread` (chat_search.py:859): Gate 1 chat context + Gate 2 message-ID validation — no settings gate.
   - `_llmToolGetMessagesByIds` (chat_search.py:925): docstring explicitly says the chat-time gate is USE_TOOLS and it is NOT gated on `ALLOW_TOOLS_COMMANDS` or `EMBEDDINGS_ENABLED` (pure DB lookup).

All four tool bodies keep the never-raise contract: top-level `try/except Exception`, failures folded into `{"done": False, "error": ...}`. Extra defensive gates (EMBEDDINGS_ENABLED, rate-limit) belong only where the tool actually consumes the gated resource (embeddings API).

title: condenseContext summary content is renderCondensedSummary JSON — test with .source identity, not .content
content:
In the simplified Condensed-Context Retrieval design, `condenseContext` (`internal/services/llm/service.py`) builds each returned summary ModelMessage as:

```python
newBody.append(ModelMessage(role="user", content=renderCondensedSummary(resDict), source=resDict))
coverage[len(newBody) - 1] = resDict
```

Two critical facts for test authors:
1. The summary message's `.content` is `renderCondensedSummary(resDict)` — a JSON string, NOT the raw summary text. Asserting `result[1].content == "summary-0"` will FAIL. The raw summary text lives in `resDict["text"]` / `coverage[i]["text"]`.
2. The SAME `resDict` object is assigned to both `ModelMessage.source` and the coverage dict entry. Therefore `result[headLen + coverageKey].source is coverage[coverageKey]` (identity check) is the strongest alignment guarantee.

This was discovered during the test rewrite pass (2026-07-13): the first pass of `TestCondenseContextCoverage` cross-checked `result[i].content == "summary-X"` and all 4 such tests failed. Fixed by replacing content assertions with `result[i].source is coverage[key]`.

For the head length: `retHead` includes the system message (if present) + any `keepFirstN` messages. With a system message and `keepFirstN=0` (bumped to 1 internally), `result[1]` is the first summary, `result[2]` is the second, etc. `result[-1]` is the tail (`keepLastN` messages).

title: mergeCondensingDicts participants ordering is list(set) — non-deterministic, compare as set in tests
content:
`mergeCondensingDicts` in `internal/bot/models/message_metadata.py` builds the merged `participants` field as `list(participants)` where `participants` is a `MutableSet[str]` (built via `.update()` from each input dict's participants). This means:

- The output `participants` list is in **hash-based set iteration order**, NOT sorted and NOT insertion order.
- The order is deterministic within a single Python process for a given set of strings, but is NOT predictable from the input order.

**Testing implication**: When asserting on `participants` in a merged CondensingDict (e.g., `randomContext["participants"]`), always compare as a `set()`, never as a list:

```python
# CORRECT — order-independent
assert set(randomContext["participants"]) == {"user0", "user1", "user2"}
# or
assert sorted(randomContext["participants"]) == ["user0", "user1", "user2"]

# WRONG — will fail intermittently
assert randomContext["participants"] == ["user0", "user1", "user2"]
```

The same applies to `generateCondencingDict` which also uses `list(participants)` from a set.

Note: `messageIds` IS order-preserving (it's a list built via `.append()` / `.extend()`), so list equality is safe for `messageIds`.

title: messageIds safe by construction in simplified design — tool messages have source=None, not EnsuredMessage
content:
Key analysis of the simplified Condensed-Context Retrieval design (source-tagging verified 2026-08-20).

In the NEW simplified design, `generateCondencingDict` (internal/services/llm/service.py:69-144) reads `message.source` per ModelMessage. The multi-emit pattern from `toModelMessageList` produces:
- **randomContext msg** → `source = CondensingDict` dict (ensured_message.py:1257)
- **N tool-history msgs** → `source = None` (emitted via `ModelMessage.fromDict(toolsMessage)` at ensured_message.py:1262; `fromDict` never passes `source`, and `ModelMessage.__init__` defaults `source=None` — lib/ai/models.py:576)
- **main msg** → `source = self` (the EnsuredMessage, ensured_message.py:1336)

So when `generateCondensingDict` walks these: tool messages (source=None) increment `messageCount` but do NOT append to `messageIdList`; only the main message (source=EnsuredMessage) appends its `messageId`. **`messageIds` has NO duplicates in practice — safe by construction, not by explicit dedup.** Duplicates would require two ModelMessages with the same EnsuredMessage as `.source`, which `toModelMessageList` never produces.

UPDATE (supersedes the old "messageCount IS still overcounted" framing): the None-source increment is now the DOCUMENTED, INTENTIONAL semantics — `CondensingDict.messageCount` is defined as "Number of processed ModelMessage positions this summary covers (includes auxiliary tool-history emissions, not just original user/assistant messages)" (message_metadata.py:134-137) and `generateCondencingDict`'s docstring (service.py:80-83) explicitly says the None-source branch "still increment[s] messageCount". The 2026-07-14 user-memory-v2 review redefined the semantics (issue I9) instead of changing the counter — it is no longer a defect.

Caveat (still valid): during the re-condense cascade (Path A, base.py:893-927), if two CondensingDict-source summaries with overlapping messageIds are in the same batch, the dict branch (`messageIdList.extend(message.source["messageIds"])`) can carry duplicates into the re-condensed dict — and `mergeCondensingDicts` does not dedup either.

title: generateCondencingDict creates service→bot coupling via isinstance(source, EnsuredMessage) — acceptable tradeoff
content:
**Architectural observation from 2026-07-13 code review (REC, not urgent).**

The simplified `generateCondencingDict` (internal/services/llm/service.py:67-139) inspects `EnsuredMessage` attributes (`.messageId`, `.sender.username`, `.date.timestamp()`) via `isinstance(message.source, EnsuredMessage)` at :109. This moves coverage-extraction logic from the bot layer (old `buildCondensingFields` reading `ChatMessageDict` keys) to the service layer.

The `EnsuredMessage` import at service.py:18 pre-existed (used by `ExtraDataDict` in `internal/services/llm/models.py`), so this isn't a NEW dependency. But the new `isinstance` check tightens the coupling: the service layer now needs to understand bot-model internals (messageId, sender.username, date.timestamp()).

**Tradeoff:** The simplification is SIMPLER (no parallel index lists, no caller-side coverage computation, no `[row] * n` tagging) but creates a service→bot coupling for source inspection. This is an acceptable tradeoff for the complexity reduction. If it becomes a pain point, the extraction logic could be moved back to a bot-layer helper that `condenseContext` calls via a callback.

**Layering note:** `internal/services/llm/` importing from `internal/bot/models/` is pre-existing (not introduced by the simplification). The new usage is within an existing dependency relationship.

title: Condensed-Context Retrieval SIMPLIFIED design — COMPLETE (code final, docs synced)
content:
As of 2026-07-13, the user manually simplified the Condensed-Context Retrieval feature, replacing the original caller-side index-range machinery with a single-layer `ModelMessage.source`-based design. The code is FINAL and GREEN (3179 tests). All project docs have been synced to match. THIS SUPERSEDES older Phase 3a/3b memories about `returnCoverage`, `indexToEntry`/`indexToEntry2`, and caller-side `buildCondensingFields` slicing.

## DELETED symbols (gone from codebase entirely — NOT orphaned)
`_condensingDictFromCoverage`, `buildRandomContextDict`, `buildCondensingFields`, `CondenseBatchCoverage` TypedDict, `CondensingMetadataDict` TypedDict, `indexToEntry`/`indexToEntry2` parallel-list machinery, the `returnCoverage` kwarg, and `@overload` stubs on `condenseContext`.

## `condenseContext` contract (`internal/services/llm/service.py`)
- Signature: `condenseContext(messages, model, *, keepFirstN=0, keepLastN=1, condensingModel=None, condensingPrompt=None, condensingSystemPrompt=None, maxTokens=None, force=False)` — NO `returnCoverage` kwarg.
- ALWAYS returns `Tuple[Sequence[ModelMessage], Dict[int, CondensingDict]]`. First = condensed message list (head + summaries + tail). Second = `Dict[int, CondensingDict]` keyed by body-index → fully-populated CondensingDicts. When no condensing occurs, second element is `{}`.
- Path C (`generateTextViaLLM`) unpacks `_messages, _ = await self.condenseContext(...)` — byte-identical behavior, ignores coverage.

## `generateCondencingDict(text, messages) -> CondensingDict` (service.py, module-level)
The coverage producer — computes coverage INSIDE `condenseContext` by reading each `ModelMessage.source`:
- `EnsuredMessage` source → extract `messageId` / `sender.username` / `date.timestamp()`.
- `dict`/`CondensingDict` source → union existing fields (re-condense cascade).
- `None` source (tool-history emissions) → `logger.warning` + skip, NOT counted in `messageCount`.
- Returns CondensingDict with `text` + conditionally-populated `messageIds` / `participants` (sorted unique) / `dateRange` (`{from:min ts, to:max ts}`, omitted if none) / `messageCount`. Does NOT set `tillMessageId`/`tillTS`.
- Wrapped in try/except → fallback `CondensingDict(text=respText)` on failure (summary preserved, coverage dropped).

Works because: `EnsuredMessage.toModelMessage` sets `source=self`; pre-existing summary replay sets `source=condensedMessage` (base.py).

## Caller flow (simplified — no parallel-list machinery)
- Path A (`getThreadByMessageForLLM`, base.py): `condensedRet, condencingDictMap = await self.condenseContext(...)`; `condenseCache.extend(condencingDictMap.values())` (or `= list(...)` for re-condense).
- Path B (`handleRandomAnswer`, llm_messages.py): `condensedRet, condencedDictMap = await self.condenseContext(...)`; `if condencedDictMap: ensuredMessage.metadata["randomContext"] = mergeCondensingDicts(condencedDictMap.values())` (SKIP write when coverage empty — user decision: nothing meaningful to persist).

## TypedDict changes (`internal/bot/models/message_metadata.py`)
- `CondensingDict`: ONLY `text` is required; ALL other fields (`tillMessageId`, `tillTS`, `messageIds`, `participants`, `dateRange`, `messageCount`) are `NotRequired`. `tillMessageId`/`tillTS` are legacy boundary markers NOT set by `generateCondencingDict` — readers use `in`/`.get()` checks.
- `renderCondensedSummary(data: CondensingDict) -> str` — signature narrowed to `CondensingDict`-only (NO legacy `str` branch). The caller (`ensured_message.py` Path B read site) pre-wraps legacy `str` rows into `CondensingDict(text=randomContext)` before calling.
- `mergeCondensingDicts(dictList) -> CondensingDict` — unions multiple: `text` = `"\n".join`; `messageIds` = concat DEDUPED via `asStr()` first-seen order; `participants` = sorted-unique set union; `dateRange` = min/max; `messageCount` = sum.
- `CondensedDateRangeDict` = `TypedDict("CondensedDateRangeDict", {"from": float, "to": float})` — functional syntax (`from` is reserved).

## Authoritative documentation locations
- **ADR-019** in `docs/llm/architecture.md` — the canonical design description (rewritten 2026-07-13 to describe the simplified design).
- `docs/llm/services.md` — `condenseContext` always-tuple return + `generateCondencingDict` documentation.
- `docs/database-schema.md` + `docs/database-schema-llm.md` — `CondensingDict` shape (only `text` required).
- `docs/plans/condensed-context-retrieval-plan-v1.md` — has a SIMPLIFIED (2026-07-13) note at top; plan body is historical (describes the old `returnCoverage`/index-range approach — do NOT follow it as current).

content:
In `condenseContext()` in `internal/services/llm/service.py`, the adaptive batch-shrink branch (~line 1230 as of 2026-08-20; line numbers drift — re-locate by the `tokensCount / summaryMaxTokens` expression):

```python
currentBatchLen = int(currentBatchLen // (tokensCount / summaryMaxTokens))
```

The formula uses `summaryMaxTokens` (= the condensing model's context size), NOT `maxTokens` (the target model's limit from the caller). This is the correct variable because batches must fit within the condensing model's context window, not the target model's. The earlier bug (which had `maxTokens` instead) has been fixed and is stable since the 2026-07-13 rewrite. Caveat kept from the original note: `summaryMaxTokens = 0` would make this a division by zero (see the separate division-by-zero-guard memory — still unaddressed).

title: condenseContext division-by-zero guard still missing (now at line 810 after rewrite)
content:
In `condenseContext()` in `internal/services/llm/service.py` (method now spans ~1081-1261; line numbers drift — re-locate by symbol):

```python
summaryMaxTokens = condensingModel.contextSize  # ~line 1185, NO guard/clamp
...
batchesCount = tokensCount // max(summaryMaxTokens - 256, summaryMaxTokens * 0.85) + 1  # ~line 1207
```

If `contextSize` is 0 (misconfigured model), the denominator becomes `max(0 - 256, 0 * 0.85) = 0`, causing `ZeroDivisionError`. Fix would be a guard like `summaryMaxTokens = max(summaryMaxTokens, 256)` between the assignment and the division. Verified still unaddressed as of 2026-08-20 (not documented in any durable doc — docs/llm/memories/condensed-context-retrieval.md and user-memory-v2-review.md do not mention it).

A second division-by-zero exposure exists in the adaptive batch-shrink branch (~line 1230):
```python
currentBatchLen = int(currentBatchLen // (tokensCount / summaryMaxTokens))
```
This is only reachable when `tokensCount > summaryMaxTokens` (the ~line 1225 check), but if `summaryMaxTokens = 0` and `tokensCount > 0`, the condition is true and this line would also crash. In practice the setup-time crash at the batchesCount division fires first.
