title: Two distinct CRON_JOB interval-gating patterns — ProxyService vs SandboxHandler, do not conflate
content:
The codebase has TWO different mechanisms for gating work inside `_dtCronJob` (the QueueService CRON_JOB handler that fires ~every 60s). They are easy to conflate in documentation — a 2026-07-18 audit found `docs/llm/memories/proxy-lifecycle.md` had wrongly attributed SandboxHandler's flags to ProxyService.

**Pattern A — ProxyService (`internal/services/proxy/service.py` + `lifecycle.py`):**
- `_dtCronJob` runs on EVERY tick. It iterates `_activeLifecycles`, starts any not-yet-started ones (checks `lifecycle.started` boolean each tick — NO one-time flag), then calls `lifecycle.onCronTick()` on each.
- Interval gating lives inside `ProxyLifecycle.onCronTick()`: uses `_tickCounter += 1` then `if self._tickCounter % healthCheckInterval != 0: return`. Pure modulo on tick count.
- `ProxyLifecycle` also has a `_starting` re-entrancy guard (distinct from `_started`).
- NO `_recoveryDone`, NO `_lastCronRun`, NO `time.time()` delta anywhere in the proxy code.

**Pattern B — SandboxHandler (`internal/bot/common/handlers/sandbox.py`):**
- Uses `self._recoveryDone = False` (one-time startup recovery flag, set True after first recovery run).
- Uses `self._lastCronRun = time.time()` + `if now - self._lastCronRun < 1800: return` (wall-clock delta gating, 1800s = 30min).
- This is the time.time()-delta pattern, NOT the modulo-counter pattern.

**Why it matters:** When documenting or reviewing either handler's cron logic, do not assume they share a mechanism. If a doc claims ProxyService uses `_recoveryDone` or `_lastCronRun`, it is describing SandboxHandler by mistake. The two patterns are intentionally different designs.

title: Durable memory drift categories beyond line numbers: dep versions and tool counts
content:
Complements memories dbec997e (line numbers rot) and 79fdc932 (file paths drift). A July 18, 2026 audit of `docs/llm/memories/chat-history-search.md` surfaced two ADDITIONAL drift-prone claim categories that the existing "avoid brittle references" memories do not name:

1. **Dependency version pins in prose** — the file claimed `numpy==2.4.6`; actual is `numpy==2.5.1` (requirements.direct.txt). Also `fastembed==0.8.0` was correct but only by luck. Dependency versions in durable memory rot on every bump. When auditing, re-verify ALL version pins against requirements.direct.txt; when writing, prefer omitting the pin and pointing at the requirements file instead.

2. **Registered-tool / registration counts** — the file claimed "3 LLM tools registered (search_messages, list_users, get_thread)" but a 4th (`get_messages_by_ids`, added for ADR-019 condensed-context) existed. Tool/registration counts go stale whenever a new tool is added to a handler. When auditing, grep `registerTool(` and count actual calls rather than trusting a stored number; when writing, avoid hardcoding tool counts — list tool names if needed but omit the cardinality.

Also confirmed again: full method signatures rot (the file claimed `embedAndSaveMessage(ensuredMessage, modelName, db) -> bool`; actual is `(self, ensuredMessage: EnsuredMessage) -> bool`). Prefer referencing the symbol + file path over transcribing the signature.

Audit verdict pattern that worked here: when a durable file is mostly accurate (anti-patterns, gotchas, test-mocking rules still valid) but has drifted on 5+ concrete claims, FIX-IN-PLACE with targeted edits rather than ARCHIVE — archiving loses the still-valid durable lessons. Do NOT update meta indexes when fixing a single file.

title: UserMemoriesHandler dual-lock concurrency: _refineLock + _accountingLock
content:
The user-memory refinement concurrency model in `UserMemoriesHandler` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/user_memories.py`) uses TWO locks, not one. Existing memories (`59e37f96`, `93c64c1c`) and the docs (`docs/llm/memories/user-memories.md` lines 624-629, `docs/llm/memories/user-memory-refinement.md` "Concurrency model") all describe only `_refineLock` and call it the "single global lock" — this is NOW STALE.

**Current truth (verified 2026-07-18):**
- `_refineLock` (`asyncio.Lock`): serializes the whole scan+dispatch in `_runSingleRefinement` / `_runMemoryRefinement`. A bail-fast check (`if self._refineLock.locked(): return`) skips a cron tick if a previous batch (a single LLM call can exceed the 60s cadence) is still running, so the provider is never flooded with concurrent refinement calls.
- `_accountingLock` (`asyncio.Lock`): serializes ALL mutations of the in-memory `_accounting` (per-(chatId, userId, threadId) new-message counter) and `_lastRefinedTS` (per-key last-refined timestamp) dicts. Acquired from BOTH `newMessageHandler` (which increments `_accounting`) and `_dtCronJob`/`_runSingleRefinement` (which reads and resets them). This prevents the read-modify-write race between the message-ingress path and the cron path.

**Why the drift matters:** `user-memories.md` actively defers to `user-memory-refinement.md`'s "Concurrency model" section as "still accurate", so the stale "no per-entry locks" / "single global lock" claim propagates. The `user-memory-refinement.md` file was corrected on 2026-07-18 to describe both locks; `user-memories.md` lines 624-629 still need the same correction (see separate memory).

Class/method renames carried over from the rolling-bio → user-memories rewrite: `UserDataHandler` → `UserMemoriesHandler` (file `user_data.py` → `user_memories.py`), `_runRefinement` → `_runSingleRefinement`. The locks and counters themselves are unchanged in purpose.

title: Known doc-drift: user-memories.md concurrency section still says "single global lock"
content:
Known unresolved documentation drift identified 2026-07-18 during audit of `docs/llm/memories/user-memory-refinement.md`.

**Location:** `docs/llm/memories/user-memories.md` lines ~624-629 (the "Concurrency model" deferral block).

**Drift:** The text says "_refineLock (single global lock)" and describes only one lock governing the refinement scan+dispatch. This is now wrong — `UserMemoriesHandler` has a SECOND lock `_accountingLock` that serializes `_accounting`/`_lastRefinedTS` mutations across `newMessageHandler` and `_dtCronJob`. See the memory "UserMemoriesHandler dual-lock concurrency" for the full current truth.

**Status:** The sibling file `user-memory-refinement.md` (which `user-memories.md` defers to as "still accurate") was corrected on 2026-07-18 to describe both locks. `user-memories.md` itself was NOT corrected in that audit pass (out of scope — the audit was constrained to a single assigned file). A future audit/edit of `user-memories.md` should apply the same correction: replace the "single global lock" framing with the dual-lock description.

**Also stale in the same section:** the JSONL-log field list. `user-memory-refinement.md`'s "11 logged fields" (incl. `model`, `elapsedTime`) was corrected to the current 12 fields (`model`/`elapsedTime` dropped; `addCount`/`deleteCount`/`searchCount` added). `user-memories.md`'s JSONL mention ("extended with tool-call counts") is directionally correct but should be reconciled with the corrected field list when touched.

title: SUPERSEDED banner ≠ archivable when successor file defers back
content:
Documentation-maintenance gotcha discovered 2026-07-18 while auditing `docs/llm/memories/user-memory-refinement.md`.

**Pattern:** A memory doc carries a `⚠ SUPERSEDED by <other>.md` banner, inviting an auditor to `git mv` it to `docs/archive/`. But the successor file (`user-memories.md`) contains deferral phrases like "unchanged from the rolling-bio system (see `user-memory-refinement.md` 'Concurrency model' — still accurate)" and "see ADR-014/015" — i.e. it actively BACK-REFERENCES the "superseded" file for durable mechanism details (concurrency model, nested-metadata-write gotcha, JSONL log mechanism).

**Lesson:** Before archiving a SUPERSEDED doc, grep the candidate successor (and the broader `docs/llm/` tree) for back-references to the file. If the successor defers to the "superseded" file for ANY still-current mechanism detail, the file is NOT archivable — it remains load-bearing. The correct action is FIX-IN-PLACE: keep the historical/rolling-bio sections marked superseded in-body, but correct the sections the successor defers to so they match current code.

**Concrete case:** `user-memory-refinement.md` could NOT be archived because `user-memories.md` defers to it for: (1) the dual-lock concurrency model, (2) the nested-metadata-write RMW + `chatUserMetadataLock()` invariant, (3) the JSONL refinement-log mechanism. The banner's "retained for historical context; do not implement from it" is contradictory with the successor's "still accurate" deferral — the durable sections MUST be kept accurate.

**Audit-process corollary:** When a single-file audit constraint forbids editing the successor, the drift found in the audited file's deferred-from sections almost certainly also exists in the successor's deferring sections (mirror drift). Track it as a follow-up rather than assuming the successor is clean.

title: MetadataDict.memories simplified to plain CompactMemoryIdsDict; injectMemories ID-extraction flow
content:
As of 2026-07-18 audit of `docs/llm/memories/user-memories.md`, verified two facts about the user_memories injection path that a prior memory doc had wrong:

**1. TypedDict shape:** `MetadataDict.memories` (in `internal/bot/models/message_metadata.py:257`) is typed as plain `CompactMemoryIdsDict`, NOT the `CompactMemoryIdsDict | UserMemoriesDict` union a memory doc claimed. The `UserMemoriesDict` content-form fallback was removed from the type annotation. The `# type: ignore[assignment]` annotations that guarded compact-metadata writes are gone.

**2. `injectMemories` ID-extraction (no per-row slimming):** Inside `MessagePreprocessorHandler.injectMemories` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/message_preprocessor.py:74`), there is NO `convertDBMemoryToSingleMemoryDict` call on short-term rows. The actual code:
- permanent memories arrive from `cache.getChatUserPermanentMemories` ALREADY as `SingleMemoryDict` with `id` key (because the cache loader at `internal/services/cache/service.py:933` calls `convertDBMemoryToSingleMemoryDict(m, keepId=True)`). IDs read via `m.get("id")` — entries without `id` silently dropped.
- short-term memories come from `db.userMemories.getLatestMemories` / `searchMemories` as raw `UserMemoryDict` with `memory_id` key. IDs read via `m["memory_id"]` — would raise KeyError if missing (no silent drop).
- The DB→`SingleMemoryDict` slimming is DEFERRED to `cache.getMemoriesByIds` at render time (`formatForLLM`), not done in `injectMemories`.

So memory `6838b064` ("metadata['memories'] content form NEVER written at runtime") is confirmed: only compact IDs are written, and the slim-to-SingleMemoryDict conversion happens lazily on read.

title: Bulk-archive of plans/ leaves stale ../../plans/ links in referencing memory docs
content:
Gotcha for memory-doc audits discovered 2026-07-18. When a "Phase 2 bulk-archive" moves implemented plans from `docs/plans/` to `docs/archive/plans/`, the rewrite pass typically only updates ONE primary link in each referencing memory file (the top-of-file "Implemented from [...]" citation). Other in-body references to the same plan elsewhere in the same doc are left pointing at the now-stale `../../plans/` path.

**Observed:** In `docs/llm/memories/user-memories.md`, line 5's link to `user-memories-v1.md` was correctly rewritten to `../../archive/plans/`, but 6 other references (lines ~11, ~657, ~753, ~791, ~793, ~797-798) still pointed to `../../plans/` — referencing `user-memories-v1.md` (3 spots), `memory-compaction-v1.md` (2 spots), and `memories-context-dedup-plan-{v1,v2}.md` (cross-refs block).

**Action for future audits of memory docs:**
- Always grep for stale `../../plans/` and `(../../plans/` references after a bulk-archive pass.
- When auditing any `docs/llm/memories/*.md`, treat stale plan paths as a FIX-IN-PLACE candidate even if the subsystem is otherwise current.
- The check: `rg '\.\./\.\./plans/' docs/llm/memories/<file>.md` should return zero after the fix.

This complements memory `8e06eaa3` (the docs/plans/ reorganization policy) and memory `fedfb55b` (deleted-identifier zero-match convention).

title: BOT_ANSWER_PROBABILITY gate ordering invariant (do not move)
content:
Architectural invariant in `LLMMessageHandler.newMessageHandler` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/llm_messages.py`): the `BOT_ANSWER_PROBABILITY` gate is placed BEFORE `handleReply` and `handleMention` (not just before `handleRandomMessage`). Verified accurate as of 2026-07-18; gate logic is at lines ~490-517 (was ~396 in older revisions — line numbers drift).

Consequence: even an explicit reply or @-mention from a bot-suffixed account is subject to probabilistic dropping. This is INTENTIONAL — prevents bot-to-bot reply loops. The rationale IS now documented in an inline comment at lines ~493-496 (a prior memory incorrectly claimed it was undocumented; that has been superseded).

Bot detection heuristic: `senderUsername.lower().endswith("bot")`. Correct false-positive examples are usernames that genuinely end in "bot": `@turbot`, `@abbot` (a real surname). NOTE: `@robotfan` is NOT a false positive — it ends in "fan", so `endswith("bot")` returns False. A prior memory and the durable doc both carried this wrong example; both corrected 2026-07-18.

Refactor warning: a future contributor might assume the gate should only affect `handleRandomMessage` (the bot-to-bot flood path) and move it after reply/mention — that would be a semantic change. `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/skills/add-handler/SKILL.md` only specify that `LLMMessageHandler` must be the last handler in the manager list; they say nothing about internal sub-handler ordering within it.

Canonical source for full details (detection, lazy `chatSettings` fetch, `randomRoll`-captured-once pattern, 10-test suite): `docs/llm/memories/bot-answer-probability.md` — verified accurate 2026-07-18. Prefer reading that doc over trusting line numbers in any memory.

title: sourceTheadId typo: live in code+config+docs, rename requires dual-key read
content:
The misspelling `sourceTheadId` (should be `sourceThreadId`) is a known, intentionally-preserved typo that lives in THREE layers simultaneously. A rename is NOT a simple find-replace — it will silently break deployments.

**Where it lives (verified 2026-07-18):**
- Code: `internal/bot/common/handlers/resender.py:71` (`__slots__`), `:91` (param), `:109` (docstring), `:123` (assignment), `:360` (usage as `job.sourceTheadId`)
- Config: `configs/00-defaults/resender.toml:8` (`sourceTheadId = 2`)
- Docs: `docs/llm/configuration.md:355` (documents the typo'd name as the config key), `docs/llm/memories/resender.md:12` (notes the typo)

**Why it persists / the rename gotcha:**
TOML config has NO schema validation — unknown keys are silently ignored. If the code is changed to read `sourceThreadId` but a deployment's `configs/local/` override still has `sourceTheadId`, the value is silently dropped (defaults to `None`) and the resender silently processes the wrong/no thread. There is no DB migration for config files. A safe rename therefore requires the code to read BOTH key names during a transition period (e.g. `config.get("sourceThreadId", config.get("sourceTheadId"))`), plus updating the default TOML and the two doc files. Flagged as a follow-up during the 2026-07-18 resender.md audit; not yet addressed.

title: For structural count claims in durable docs, drop the number rather than annotate
content:
Refinement to convention f495e63e ("Annotate point-in-time counts in durable docs — don't chase updates"). Discovered during the 2026-07-18 audit of `docs/llm/memories/use-tools-filtering.md`.

f495e63e's guidance ("annotate with a point-in-time parenthetical, don't keep updating") works well for counts that are pure snapshots (test counts, file counts, link counts at an event time). But it is awkward for STRUCTURAL/RELATIONAL count claims — where the number documents a 1:1 relationship rather than an event outcome.

Concrete case: `use-tools-filtering.md` stated "the `ToolName` StrEnum has 19 members, one per registered LLM tool" to convey the enum↔tool correspondence. The count drifted to 22 (members added: EXAMPLE, DO_TAROT_READING, DO_RUNES_READING) and the registerTool call-site count (also 19) and test count (20→21) drifted with it. Annotating as "19 members, one per tool (as of 2026-07-04)" is ugly and still leaves the count stale-looking.

The clean fix (validated by the audit's own follow-up note "consider dropping the absolute count entirely"): **drop the absolute number and state the relationship qualitatively** — e.g., "one member per registered LLM tool" / "one `registerTool(name=...)` call site per ToolName member." The 1:1 invariant is what matters; the integer is incidental and will always be stale.

Decision rule when auditing a durable doc with a drifted count:
- If the count documents an EVENT outcome (campaign results, snapshot metrics) → annotate with "(as of YYYY-MM-DD; counts drift)" per f495e63e. Preserve the historical figure verbatim.
- If the count documents a STRUCTURAL relationship (N members ↔ N things) → drop the number, keep the relationship statement.
- If the count is load-bearing as an exact current figure with no relationship to express → it should not be in a durable memory doc at all (belongs in generated/linted output).

This applies to all enum-size and call-site-count claims in `docs/llm/memories/`. These rot on every member addition and are the highest-frequency drift source in that tree.

title: get_messages_by_ids extra={"items":{"type":"string"}} is COMMENTED OUT — runtime str coercion is the safety net
content:
The `extra={"items": {"type": "string"}}` line at internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py:363 is COMMENTED OUT (`# extra={"items": {"type": "string"}},`) — verified still true 2026-08-20. The `message_ids` parameter is declared as a plain ARRAY with no item-type enforcement in the emitted JSON schema. This corrects memory 0b98d4a1's claim that the schema carries the items override.

The actual safety net (never-raise when the model violates the implicit string schema): the handler does `str(mid).strip()` + `MessageId(midStr)` coercion at runtime (chat_search.py:985-999). Input is de-duped via a `seen: set[str]` (first-seen order), blank/None entries dropped, clamped to MAX_GET_MESSAGES_BATCH=32 (constants.py:281).

RESOLVED since the original 2026-07-18 note: the previously-stale source text at chat_search.py:974-982 (inline Gate-2 comment) has been FIXED — it now correctly states the `extra=` override is COMMENTED OUT and that the str-coercion is the actual safety net. There is no longer a doc/code mismatch in chat_search.py itself.

Remaining stale reference: docs/llm/memories/condensed-context-retrieval.md:87 carries a drift-note claiming "the source docstring at chat_search.py:975-977 still describe extra=... as live — both stale" — that note is itself stale now.

Return shape (re-confirmed): `{"done": True, "messages": [...], "notFound": [...], "count": N}` on success, `{"done": False, "error": "..."}` on failure.

If someone re-enables the `extra=` line (uncomments :363), this memory becomes stale — re-verify against chat_search.py:363 at that time.

title: Durable markdown memory audit: 36 docs/llm/memories/*.md files, one-per-subagent
content:
A coordinated teamlead-driven audit campaign (active as of 2026-07-18) targets the durable markdown memory files at `docs/llm/memories/*.md` — a DIFFERENT memory system from the `.opencode/memory.jsonl` session memory covered by the existing `memory-audit-workflow` memories.

**Workflow shape:**
- 36 subsystem-memory files audited, ONE file per subagent (parallel dispatch).
- Each subagent does a deep-audit: verify every concrete claim in the assigned `.md` file against current code (file paths exist, section numbers resolve, drift examples still absent, historical counts framed as past-tense).
- Mode is `implement`: edit ONLY the assigned file in-place.
- Verdict is one of: **KEEP** (accurate, no edits), **FIX** (enumerate every change with line refs + before/after), **ARCHIVE** (lesson is dead → `git mv docs/llm/memories/<file>.md docs/archive/llm-sessions/`).
- Constraints: no `make lint`/`make test`; camelCase; preserve existing voice/structure; AGENTS.md applies.
- Expected output format: (1) verdict line, (2) per-claim verification log, (3) fixes applied, (4) stale claims intentionally not fixed with rationale, (5) follow-up cross-file flags for teamlead.

**Key distinction for future audits:**
- Historical counts (e.g. "78-file review", "2635+ tests green") framed as past-tense observations from a specific dated campaign CANNOT drift — do not flag them.
- Structural references (file paths, section numbers like §4.2.1/§6/§6.1 in `reviewing-large-changes.md`) CAN drift — verify they still resolve.
- "Drift examples" cited as historical lessons (e.g. `get_summary` tool, `asyncio.run()` in wrong place, `initialize(queueService, configManager)`) should be checked for continued absence from shipped code; their absence reinforces the lesson rather than invalidating it.

**Verified as KEEP on 2026-07-18:** `docs/llm/memories/large-review-campaign.md` (1548 bytes) — all cross-refs resolve (`teamlead-memory.md`, `reviewing-large-changes.md` §4.2.1/§6/§6.1), all drift examples still absent from production code, no edits needed.

Cross-references for the audit target set: `docs/llm/memories/index.md` (catalog), `docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md` (live compact memory that points into the per-subsystem files).

title: asyncio.run() confined to scripts/tests — absent from internal/ bot and service code
content:
Verified 2026-07-18 during a memory audit: `asyncio.run(...)` appears ONLY in top-level CLI entry points and tests, never in the bot/service production code path. This is a codebase convention (not in AGENTS.md) worth treating as a smell signal during review.

**Where it legitimately lives (verified via `rg 'asyncio\.run\('`):**
- `scripts/reproduce_llm_dialog.py`, `scripts/run_llm_debug_query.py`, `scripts/check_tool_calling.py`, `scripts/check_image_parsing.py`, `scripts/list_models.py`, `scripts/reproduce_layout_extraction.py`, `scripts/aiodocker_demo.py`, `scripts/check_structured_output.py` — all as `sys.exit(asyncio.run(main()))` or `asyncio.run(main())` at module bottom.
- `lib/aurumentation/` — same pattern.
- Various `tests/` files.

**Where it does NOT appear (and should not):**
- `internal/bot/` (telegram, max, common) — no `asyncio.run()`.
- `internal/services/` (cache, llm, queue_service, storage, proxy) — no `asyncio.run()`.

**Rationale:** The app is a single-process async application with one event loop managed by the application entry point (`main.py` → `GromozekBot` → platform `BotApplication`). Bot and service code runs under that loop; calling `asyncio.run()` inside it would create a nested/sibling loop and break. Scripts are standalone CLI entry points that need to spin up their own loop.

**Review signal:** Seeing `asyncio.run()` in `internal/` bot or service code is a documentation-drift smell and likely a real bug — flag it. This is also why historical "documentation drift" lessons (e.g. in `docs/llm/memories/large-review-campaign.md`) cited `asyncio.run()` as an example of docs describing code that doesn't match shipped reality.

Note: also verified that no `initialize(queueService, configManager)` signature exists anywhere — actual `initialize()` signatures are `(self)`, `(self, bot)`, `(self, proxyConfigDict, loop)`. And no `get_summary`/`GET_SUMMARY` tool exists in production code (only in archived plan docs).

title: Inbound-link DESCRIPTION drift: editing a memory file stale-izes its descriptor in index files
content:
A drift class not covered by existing cross-reference memories (90a8e2f5, dbec997e, 79fdc932 all cover OUTBOUND links breaking): when you edit the substance of a memory file (e.g. `docs/llm/memories/docs-reorg-lessons.md`), the link DESCRIPTIONS in files that link INTO it become stale, even though the link target itself still resolves.

Concrete case (2026-07-18): `docs-reorg-lessons.md` was edited to drop "source-tree README" claims (READMEs are no longer a hotspot). But two inbound descriptors still summarize it with "source-tree README/codedoc references":
- `docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md:214`
- `docs/llm/memories/index.md:26`

The links resolve fine; the prose summaries are wrong.

Why this matters for audits: when the audit scope is "edit ONLY the target file," these descriptor-drift cases CANNOT be fixed in-place — they must be flagged for a follow-up sweep by whoever owns the index files. The right action during a single-file audit is to record each stale descriptor with its file:line and the suggested rewording, in the "cross-file flags" section of the audit report.

General rule for memory maintenance: when you change what a file is ABOUT, grep for inbound links to it (`grep -rn "<filename>" docs/`) and reconcile the descriptors, not just the link targets.

title: docs/llm/memories/*.md date convention: title=lesson date, subtitle=extraction+reverification, inline as-of stamps
content:
Confirmed convention (2026-07-18, observed across sibling memory files during the durable-markdown audit) for dating the files under `docs/llm/memories/*.md`. Distinct from the live `docs/llm/*.md` footer-bumping rule (memory bc97727f) and the SUPERSEDED banner rule (memory 909dc68a).

**Three date roles, never collapsed:**
1. **Title H1 date** = lesson-CAPTURE date (when the lessons were originally learned). Stays FIXED across re-verifications. Example: `# Documentation Audit Lessons (2026-06-28)` keeps 2026-06-28 even though re-verified 2026-07-18. Sibling `# Docs Reorg Lessons (2026-07-04)` likewise keeps its lesson date. Do NOT bump the title date on re-verification — that would erase provenance.
2. **Subtitle date(s)** = extraction date + re-verification date(s), accumulated. Example: `Archived durable notes from [link] (extracted 2026-07-18; re-verified 2026-07-18 during the second docs audit, with inline as-of stamps on re-checked claims)`. Append a new `; re-verified YYYY-MM-DD …` clause on each re-audit pass.
3. **Inline `as-of YYYY-MM-DD` stamps** on individual time-sensitive claims that were re-checked this pass (line counts, file counts, version pins). Example: `723-line (as of 2026-07-18; this count itself drifts)`. Claims WITHOUT an as-of stamp should be read as "not re-checked this pass" — the subtitle's as-of-stamp note makes this contract explicit to future readers.

**Why this matters:** an auditor reading a memory file needs to tell apart (a) when the lesson was learned, (b) when the file was last touched, (c) which specific concrete claims were re-verified vs left stale-intentionally. Collapsing these into a single "last updated" date loses that signal.

title: docs/other/yc-ai-sdk/index.md is an SDK API reference, NOT a file-tree index — name misleads
content:
Gotcha discovered 2026-07-18 during the documentation-audit.md re-verification. `docs/other/yc-ai-sdk/index.md` (8088 bytes) is NAMED `index.md` but is NOT a file-tree index. It is a version-pinned YC AI Studio SDK API reference (SDK v0.20.2, per memory 7635bdd9 — requirements now pin 0.22.0, so the doc is already frozen-behind).

**The error it caused:** `docs/llm/memories/documentation-audit.md` line 5 lumped it with `docs/llm/index.md` and `docs/llm/memories/index.md` under "Three index.md files … All three must be kept in sync with the file tree." That rule is correct for the first two (genuine file-tree navigation indexes) but WRONG for the yc-ai-sdk one, which needs full revision on SDK upgrades — not routine tree-sync maintenance. The claim was softened in the 2026-07-18 fix.

**Rule for future audits:** do not assume a file named `index.md` is a tree-sync index. Verify its actual function before applying tree-sync maintenance rules. As of 2026-07-18, exactly TWO of the three `index.md` files in the repo are tree-sync indexes (`docs/llm/index.md`, `docs/llm/memories/index.md`); the third (`docs/other/yc-ai-sdk/index.md`) is a version-pinned SDK reference.

**Follow-up flag for teamlead:** if/when the YC AI Studio SDK is upgraded, `docs/other/yc-ai-sdk/index.md` (and the 7 sibling files in that bundle) need a full revision pass, not the tree-sync treatment.

title: Audit distinction: inline illustrative examples are pattern illustrations, not current-truth claims
content:
Methodology refinement for durable-markdown audits (extends memory 3f4d5242, which already covers "historical counts framed as past-tense cannot drift"). Observed 2026-07-18 auditing `docs/llm/memories/documentation-audit.md`.

**The distinction:** when a memory file cites a specific value INSIDE an illustrative example of a PATTERN, that value is not a current-truth claim even though it looks concrete. Do not flag it as drift, and do not "fix" it to current values — doing so erases the historical lesson.

**Concrete instances from documentation-audit.md (all left as-is, correctly):**
- Line 9: "method names change in code but not in doc examples (e.g., `setUserData` → `addUserData`)" — but `setUserData` is currently the LIVE name (in `tests/fixtures/database_fixtures.py:195`, `tests/fixtures/service_mocks.py:266`). The example direction has flipped over time; it's illustrating the rename-drift PATTERN with a historical instance, not asserting current API shape.
- Line 15: "the same stale value appears in multiple docs (e.g., 12 repos, manager.py:249, RateLimiterManager:12)" — but current repo count is 16. These illustrate the cross-file-stale-value PATTERN; the lesson (fix ALL instances at once) is what matters.

**How to tell illustrative from truth-claim:** illustrative examples are typically introduced by "e.g.", "such as", "for example", or are parenthetical; they demonstrate a category of problem rather than census the codebase. Truth claims stand alone as bare assertions ("there are 12 repos", "the file is 732 lines").

**Counterpoint — when the example SHOULD be updated:** if an illustrative example has become actively misleading (e.g., names a method that no longer exists AT ALL and a reader would chase a dead reference), soften to "e.g., past method renames like X→Y" rather than deleting. Preserve the lesson, reduce the confusion.

title: code-reviewer.md still has cat * and sed -n * in bash allowlist (edit-bypass vector, 7+ days open)
content:
Identified 2026-07-18 (re-flagged; originally noted in `docs/llm/memories/skills-agents-audit.md:23` on 2026-07-11, still open 7 days later).

**Concern:** `.opencode/agents/code-reviewer.md` bash allowlist (current state at lines 113, 118) still permits:
- `"cat *": allow` — allows `cat > file.py` (redirect-write), `cat >> file.py` (append), bypassing the agent's review-only identity and the edit-deny policy
- `"sed -n *": allow` — allows `sed -n` patterns, including variants with `-i` (in-place edit) — also a write vector

This is the same bypass class that was already resolved for `make format` / `make format lint` (per memory `4a514104`, applied 2026-07-14). The `cat *` and `sed -n *` entries were left in place at that time as a follow-up consideration.

**Why this matters:** the code-reviewer agent is supposed to be review-only (cannot edit source files via the edit tool). But `cat > file.py` and `sed -i ... file.py` are functionally equivalent to edits via the bash tool, defeating the intent.

**Recommended fix:** narrow these patterns further or remove them. `cat` for read-only inspection is already covered by Read/Grep/Glob tools; `sed -n` for range-printing is covered by Read with offset/limit. Neither wildcard pattern is needed for legitimate review work.

**Why not fixed in this audit:** the skills-agents-audit memory was the assigned file; editing `code-reviewer.md` was out of scope.

title: Audit convention: historical snapshots in memory files are point-in-time, do not "fix" them to current state
content:
Established 2026-07-18 during the durable-markdown memory audit campaign (one-per-subagent audit of `docs/llm/memories/*.md`).

**Rule:** when auditing a memory file that contains both (a) current-state factual claims and (b) historical/point-in-time snapshots, treat them differently:

- **Current-state claims** (e.g., "X is at line N", "Y is enabled", "Z count is N") → verify against current code and FIX drift.
- **Historical snapshots** (e.g., references inside `[RESOLVED YYYY-MM-DD]` / `[BROKEN LINKS RESOLVED YYYY-MM-DD]` / `[COMPLETED YYYY-MM-DD]` sections, or any paragraph that documents where a bug WAS at fix time) → leave as-is. These are provenance, not current-state assertions. "Fixing" them to match current code would erase their historical value.

**Concrete application (skills-agents-audit.md, 2026-07-18):**
- Fixed: `user_memories.py:1306` → `:~1026` (read as current fact)
- Fixed: "TODO markers, 63 total" → "60 total as of 2026-07-18 (was 63 at audit time)" (kept original as anchor)
- Left: `base.py:193-200`, `base.py:352,742,1804`, `chat_settings.py:171-194` in a `[RESOLVED]` narrative — these are where the bug WAS verified at fix time
- Left: "376 broken links / 22 files" under `[BROKEN LINKS RESOLVED 2026-07-11]` — point-in-time snapshot

**Rationale:** treating moving-target references as needing correction defeats the purpose of an audit memory. The file is a snapshot of understanding at a moment; future drift is expected and tracked by re-audit, not by silently rewriting history.

**Related convention:** memory `49b5f7d3` covers the `~` prefix and grep-able symbol anchor convention for forward-looking skill-doc line refs (a different concern — preventing drift rather than managing historical refs).

title: Durable memory drift category: file-scope/category counts rot silently (extends tool-count lesson)
content:
Third drift-prone claim category beyond line numbers (dbec997e), file paths (79fdc932), dep versions + tool counts (2d7a1148). Surfaced 2026-07-18 auditing `docs/llm/memories/any-type-cleanup.md`.

**The category:** file-scope / category cardinality claims — e.g. "~20 files use `Dict[str, Any]`", "N occurrences of pattern X", "~M handlers register this tool". These rot silently and monotonically as the codebase grows: there is no commit signal (unlike a dep bump), no compile error (unlike a moved symbol), and no test breakage. The number just becomes wrong without any breadcrumb.

**Concrete case:** `any-type-cleanup.md` GENUINE-patterns bullet claimed `Dict[str, Any]` appears in "~20 files, excluded from audit scope". Re-derivation 2026-07-18: 75 files (internal/+lib/) — ~3.75× growth in 20 days. The policy conclusion ("JSON-shaped dicts are the legit AGENTS.md generic-container escape hatch, excluded from audit scope") is STILL correct; only the count misled.

**Why it matters:** a future auditor reading "~20 files" might scope a cleanup pass at that size; the real scope is nearly 4× larger. Cardinality claims silently distort future planning even when the surrounding policy is sound.

**Lessons:**
- When WRITING durable memory: avoid hardcoding scope counts. Prefer the qualitative claim ("excluded from audit scope") over the quantitative ("~20 files"). If a number is load-bearing, frame it as a dated snapshot, not a current-truth claim.
- When AUDITING: re-derive any scope count via grep rather than trusting the stored number. `rg -l 'Dict\[str, Any\]' internal/ lib/ | wc -l` takes one command.
- Same rule applies as 2d7a1148 for tool counts: list the names if useful, omit the cardinality.

Note: this does NOT apply to counts that describe a FIXED historical event (e.g. "61 usages found in the 2026-06-28 audit" — that's a frozen fact about the past, not a current-state claim, and cannot drift). See also the methodology note in `234a2d41` (inline illustrative examples vs current-truth claims).

title: Adding a dep-usage test file requires 4-site lockstep update
content:
Convention discovered 2026-07-18 during the `dependency-usage-tests.md` memory audit. Adding a new file under `tests/dependencies/` (the sanctioned home for dependency-usage regression tests per `docs/llm/testing.md` §1) is a FOUR-SITE lockstep change, analogous to the `add-chat-setting` 4-site rule and the `add-llm-tool` 4-site rule. The four EXTERNAL sites that must update together (in addition to the new test file itself) are:

1. **`docs/llm/memories/dependency-usage-tests.md`** — the durable memory file; its header line ("N files, M tests") and per-library coverage claims must reflect the addition.
2. **`docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md`** (~line 226) — summary blurb repeating "N files, M tests".
3. **`docs/llm/memories/index.md`** (~line 23) — second summary blurb repeating the same count.
4. **`docs/llm/testing.md`** (§1 "Sanctioned exception" paragraph, ~line 36) — enumerates the pinned libraries and the test count.
5. **`CHANGELOG.md`** (`## [Unreleased]` → Added) — one-line entry per the changelog rule.

(Miss any of these and the counts/coverage claims drift apart across docs — exactly the half-wired failure mode the add-chat-setting rule exists to prevent.)

**Current gap flagged:** `pillow==12.3.0` (added to `requirements.direct.txt` Runtime section for the `input_image_format` feature, used at `lib/ai/models.py:48` `from PIL import Image`) has ZERO dep-usage coverage. title: Line-number refs in memory files drift — use symbol-relative refs with "currently :N" guard
content:
Discovered during the 2026-07-18 durable-markdown-memory audit campaign (auditing `docs/llm/memories/*.md`). This is a DISTINCT drift class from the section-number drift already noted in memory `3f4d5242` (which covers §4.2.1/§6/§6.1 references).

**The drift class:** Memory files that cite source-code locations as `file.py:NNN` (bare line numbers) go stale on every non-trivial commit to the referenced file. Concrete cases found in `docs/llm/memories/user-memory-v2-review.md` during the 2026-07-18 audit:
- `MAX_GET_MESSAGES_BATCH=32 (constants.py:258)` — actual location had drifted to `internal/bot/constants.py:253` (one-line drift).
- `condenseContext batchLength must be floored at 1 (service.py ~812)` — actual location had drifted to `internal/services/llm/service.py:1091-1092` (~280-line drift).
Both invariants themselves were STILL LIVE and correct in the code; only the line numbers were wrong.

**Reusable fix shape:** When correcting a stale line ref in a durable memory/doc, do NOT just hardcode the new line number — it will drift again. Use this phrasing instead:
```
`MAX_GET_MESSAGES_BATCH=32` (`internal/bot/constants.py`, currently `:253` — line drifts, re-locate by symbol)
```
The three load-bearing parts: (1) full module path so the file is unambiguous, (2) "currently :N" framed as a point-in-time snapshot not a promise, (3) "line drifts, re-locate by symbol" tells the next reader/auditor to grep by symbol name rather than trust the number.

**Distinguish from non-fixable historical snapshots:** This fix applies ONLY to line refs that POINT AT CURRENT CODE. Historical counts framed as past-tense observations from a specific dated campaign (e.g. "28 commits, 140 files", "3201 tests green") CANNOT drift and must be preserved verbatim — they are the historical record, not live pointers. This distinction is already in memory `3f4d5242`; the line-ref case is the new addition.

**Audit-campaign applicability:** All 35 remaining memory files in the `docs/llm/memories/*.md` audit should be checked for the same `file.py:NNN` / `file.py ~NNN` anti-pattern. When found, apply the same fix shape rather than either (a) silently updating the number or (b) deleting the reference.

title: HandlersManager.shutdown() docstring claims "drops queues" but implementation does not
content:
Verified docstring-vs-implementation drift in `HandlersManager.shutdown()` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/manager.py`), surfaced during the 2026-07-18 audit of `docs/llm/memories/shutdown-state-dump.md`.

**The drift:** The `shutdown()` docstring reads "Signals shutdown to all chat queues, awaits in-flight handler tasks, and drops queues." — but the implementation never explicitly clears `self.chatStates` or any per-chat `queue` deque. The actual sequence is:
1. `self._shutdownEvent.set()`
2. `await self._dumpAllState()`
3. For each `chatState`: acquire `chatState.lock`, set `chatState.shutdownEvent`
4. `await asyncio.gather(*self.handlerTasks)`

There is no step that empties/discards the deques. "Drops queues" is only true in the loose sense that in-memory deques vanish when the process exits (queues are not persisted/flushed). A reader taking the docstring literally could wrongly assume queues are explicitly cleared mid-shutdown.

**Severity:** low. The inline code comment `# Dump state before draining queues` and the sibling doc `docs/llm/handlers.md` §"Shutdown state dump" both use this same loose "drain/drop" terminology, so the codebase is internally consistent in its phrasing — the drift is docstring-vs-behavior, not doc-vs-doc.

**Note:** This finding is NOT reflected in the existing architecture memories (`747966fe`, `1a7b816b`), which correctly describe the actual event-based sequence without claiming queues are dropped. The durable memory file `docs/llm/memories/shutdown-state-dump.md` was also confirmed accurate on 2026-07-18 (KEEP verdict) — it carefully avoids the "drops queues" claim, using "before per-chat queues are drained" to match the code's own comment.

Fix would require editing `manager.py` (out of scope for a markdown-only audit). Flagged for a future code edit.

title: Session-memory `date` labels can drift from actual commit dates — verify against git
content:
When auditing durable/session memories that reference a specific historical event, do NOT trust the `date` label on session-analysed entries (`.opencode/memory.jsonl`) as the event date. The session-analyser stamps the `date` field with its OWN run date, which can be days off from the event it describes.

Concrete case: the repo-wide "dedoodization" pass. The actual commit `81919f8 "Dedoodie the code"` is dated **2026-07-02 22:19:25 +0300** (verified via `git show -s --format='%ci' 81919f8`). The durable file `docs/llm/memories/dedoodization.md` correctly states 2026-07-02. But the session-analyser memory entry `bb8fbcb6-…` in `.opencode/memory.jsonl` stamps the same event as **2026-07-04** — the date the analyser ran, not the date the dedoodization happened.

Actionable rule for memory curation/audits: when two sources disagree on an event date, `git show -s --format='%ci' <SHA>` (or `git log --format='%ci' -- <path>`) is the source of truth, not the memory's `date:` label. Treat session-analyser `date` labels as "when this memory was written", not "when the described event occurred".

title: Audit heuristic: memory-file aggregate counts can be internally inconsistent (total ≠ sum of per-item breakdown)
content:
Discovered during the 2026-07-18 audit of `docs/llm/memories/max-webhook-support.md`. This is a DISTINCT defect class from the line-number drift (3b3c3297) and link drift (90a8e2f5, 335547c2, dbec997e) classes already documented.

**The defect:** A memory file states an aggregate count AND a per-item breakdown, but the aggregate does not equal the sum of the per-item counts. This indicates a WRITE-TIME arithmetic error, not time-based drift. Both the aggregate and the per-item counts may be individually wrong.

**Concrete instance:** The memory claimed "51 tests total" with per-file counts of 14 + 19 + 3 + 6 + 14 = 56 (not 51). The total was wrong even at the time of writing. By 2026-07-18 the actual count had further drifted to 59 (test_app.py grew 19 → 22).

**Diagnostic heuristic for auditors:** When a memory file has BOTH an aggregate count and a per-item breakdown, always verify that `sum(per-item) == aggregate`. If they disagree:
1. The aggregate is a write-time error — distrust it entirely.
2. The per-item counts may ALSO have drifted independently since writing — re-verify each against current source.
3. Recount from scratch using `pytest path/ --collect-only -q | tail -1` for test files, or `rg -c 'def test_' file.py` per file.

**Why this matters:** An auditor who only spot-checks the aggregate against current source (e.g. "memory says 51, actual is 59, update to 59") may miss that the per-item breakdown is ALSO wrong (the memory said 19 for a file that now has 22). Always cross-validate aggregate against breakdown first, then verify each per-item count against source.

title: Agent mistake in services.md audit: disputed correct _persistMemoryEntry-removed cross-flag
content:
During the `docs/llm/services.md` audit (2026-07-18), the software-developer agent INCORRECTLY disputed a cross-file flag from Wave 2's chat-users-cache.md. The flag correctly stated that `_persistMemoryEntry` was a removed symbol (code-side drift: the `chatUserMetadataLock()` docstring at `internal/services/cache/service.py:1134-1153` still references it).

The agent's erroneous conclusion in its final report:
> "Wave 2's chat-users-cache.md flag claimed `_persistMemoryEntry` was "removed" but it still exists (in `user_memories.py`, referenced from `base.py:1174` and ADR-014/015 docs). The cross-flag appears to be incorrect"

This is WRONG. Per memory 5fbb7e65 (2026-07-14, more authoritative), `rg "def _persistMemoryEntry"` returns NOTHING — the method definition was removed during the Phase 4a v2 refinement rewrite. The cursor-persist logic is now INLINE in `UserMemoriesHandler._runSingleRefinement`.

**Root cause of the mistake:** The agent ran `rg "_persistMemoryEntry"` (plain text search) and found matches in comments/docstrings/other docs (user_memories.py:175 comment, tasks.md:493, memories/user-memory-refinement.md:65, chatUserMetadataLock docstring). It then concluded the method "still exists." But these are all STALE REFERENCES to a removed symbol, not proof the `def` exists.

**Correct verification method:** To determine if a symbol EXISTS, run `rg "def <symbol>"` (for functions/methods) or `rg "class <symbol>"` (for classes) or `rg "<symbol> ="` (for assignments). A plain `rg "<symbol>"` only proves the NAME appears somewhere, which includes stale comments, docstrings, and other docs. "Referenced in" ≠ "exists as a definition."

**Impact:** The agent's final report marked this as a resolved non-issue ("cross-flag appears to be incorrect"), which could mislead future readers of the audit output. The actual cleanup work (removing stale `_persistMemoryEntry` references from the chatUserMetadataLock docstring and other docs) is still pending.

title: ProxyService.initialize calls setGlobalProxyConfig internally — not before it
content:
Architectural detail verified during the `docs/llm/services.md` audit (2026-07-18). `ProxyService.initialize(proxyConfigDict, loop)` at `internal/services/proxy/service.py:23` ITSELF calls `ProxyHelper.getInstance().setGlobalProxyConfig(proxyConfigDict)` at `proxy/service.py:103`. The `setGlobalProxyConfig` call happens INSIDE `initialize`, not before it.

This means any documentation saying `initialize` is "called once from main.py after setGlobalProxyConfig" is WRONG. The correct description is simply "called once from main.py" — `initialize` is responsible for setting the global proxy config itself.

**Fix applied in services.md (line 366):** Changed the comment from `# Initialize (called once from main.py after setGlobalProxyConfig)` to `# Initialize (called once from main.py)`.

**Additional param naming:** The actual parameter is named `proxyConfigDict` (not `proxyConfig`), per the signature `def initialize(self, proxyConfigDict: Dict[str, Any], loop: asyncio.AbstractEventLoop) -> None:`. services.md line 377 was updated to match.

This is distinct from memory fc203d2a (which covers `getGlobalProxyConfig`'s None guard + simple return) and memory 165bbb06 (which covers the `setGlobalProxyConfig` docstring "or None to clear" inaccuracy). Those memories cover the ProxyHelper side; this covers the ProxyService caller side.

title: HTTP API clients take proxyConfig directly — NOT proxyKwargs dict
content:
Verified 2026-07-18 during docs/llm/libraries.md audit. The HTTP API client classes `OpenWeatherMapClient` (lib/openweathermap/client.py) and `GeocodeMapsClient` (lib/geocode_maps/client.py) both accept proxy configuration as a **`proxyConfig: Optional[ProxyConfig]`** keyword argument on their constructors — a `ProxyConfig` OBJECT, not a `proxyKwargs` dict.

This contradicts what docs/llm/libraries.md claimed before the 2026-07-18 fix (it described a `proxyKwargs` dict and a manual `ProxyConfig.fromServiceConfig() → getCombined() → toKwargs()` flow). That description is wrong for these clients.

**Correct wiring pattern** (seen at `internal/bot/common/handlers/weather.py:80-86, 119`):
```python
proxyConfig = ProxyService.getInstance().resolveProxy(serviceConfig, serviceLabel)
client = OpenWeatherMapClient(apiKey=..., proxyConfig=proxyConfig)
```
`ProxyService.resolveProxy(serviceConfig, serviceLabel)` returns a `ProxyConfig` directly (it internally calls `ProxyConfig.fromServiceConfig()`). The `ProxyConfig` object is passed straight to the client — the client does NOT call `toKwargs()` itself for proxy setup at construction; it holds the ProxyConfig and resolves httpx kwargs lazily when building its httpx.AsyncClient.

**Related negative claim:** `LLMManager.__init__(config, *, statsStorage=None)` does NOT accept a `proxyConfig` kwarg either. LLM providers (`BasicOpenAIProvider`, `OpenrouterProvider`) resolve proxy internally from their own service config via `ProxyConfig.fromServiceConfig(self.config)`. The LLM-provider proxy pattern IS documented in existing memory ebb7a9e5; this memory covers the HTTP-API-client side, which is a different surface.

**Audit recommendation:** The `fromServiceConfig + getCombined + toKwargs` misconception may also appear in other docs/llm/ files touching proxy-using clients. Grep for `rg "ProxyConfig.fromServiceConfig.*getCombined.*toKwargs" docs/llm/` to find more drift.

title: OpenWeatherMapClient public methods — getCoordinates/getWeather/getWeatherByCity
content:
Verified 2026-07-18 during docs/llm/libraries.md audit. `OpenWeatherMapClient` (lib/openweathermap/client.py) exposes exactly three public async methods. There is NO `getCurrentWeather()` or `geocode()` method — docs/llm/libraries.md previously invented both names and was fixed.

Actual public API:
- `getCoordinates(city: str, country: Optional[str] = None, state: Optional[str] = None, limit: int = 1) -> Optional[GeocodingResult]` (line 151) — uses the OpenWeatherMap Geocoding API; results cached via `geocodingCache`.
- `getWeather(lat: float, lon: float, exclude: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> Optional[WeatherData]` (line 239) — the main weather fetch by coordinates.
- `getWeatherByCity(...)` (line 388) — convenience wrapper that geocodes then fetches weather.
- Internal: `_makeRequest(url, params) -> Optional[dict]` (line 434).

Constructor signature (line 102):
```python
OpenWeatherMapClient(
    apiKey: str,
    weatherCache: Optional[CacheInterface[str, WeatherData]] = None,
    geocodingCache: Optional[CacheInterface[str, GeocodingResult]] = None,
    geocodingTTL: Optional[int] = 2592000,   # 30 days
    weatherTTL: Optional[int] = 1800,        # 30 minutes
    requestTimeout: int = 10,
    defaultLanguage: str = "ru",
    rateLimiterQueue: str = "openweathermap",
    proxyConfig: Optional[ProxyConfig] = None,
)
```
There is NO `cacheTtl` constructor parameter (docs/llm/libraries.md previously claimed `cacheTtl=3600` in its example and was fixed). Caching TTLs are split into `geocodingTTL` and `weatherTTL`.

Note: the GeocodeMapsClient surface (search/reverse/lookup) is already documented in existing memory daa23b59.

title: Reference docs can rot into teaching forbidden patterns — database.md §6 case study
content:
Doc-quality lesson from the 2026-07-18 audit of `docs/llm/database.md`.

**The failure mode:** §6 "Adding Methods to `Database`" had accumulated examples that taught the EXACT OPPOSITE of current AGENTS.md SQL portability rules:
- Used sync `with self.db._getConnection()` (the old sync pattern — no longer exists)
- Used raw `cursor.execute("... WHERE chat_id = ?", (chatId,))` (raw sqlite3 — explicitly forbidden; must go through `BaseSQLProvider`)
- Used `?` positional placeholders (must use `:named`)
- Constructor signature `def __init__(self, db: 'Database')` (actual is `manager: DatabaseManager`)
- Registration `self.myRepository = MyRepository(self)` (actual is `MyRepository(self.manager)`)

All fixed in this audit to use `async` + `await self.manager.getProvider(...)` + `BaseSQLProvider.executeFetchOne` + `:named` placeholders + `dbUtils.sqlToTypedDict`.

**Generalisable lesson:** Reference docs that teach patterns (not just describe APIs) are high-risk for this class of drift. When the underlying conventions change, the doc silently becomes an anti-tutorial. Two structural mitigations:
1. Reference docs should show MINIMAL code — prefer signatures + links to real source over inline examples.
2. Code examples in docs should be paired with the rule they satisfy, so a reader (or auditor) can immediately spot contradiction.

**Related anti-pattern in the same audit:** the migration recipe in §4 used `Migration016AddUserPreferences` as its "next migration" example, but `migration_016_add_stat_tables.py` already exists. Concrete version/number references in doc examples collide with real artifacts and mislead. Now bumped to 025. Prefer placeholder syntax (`Migration_NNN_*`) or clearly-fictional names over real-ish numbers.

title: Bayes filter class is NaiveBayesFilter — NOT BayesFilter
content:
Verified 2026-07-18 during docs/llm/libraries.md audit. The spam-classification class in `lib/bayes_filter/bayes_filter.py` is named **`NaiveBayesFilter`** (class declaration at line 135; `__init__` at line 169). It is exported from `lib/bayes_filter/__init__.py` as `NaiveBayesFilter`, alongside `BayesConfig` and `SpamScore`.

docs/llm/libraries.md previously referred to the class as `BayesFilter` throughout its section and was fixed on 2026-07-18.

Constructor:
```python
NaiveBayesFilter(storage: BayesStorageInterface, config: Optional[BayesConfig] = None) -> None
```

**Negative claim:** There is NO `dataSource` parameter on `NaiveBayesFilter` or `BayesConfig`. docs/llm/libraries.md previously claimed "`BayesFilter` supports `dataSource` parameter for multi-source routing" — this is fabricated; the claim was removed. Storage routing (per-chat vs global) is controlled solely by `BayesConfig.perChatStats` (bool) and the storage implementation (`DatabaseBayesStorage` in internal/database/bayes_storage.py), not by a `dataSource` argument.

`BayesConfig` defaults (all verified): alpha=1.0, minTokenCount=2, perChatStats=True, defaultThreshold=50.0, minConfidence=0.1, maxTokensPerMessage=2000.

title: LLMToolCall.errorMessage field is non-serialized — not in __str__/toDict()
content:
Verified 2026-07-18 during docs/llm/libraries.md audit. `LLMToolCall` (lib/ai/models.py:499) has an `errorMessage: Optional[str] = None` field that carries provider-side error context for a tool call, but it is deliberately **NOT included in `__str__()` or `toDict()`** serialization.

This means: if you inspect a `LLMToolCall` via its dict/str form (e.g. for logging or JSON serialization in tool-result plumbing), the error reason is silently dropped. To see whether a tool call errored, you must access `.errorMessage` directly on the object — it will not appear in serialized/round-tripped representations.

Full LLMToolCall field surface (line 499):
- `id: str`
- `name: str`
- `parameters: Dict[str, Any]` (the tool call arguments)
- `errorMessage: Optional[str] = None` (non-serialized — see above)

Note: `ModelMessage` has a `toolCallId` field (distinct from LLMToolCall.id); do not confuse the two. The `toolCallId` on ModelMessage links an assistant/tool message pair; `LLMToolCall.id` is the id assigned to a tool invocation within a model run result.

Related Wave 4 slots on adjacent classes: `ModelMessage` now has a `source` slot (lib/ai/models.py:550) used by llm-messages-handler for tracking original message provenance; `ModelRunResult` has a `roundLimitHit` slot (lib/ai/models.py:965). These were added to docs/llm/libraries.md in the same audit.

title: Divination API: drawSymbols requires supportsReversed kwarg; classmethods resolveLayout/draw
content:
Verified 2026-07-18 during docs/llm/libraries.md audit. The divination library API surface (lib/divination/) was previously mis-documented in libraries.md's "Usage from a handler" example, which called `resolveLayout(system, "three_card")` and `drawSymbols(system, layout, question=...)`. Both calls are wrong.

**Module-level `drawSymbols`** (lib/divination/drawing.py:15):
```python
def drawSymbols(
    deck: Sequence[Symbol],
    layout: Layout,
    *,
    supportsReversed: bool,   # keyword-only, REQUIRED
    rng: Optional[random.Random] = None,
) -> Tuple[DrawnSymbol, ...]
```
- First arg is `deck` (a sequence of `Symbol`), NOT a system instance.
- `supportsReversed` is **keyword-only and required** — there is no default. Tarot passes True; runes pass False (runes have no reversed semantics).
- There is NO `question` parameter.

**Module-level `resolveLayout`** (lib/divination/layouts.py:70):
```python
def resolveLayout(name: str, *, layouts: Sequence[Layout]) -> Optional[Layout]
```
- Takes `name` FIRST, then keyword-only `layouts`. Calling it positionally as `resolveLayout(system, "three_card")` is wrong.

**Preferred: BaseDivinationSystem classmethods** (lib/divination/base.py):
- `BaseDivinationSystem.resolveLayout(cls, name: str) -> Optional[Layout]` (line 180) — classmethod; no instance needed. Match is case/dash/underscore/space-insensitive against id + aliases.
- `BaseDivinationSystem.draw(cls, layout: Layout, *, rng: Optional[random.Random] = None) -> Tuple[DrawnSymbol, ...]` (line 194) — classmethod; delegates to `drawSymbols` internally, supplying the system's own deck and `supportsReversed`.
- `BaseDivinationSystem.availableLayouts(cls) -> Sequence[Layout]` (line 171).

There is NO instance-level `read()` method on BaseDivinationSystem. Correct handler usage:
```python
from lib.divination import TarotSystem
layout = TarotSystem.resolveLayout("three_card")
drawnSymbols = TarotSystem.draw(layout)
```
Concrete systems are `TarotSystem` (lib/divination/tarot.py:16) and `RunesSystem` (lib/divination/runes.py:14); both subclass `BaseDivinationSystem` (lib/divination/base.py).

title: DIVINATION_DISCOVERY_STRUCTURE_PROMPT does not exist — real keys are DIVINATION_PARSE_STRUCTURE_SYSTEM_PROMPT + DIVINATION_PARSE_STRUCTURE_PROMPT
content:
Doc-fabrication drift class (corrected in `docs/llm/configuration.md` 2026-07-18 audit). The name `DIVINATION_DISCOVERY_STRUCTURE_PROMPT` / `divination-discovery-structure-prompt` was invented in docs — it does NOT exist in the `ChatSettingsKey` enum or any TOML config. The real keys are:

| Real enum member | String value | chat_settings.py | bot-defaults.toml |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DIVINATION_PARSE_STRUCTURE_SYSTEM_PROMPT` | `divination-parse-structure-system-prompt` | ~357 | ~331 |
| `DIVINATION_PARSE_STRUCTURE_PROMPT` | `divination-parse-structure-prompt` | ~359 | ~343 |

Both live on page `BOT_OWNER_SYSTEM`. The `divination-parse-structure-prompt` template uses THREE placeholders: `{systemId}`, `{layoutName}`, `{description}` (not just `{description}` as the doc claimed). The companion discovery keys are `DIVINATION_DISCOVERY_SYSTEM_PROMPT` and `DIVINATION_DISCOVERY_INFO_PROMPT` (these are real; `INFO_PROMPT` placeholders are `{systemId}`, `{layoutName}`).

General lesson: when a docs table lists a single "structure" key alongside "info"/"system" entries, suspect it's actually two keys (system + template) — the parse-pipeline convention in this repo splits system instruction from user-template for every LLM call.

title: channel-defaults IS consumed — loaded via ChatType enum iteration in HandlersManager.__init__
content:
`[bot.channel-defaults]` in `configs/00-defaults/bot-defaults.toml` (line 45) looks like it might be dead config because no code reads the literal string `"channel-defaults"`. It is NOT dead. `HandlersManager.__init__()` (`internal/bot/common/handlers/manager.py` ~line 453) iterates over `for chatType in ChatType:` and reads `botConfig.get(f"{chatType.value}-defaults", {})` for each — so `channel-defaults`, `private-defaults`, `group-defaults` are all loaded the same way, just by enum value.

Same goes for `private-defaults` / `group-defaults` — they're not referenced by literal name anywhere either; they're all loaded by the enum-driven loop. Adding a new `ChatType` value automatically requires a matching `{value}-defaults` TOML section (or the loop silently gets `{}` for it).

Config doc tables (e.g. `docs/llm/configuration.md` `[bot]` section) must list all four: `defaults`, `private-defaults`, `group-defaults`, `channel-defaults`, plus `tier-defaults` (loaded separately at manager.py ~463 via `botConfig.get("tier-defaults", {})` keyed by tier name).

title: Three distinct default layers for chat-search tools — LLM-tool hardcoded vs config vs slash-command
content:
Doc-writing gotcha (root cause of multiple drifts in `docs/llm/configuration.md`'s `[search-history]` section, fixed 2026-07-18). The chat-search handler has THREE independent default mechanisms that are easy to conflate:

**`search_messages` LLM tool** (`_llmToolSearchMessages`, `internal/bot/common/handlers/chat_search.py`):
- `limit` default = **5** (hardcoded in signature, clamped `max(1, min(n, 100))`)
- `max_age_days` default = **None** (passed straight through; NO auto-fallback to config)

**`list_users` LLM tool** (`_llmToolListUsers`):
- `limit` default = **20** (hardcoded, clamped `max(1, min(n, 200))`)

**`/users` slash command** (`_handleUsersCommand`, different code path):
- `limit` default = **50**

**`/search` slash command** + `[search-history.defaults]` config:
- `max-results` = **10** → slash-command `limit`
- `default-days` = **30** → slash-command `days` (via `self._defaultDays`)

Two concrete drifts this caused: (a) doc said `search_messages` "limit defaults to `[search-history.defaults].max-results` (10)" — WRONG, LLM tool doesn't read that config; (b) doc said `list_users` "limit defaults to 50" — WRONG, conflated with the slash command.

Rule for documenting any chat-search parameter: specify which of the three paths (LLM tool / slash command / config) the default comes from, and never borrow a slash-command default to describe an LLM-tool parameter. Existing memory 6381f68c covers one specific instance (the hardcoded upper bound of 100); this entry generalizes the pattern.

Related ground truth: ChatSearchHandler registers exactly **4** LLM tools (`search_messages`, `list_users`, `get_thread`, `get_messages_by_ids`) — see memory f7d6d6f3.

title: POLL_INTERVAL=0.5 is a hardcoded constant in webhook receiver, NOT a config key
content:
Correction of an inaccurate cross-file flag. The Phase 3a / Wave 5 audit flag for `docs/llm/configuration.md` listed `poll-interval = 0.5` as if it were a `[webhook-receiver]` config key. It is NOT — there is no `poll-interval` key in `configs/00-defaults/webhook-receiver.toml`.

The `0.5` value comes from a module-level Python constant `POLL_INTERVAL = 0.5` at `internal/max_webhook_receiver/app.py:47`, used by the long-poll `handleGetUpdates` loop (sleeps `POLL_INTERVAL` between empty-result retries). It is not user-tunable via TOML.

When documenting webhook-receiver config, the actual configurable timing keys are the ones in `webhook-receiver.toml` (e.g. `poll-interval` is NOT among them). If a doc ever needs to reference the 0.5s cadence, cite it as a code constant, not a config default. (The flag's other claims — `enable-cleanup = true`, `unregister-webhook = false` config default with code default `True` per memory e6112afd, `register-webhook = true`, 14 active + 2 commented TLS keys — are accurate.)

content:
In `docs/llm/reviewing-large-changes.md`, Section 7 Appendix describes 5 batches (A-E) while Section 4.2.1 "Real-World Example" describes 6 batches (A1, A2, B-E). This is NOT a documentation bug to "correct."

title: _persistMemoryEntry stale refs: 3 locations remain open (tasks.md FIXED 2026-07-18)
content:
Durable documentation convention (confirmed across the 2026-07 _persistMemoryEntry cleanup, verified fully resolved 2026-08-20): when a method is renamed or inlined (e.g. `UserMemoriesHandler._persistMemoryEntry` inlined into `_runSingleRefinement`'s cursor-persist block), the project pattern is to reference the NEW symbol and add an inline "(formerly a standalone `X` method)" historical pointer — see architecture.md ADR-014/015, internal/services/cache/service.py:1204, internal/bot/common/handlers/base.py:1212, docs/llm/memories/user-memory-refinement.md:65, tests/bot/common/handlers/test_user_memories.py:819/855.

title: ConfigManager.getProxyConfig() returns ProxyConfigDict (not Dict[str, Any])
content:
`ConfigManager.getProxyConfig()` (internal/config/manager.py:508) returns `ProxyConfigDict`, NOT `Dict[str, Any]`. The `ProxyConfigDict` TypedDict is imported from `lib/proxy/__init__.py` (see memory `256d3a87` for the dual-context `enabled` vs `use-proxy` ambiguity of that type).

This was found 2026-07-18 during the `docs/llm/configuration.md` audit: the ConfigManager methods table (§3, line ~846) incorrectly listed the return type as `Dict[str, Any]`. Now corrected to `ProxyConfigDict`. This is the ONLY `get*Config()` method on ConfigManager that returns a concrete TypedDict rather than `Dict[str, Any]` — `getRateLimiterConfig()` returns `RateLimiterManagerConfig` (also a concrete type), but all others (`getBotConfig`, `getDatabaseConfig`, `getLoggingConfig`, `getModelsConfig`, `getGeocodeMapsConfig`, `getOpenWeatherMapConfig`, `getYandexSearchConfig`, `getStorageConfig`, `getStatsConfig`, `getSearchHistoryConfig`) return plain `Dict[str, Any]`.

When documenting ConfigManager methods, always grep the actual signature in `internal/config/manager.py` rather than assuming `Dict[str, Any]`.

title: Sandbox handler uses 3 distinct readFile maxBytes caps — only 2 are named constants
content:
The sandbox handler (`internal/bot/common/handlers/sandbox.py`) reads container output with THREE different byte caps depending on the call site. Only two of them are named constants (per memory 5ec0085c); the third tier uses inline hardcoded literals that are easy to miss when adding new read paths:

1. **`MAX_SANDBOX_READ_FILE_BYTES = 65536` (64 KB)** — used ONLY by `_llmToolSandboxReadFile` (the `sandbox_read_file` LLM tool). Imported from `internal/bot/constants.py`.
2. **`MAX_SANDBOX_SEND_BYTES = 20 * 1024 * 1024` (20 MB)** — used ONLY by `_llmToolSandboxSendFile` (the `sandbox_send_file` LLM tool), read as `maxBytes=MAX_SANDBOX_SEND_BYTES + 1` then enforced. Imported from `internal/bot/constants.py`.
3. **Inline hardcoded `maxBytes=4096`** — used for stdout/stderr reads in BOTH `_llmToolRunSandboxCode` (the `run_python` LLM tool, sandbox.py:317,328) AND the `/run` slash command response builder. NOT a named constant.
4. **Inline hardcoded `maxBytes=3000`** — used ONLY by the `/sandbox read` slash command (human-facing, not an LLM tool). NOT a named constant.

Additionally, the `/run` slash command response truncates the combined output at `maxLength=3000` (sandbox.py:740) — a separate display-truncation budget distinct from the read cap.

**Gotcha for new read paths:** If you add a new sandbox read site, pick the matching cap deliberately. The LLM tool path uses the 64 KB constant; human slash commands use 3000–4096 inline literals. Mixing them up (e.g. giving an LLM tool the 3000 cap) silently throttles model-visible output.

Verified 2026-07-18 during the docs/llm/sandbox.md audit (8 fixes applied, FIX-in-place verdict).

title: Sandbox slash commands inventory: /run|/python + /sandbox files|read|status|packages|install
content:
Human-facing sandbox slash commands registered in `internal/bot/common/handlers/sandbox.py` (verified 2026-07-18):

- **`/run <code>`** (alias: **`/python`**) — execute Python in sandbox. `commands=("run", "python")`.
- **`/sandbox files [path]`** — list workspace files.
- **`/sandbox read <path>`** — read a workspace file (uses inline `maxBytes=3000`).
- **`/sandbox status`** — show session status.
- **`/sandbox packages`** — list installed Python packages (human-facing counterpart to the `sandbox_list_libraries` LLM tool, memory c83044a8). Help string: ` <files|read|status|install> [args]` (note: the help string omits `packages` from the enumerated subcommands even though the command dispatches it — minor doc-string drift).
- **`/sandbox install <packages...>`** — install packages (admin only; wraps `SandboxManager.installRuntimeLibraries()`, memory 83ff0f87 — NOT exposed as an LLM tool).

The `/sandbox` command is registered with `visibility={CommandPermission.PRIVATE}`, `availableFor={CommandPermission.DEFAULT}`, `category=CommandCategory.TOOLS`.

Distinct from the 5 LLM tools (`run_python`, `sandbox_list_files`, `sandbox_read_file`, `sandbox_send_file`, `sandbox_list_libraries`) which are model-invoked, not human-invoked.

title: TOML config key casing is inconsistent across config sections: snake_case vs kebab-case
content:
TOML config key casing conventions are NOT uniform across the repo. An agent editing config files must verify the casing used in the SPECIFIC config section rather than assuming consistency.

Observed conventions:
- **AI models config** (`configs/00-defaults/openrouter-models.toml`, `yc-openai-models.toml`, `yc-sdk-models.toml`, `fastembed-models.toml`) uses **snake_case**: `model_id`, `model_version`, `support_tools`, `support_text`, `support_images`, `temperature`, `context`, `provider`, `enabled`. Table structure is `[models.models."provider/model-id"]`. Accessed in Python via `modelConfig["model_id"]` (see `lib/ai/manager.py` ~line 171).
- **Providers config** (`configs/00-defaults/providers.toml`) uses **snake_case**: `type`, `folder_id`, `api_key`. Table structure is `[models.providers.NAME]`.
- **Sandbox config** (`configs/00-defaults/sandbox.toml`) uses **kebab-case**: `root-dir`, `base-url`, `run-image-tag`, `dir-mode`. These kebab-case TOML keys map to camelCase Python dataclass fields via a `@classmethod fromDict()` method. (See existing memories on sandbox-config / configuration.md drift.)

This caused a real bug in `docs/product-page.md`: the marketing copy fabricated a TOML example using camelCase keys (`[[ai.models]]` with `group`, `apiType`, `modelId`) that don't exist anywhere — wrong table structure, wrong field names, wrong casing. The real schema is `[models.models.NAME]` with snake_case `model_id`/`provider`.

Note: AGENTS.md's camelCase rule applies to **Python identifiers** (variables, args, fields, functions, methods, classes). It does NOT apply to TOML config keys, which are data/strings, not Python identifiers. Do not extend the Python camelCase convention to TOML config keys — check the actual file first.

Practical rule: before writing or documenting any TOML config snippet, grep the corresponding `configs/00-defaults/*.toml` file to confirm the exact key names and casing for that section.

title: Reference docs fabricate API surface — distinct from teaching forbidden patterns
content:
A documentation-drift failure mode confirmed across two files (database.md §6 audit 2026-07-18 and sql-portability-guide.md audit 2026-07-18): illustrative/example code blocks in docs FABRICATE API that does not exist in the codebase, or use wrong identifiers. This is distinct from "teaching forbidden patterns" (memory 5e8a7fc1) — fabricated API would simply TypeError/NameError if copy-pasted.

Specific instances found in docs/sql-portability-guide.md (all fixed in the 2026-07-18 audit):
1. **Invented `executeUpsert()` method** — does not exist on BaseSQLProvider. Real method is `upsert()`.
2. **`getCurrentTimestamp()` shown as a provider method returning a SQL expression** (`sqlite_provider.getCurrentTimestamp()` asserted to contain `datetime('now')`). Reality: module-level function in `internal/database/utils.py`, returns `datetime.datetime`, NOT a SQL expression.
3. **Wrong class name `BaseProvider`** in class declarations and imports. Real class is `BaseSQLProvider`.
4. **snake_case kwargs in `upsert()` examples** — `conflict_columns=`, `update_expressions=`. Real signature uses camelCase: `conflictColumns=`, `updateExpressions=`. Violates both the project hard rule AND won't run.
5. **Raw string `"excluded.updated_at"`** in updateExpressions where the doc's own contract mandates the `ExcludedValue()` marker.

Root cause: example/illustrative code in docs is written from memory rather than copied from (or verified against) real call sites. Because these are in "Recommended Solution" / "Usage Example" / test-scaffold blocks, no CI catches them — they only fail when a developer copy-pastes the example into real code.

Mitigation pattern that worked in this audit: grep the codebase for each API symbol referenced in doc code blocks (method name, class name, kwarg name, import path) and flag any that return zero matches outside docs. This is cheap and catches fabrication reliably.

When auditing any reference doc, verify EVERY symbol in code blocks against the real source, not just the prose claims — fabrication is the failure mode that prose-review misses.
