title: Docs metadata policy: YAML front matter in docs/ (Phase 4)
content:
Owner-ratified metadata policy for Gromozeka docs (Phase 4 of the markdown-mcp-driven docs rewrite), first applied 2026-09-06 to the 13 core files under docs/llm/:

- `category` REQUIRED on every doc file, from a CLOSED set: {design, plan, process, guide, reference}.
- `title` added ONLY where the H1/filename stem is inadequate — default is NO title.
- `description` ONLY on designated entry points, one line each. Entry points: docs/llm/index.md ("Index and quick reference for the agent documentation set — start here before non-trivial work.") and docs/llm/memories/index.md (handled by a different agent).
- `tags`: NONE.
- Merge into existing YAML front matter if present; else create at the very top: `---`, category (then optional description), `---`, blank line before content. NO other content changes in the same edit.
- Scope exclusions: docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md (teamlead-owned) and anything under docs/llm/memories/.

Rationale: front matter feeds markdown-mcp search/navigation (doc_list/doc_search filter by category/tag). Category assignments for docs/llm: index.md=guide(+description); handlers/libraries/services/database/configuration/testing/sandbox/tasks.md=guide; architecture.md & aurumentation.md=reference (ADR record / golden-data reference); changelog.md & reviewing-large-changes.md=process. As of 2026-09-06 none of the 13 had pre-existing front matter (all created, none merged).

title: markdown-mcp doc_write cannot edit front matter — edit via anchored H1 replacement
content:
The markdown-mcp `doc_write` tool cannot create or modify YAML front matter:
- `overwrite` replaces content AFTER the front-matter block (block itself untouched).
- `prepend` inserts after the front-matter block — on a file that already has front matter this creates a second pseudo-front-matter block in the body (wrong); on a file without front matter it lands at the top and the inserted block effectively becomes the front matter.
- `doc_section_edit` operates on parsed sections; front matter is not a section.

Working pattern (used for all 13 docs/llm files in Phase 4, 2026-09-06): plain `edit` anchored on the file's unique H1 first line — oldString = the H1, newString = front-matter block + blank line + H1. Yields additions-only diffs (4 lines per file, 5 with description), zero content drift, byte-identical rest of file. Verification: `git diff --numstat` must show additions-only; `doc_lint` needs no index (reads disk) so it validates immediately; `make check-docs` link checker (scripts/check_docs.py) treats the leading `---` fence harmlessly — 0 broken links across 139 files after the change.

Also: only a `---` fence at byte 0 is parsed as front matter; existing `---` horizontal rules later in the body are unaffected.

title: YAML front-matter values containing ': ' must be double-quoted
content: In YAML front matter, a `description` (or any value) containing `: ` (colon + space) cannot be an unquoted plain scalar — strict parsers (PyYAML, as used by python-frontmatter / markdown-mcp indexing) fail with "mapping values are not allowed here". Fix: double-quote exactly those values; the text stays verbatim and quoted/unquoted values parse to the same string. Real examples from the Phase 4 docs rollout (2026-09-06): `description: "End-to-end developer guide: setup, architecture, handlers, services, libraries, testing, and deployment."` and `description: "Reference index for the database layer: schema, repositories, migrations, and SQL portability."`. Values without colon-space (e.g. "Product overview of Gromozeka for end users.") stay unquoted. Do not reword owner-supplied description text to dodge colons — quoting is the standard fix and adds no keys.

title: markdown-mcp CAS tokens: no bash shasum; doc_read dumps full file — prefer edit pattern for batches
content:
Addendum to memory 058b23e8 (markdown-mcp front-matter editing). For files WITHOUT front matter, `doc_write` op=prepend works perfectly: content `---
category: X
[description: Y]
---

` inserts literally at byte 0 with the trailing blank line preserved (verified byte-exact via disk read on docs/product-page.md), and doc_write reindexes in-call, returning the new sha256 + outline. The reason the plain-edit pattern is still preferred for batches: prepend is CAS-gated (expected_sha256), and the only token sources are (a) doc_read — which returns the FULL file content with no size limit, flooding context on 1000+ line docs — or (b) `shasum`/`sha256sum`, which are NOT on the docs-writer bash allowlist (allowed: make lint*, make check-docs*, rg, grep, ls, git diff/log/show/status/ls-files, wc; everything else denied). Rule of thumb: one-off small file → doc_write prepend (gets index freshness for free); batch over large files → plain edit anchored on the unique H1, accept index staleness until the phase-level reindex (doc_lint and doc_read serve from disk, so verification is unaffected either way).

title:
markdown-mcp prepend: single trailing 
 is consumed — use 

; sha via truncated doc_read files
content:
Two refinements to memory 31139509 (markdown-mcp CAS/prepend workflow), discovered applying front matter to the 20 docs/design + docs/plans files 2026-09-06:

1. Prepend newline failure mode: `doc_write` op=prepend consumes the content's final `
` as the last line's terminator. Prepending `---
category: X
---
` yields NO blank line between the front matter and the body. The double newline in `---
category: X
---

` is what lands the required blank separator (verified byte-exact via git diff). The pilot file (docs/design/chat-accessibility-tracking.md) had to get its blank line via a follow-up plain `edit` because of this.

2. CAS tokens for large files without context flooding: `doc_list` does NOT expose sha256; only `doc_read` does (JSON head `{"mode": "disk", "sha256": "..."}`). doc_read outputs over ~52 KB are truncated and saved to `/Users/vgoshev/.local/share/opencode/tool-output/tool_<id>` — the transcript then shows only a short notice, so PARALLEL doc_reads over many large files are context-cheap. Extract all tokens afterwards in one allowlisted call: `rg -o '"sha256": "[a-f0-9]{64}"' <saved-file-1> <saved-file-2> ...` (output is filename-prefixed, unambiguous mapping). This makes the MCP prepend path viable for whole batches of 1000+ line docs, with in-call reindex (`reindex.status: indexed`) for free — relaxing the earlier "prefer plain edit for batches" rule when index freshness matters and the tool-output truncation workaround is available.

title: markdown-mcp: section-scoped doc_read returns the FILE-level sha256 — token-efficient CAS workflow
content:
Refinement of memories 31139509 / 084f0031 (markdown-mcp CAS workflow). Discovered 2026-09-06 while applying front matter to 25 docs/llm/memories/ files:

- A SECTION-scoped `doc_read` (file_path + section_slug) returns the FILE-level sha256 in the top-level JSON, while `data` holds only the small section body. Verified: CAS-gated `doc_write` calls succeeded using these section-read tokens — they are true file-byte CAS tokens, not section hashes. So the efficient path for LARGE files is: `doc_outline` (section slugs, compact) → section-scoped `doc_read` (tiny body + file sha) → `doc_write`. No full-file dump needed.
- `doc_outline` and `doc_list` do NOT include sha256 — only `doc_read` (full or section) yields the CAS token.
- Full `doc_read` is required only for SECTIONLESS files (no `##` headings). In docs/llm/memories/ these 9 are sectionless: stats-subsystem, stt-media-transcription, max-webhook-receiver-extraction, skills-agents-audit, llm-messages-handler, llm-tool-call-healing, llm-user-message-format, review-fix-lessons, shutdown-state-dump — they are also not section-addressable via `doc_section_edit`/section reads (only whole-file ops work on them).
- If a full doc_read output exceeds the output limit it is truncated and saved to ~/.local/share/opencode/tool-output/<id>; the sha256 sits near the head of that JSON and is recoverable with a limit-1 read (see memory 084f0031).
- Caveat: section-read sha comes from the index (source: "index"); if a file changed on disk without reindex, the CAS gate aborts safely (no partial write) — fall back to full doc_read, which serves source: "disk" with a fresh sha.

title: markdown-mcp serve holds SQLite writer lock (blocks index --force); lint silent on success; read uses docs-root-relative paths
content:
Operational gotchas for the markdown-mcp CLI (v1.6.0, ~/bin/markdown-mcp), discovered 2026-09-06 during Phase 4 verification:

1. **Writer-lock conflict with `markdown-mcp serve`:** the long-running `markdown-mcp serve` MCP server (separate process, e.g. PID from `ps`) holds the SQLite writer lock for its lifetime, so `markdown-mcp index --force` (atomic full rebuild) refuses with "index not attempted: writer lock not acquired within 10s (held by holder PID NNNN)". Incremental `markdown-mcp index` still works fine and is sufficient to confirm tree/index sync (its `skipped=N` should equal the discovery-set size). To run a forced rebuild, stop the serve process first.

2. **Consequence — excluded-tree rows linger:** incremental sync never re-discovers excluded paths (per `.markdown-mcp.toml` `[docs].exclude = ["archive/", "other/", ...]`), so it cannot purge index rows for files that later became excluded. E.g. after `other/` exclusion, `markdown-mcp list` still showed 10 `docs/other/` rows even though incremental index reported deleted=10 (those were unrelated stale rows). Harmless: lint parses the tree (not the index) and `categories` omits uncategorized rows — but the only real purge is `index --force` once the serve lock is free.

3. **lint is silent on success:** zero findings = NO output at all + exit 0; any finding = exit 1. A bare `markdown-mcp lint; echo $?` with empty stdout is a passing result, not a no-op.

4. **CLI `read` takes docs-root-relative paths:** `markdown-mcp read llm/teamlead-memory.md`, NOT `docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md` (the latter errors "File not indexed" even though `categories` lists the file). Paths shown by `list`/`categories` are already docs-root-relative.

(Note: the fact that lint itself respects `[docs].exclude` is already recorded separately — this entry covers only the lock/semantics behaviors.)

title: zsh does not word-split unquoted $var — verification loops can silently no-op
content:
Agent mistake made and corrected 2026-09-06 (Phase 4 docs verification): a coverage value-validation loop run under **zsh** silently produced a meaningless result because unquoted `$files` was passed to grep as ONE argument with embedded newlines (grep then errored "File name too long" and output nothing — which superficially looked like "0 missing").

The zsh rule: unlike bash, zsh does NOT word-split unquoted parameter expansion (`$var`, `$array`) by default (no SH_WORD_SPLIT). Command substitution `$(...)` IS word-split, which is why `grep -L -m1 '^category:' $(git ls-files ...)` worked while the loop over `$files` did not.

Lesson: when writing verification loops/macros in this environment's zsh, never rely on unquoted `$var` word-splitting. Use explicit forms: `"${(f)var}"` (split on newlines), `print -l`, `echo $var | xargs`, or re-run the command substitution inline. Also: always sanity-check that a "clean" verification output is actually a valid run (empty output from a broken invocation looks identical to empty output from a passing check) — confirm exit codes/line counts mean what they appear to mean before reporting PASS.

title: check_docs.py validates file targets only — anchors unchecked; lint baseline is 9 findings all in other/
content:

It does NOT validate anchor/heading targets. Consequence: in-file anchor links can dangle silently — the real example found is docs/database-schema.md's `chat_info.bot_status` row linking `[ChatBotStatus](#chatbotstatus)` while schema.md has no ChatBotStatus heading (it exists only in database-schema-llm.md). 2. markdown-mcp doc lint baseline (2026-09-06): the tree has exactly 9 pre-existing findings, ALL in `other/` (duplicate-slug in `other/geocode-maps/Geocode-Maps-API.md` and `other/yc-ai-sdk/...`); everything under `docs/` is lint-clean. title: Bash permission rules: single allowlisted commands only, no `;` or pipes
content:
In opencode sessions on this repo, bash is deny-by-default with allowlisted command prefixes (e.g. `make lint*`, `make check-docs*`, `rg*`, `grep*`, `ls*`, `git diff/log/show/status/ls-files*`, `wc*`). Compound commands are denied even when every part is individually allowlisted: chaining with `;` or piping into `sort/awk/uniq` both failed with permission errors.

Operational lesson: run exactly one allowlisted command per bash call; for search/aggregation use the dedicated Grep/glob/read tools instead of shell pipes. A single-purpose `rg` pattern per call works fine.

title: Docs emoji policy: strip authorial decoration, keep code-fence/inline-code/primary-source/diagram/arrows
content: Owner-ratified + teamlead-ruled policy governing Phase 6 emoji normalization of living docs in the gromozeka docs rewrite (2026-09-06). STRIP emoji that is authorial decoration in prose/headings. KEEP emoji that is: (a) inside code fences; (b) inside inline code spans; (c) quoting primary sources (bot output strings, config values); (d) diagram glyphs (▼ ► ◀ ▲ ──▶ etc.); (e) arrows (→ ← ⇒). Stripping must leave wording that carries the meaning alone (e.g. `**Status**: ✅ RESOLVED` → `**Status**: RESOLVED`; `**❌ Avoid**:` → `**Avoid**:`); never leave empty emphasis or doubled spaces. Scope of change is emoji characters + immediately adjacent stray whitespace ONLY — no rewording, reflow, or heading-level changes. Procedural requirement: when removing emoji from HEADINGS, first repo-grep for inbound anchor links to the old slugs (`filename.md#fragment`, `#emoji`-style anchors, and internal `](#` self-anchors) and repoint if any exist — the Phase 6 pass found zero inbound links for docs/database-README.md's 11 emoji headings, so none were needed. Applied to docs/database-README.md, docs/sql-portability-guide.md, docs/database-multi-source.md, docs/documentation-review-process.md (46 emoji stripped, 8 keep-class instances preserved).

title: Gotcha: emoji-only edits can silently re-indent lines — verify every hunk with git diff
content: During the Phase 6 emoji strip of docs/sql-portability-guide.md, four edit calls on indented list lines (L1390-1393, sub-bullets with 4-space indent) were issued with inconsistent leading whitespace between oldString and newString: the oldStrings matched (file had 4 spaces) but the newStrings carried 5 spaces, silently re-indenting all four lines. The edit tool gives no feedback for this — edits succeed as long as oldString matches; the new text is inserted verbatim. This violated the task's hard constraint "only emoji + adjacent stray whitespace removed" and was caught only by reviewing `git diff` per file, where the `+` lines showed one extra leading space vs the `-` lines. Fix: restore the EXACT original indentation (not a "normalized" one — sibling bullets used 3 spaces, a pre-existing quirk that must be preserved, not unified). Lessons: (1) for byte-scoped normalization edits, run `git diff <file>` afterwards and treat any non-emoji change in a hunk as a defect; (2) build edit oldString/newString by copying exact bytes from a fresh read of the region, never re-typing indentation; (3) post-edit verification must include both an emoji re-sweep (only keep-class should remain) and a whitespace/diff review.

title: Emoji sweep patterns miss ℹ️ (U+2139) and FE0F variation selectors; distrust scan counts, verify fences
content: Technique gotchas from the Phase 6 emoji sweep of gromozeka docs (ripgrep with unicode classes): a broad pattern like [\x{1F000}-\x{1FAFF}\x{2600}-\x{27BF}\x{2B00}-\x{2BFF}] MISSES ℹ️ (U+2139 U+FE0F, lives in 2100-214F) — add \x{2100}-\x{214F} or a dedicated pattern, otherwise "all emoji removed" claims are wrong. Emoji with variation selectors (🗂️ = U+1F5C2 U+FE0F, 🛠️ = U+1F6E0 U+FE0F) must have the U+FE0F stripped together with the base character or a stray invisible selector remains in the heading/file. Also: task-brief scan counts can be approximate — the Phase 6 brief said ✅×19 prose markers in docs/sql-portability-guide.md but the fence-verified count was ×20 (plus ℹ️×2 the first pattern missed). The governing authority is per-line verification: read the context around every hit to confirm it is prose (strip) vs inside a code fence or inline code (keep) — e.g. sql-portability-guide.md L1623 ✅ / L1630 ❌ were fence comments (fence spans L1620-1632) and documentation-review-process.md L368 was inside a ```markdown template fence while L403 was an inline-code span; both kept while the visually similar prose L404/L598 were stripped.

title: check_docs.py link-target resolution semantics: :NN suffix stripped, leading / = repo root
content:
`scripts/check_docs.py` (the `make check-docs` gate) resolves markdown link targets with these rules, discovered while repairing 12 links in docs/developer-guide.md:

1. **Trailing `:NN` line suffixes are stripped** before resolution (`re.sub(r":[0-9]+(?:[-,][0-9]+)*$", ...)`), so targets like `pyproject.toml:59` or `main.py:31` are sanctioned link forms — keep the suffix, it resolves to the bare file.
2. **Leading `/` resolves against the repo root**, not the filesystem root.
3. Bare relative paths resolve against the markdown file's own directory.

The dominant convention in `docs/developer-guide.md` (confirmed 2026-09-06): **leading `/` for repo-root targets** (dozens of sibling links like ``[`CacheService`](/internal/services/cache/service.py:88)``), **bare relative for docs-internal links** (e.g. `llm/architecture.md`, `design/custom-modules-design.md`). This convention also holds in `docs/llm/memories/` (existing memory c7a76036).

Gotcha when following task briefs: a brief claimed repo-root targets from `docs/` need `../../` — wrong arithmetic, `docs/` is one level deep so it would be `../`. The leading-`/` form sidesteps depth entirely. Always verify against the checker (`_resolveTarget` in check_docs.py), not the brief.

title: check-docs blind spot: links inside code fences are invisible; unfencing surfaces stale links
content:
`make check-docs` does not extract links from inside fenced code blocks, so broken links can hide inside fences for a long time and the gate still reports 0 broken. Concrete case (2026-09-06, Phase 6): a previously-unfenced ▼-diagram in `docs/developer-guide.md` (~L798-831) was fenced to fix rendering; the unfencing un-swallowed ~2000 lines of content that had been sitting inside a phantom (unclosed) code block, suddenly exposing 12 links the checker had never seen.

The exposed links were broken because the content had been **copied from a doc living one directory deeper** (its original `../../` and `../design/...` prefixes were stale relative to `docs/developer-guide.md`). Corollaries:
- Un-fencing / restructuring fenced content in docs is a broken-link trigger — run `make check-docs` immediately after.
- When copying doc sections between files at different directory depths, re-derive every relative link; prefer the leading-`/` repo-root form for repo-root targets (see check_docs.py resolution-semantics memory) to make links depth-independent.
- The "missing design doc" `custom-modules-design.md` was never missing — it lives at `docs/design/custom-modules-design.md`; only the prefix was wrong. Locate targets on disk before assuming a doc is gone.

title: markdown-mcp: killed `index --force` leaves partial rebuild (stale rows resurrected) — repair with plain incremental index
content:
Phase 7 closeout, 2026-09-06. Refines memories 31c1e6d2 (Phase 4) and c99af5b7 (Phase 1) about the markdown-mcp index/serve lock interplay:

1. **`--force` does not always refuse in 10s.** With `markdown-mcp serve` (PID 57319) holding the SQLite writer lock, `markdown-mcp index --force` did NOT exit with "writer lock not acquired within 10s" — it BLOCKED indefinitely and had to be killed by the shell timeout (5 min). Don't assume a fast refusal; use a bounded timeout.

2. **A killed mid-rebuild `--force` leaves the index WORSE, not untouched.** After the killed force attempt, doc_list showed 110 rows with the 10 stale `docs/other/` rows RESURRECTED (two-pass rebuild: full scan inserts first, exclusion prune happens last — killed before prune). The pre-force clean state was 100 rows.

3. **Repair: plain `markdown-mcp index` fixes it.** The incremental run reported `indexed=0 skipped=100 deleted=10 errors=0` and restored the clean 100-row index (0 `other/`, 0 `archive/`, 3 `docs-playbook/` rows). So incremental deletion of excluded-tree rows IS possible (deleted=10 matched the actual purge) — this contradicts the earlier claims that incremental "never re-discovers excluded paths" and that only `--force` can purge. Don't leave a killed `--force` un-repaired; always follow with an incremental run and verify row counts via doc_list globs.

title: .markdown-mcp.toml [read]-section drift investigated and reverted (Phase 7); verification recipe for recurrence
content:
During Phase 7 (2026-09-06) the working tree had uncommitted drift in `.markdown-mcp.toml`: an added `[read]` section with `section_read_cap = 8192` / `disk_read_cap = 65536`. Disposition: REVERTED (`git checkout --`), with these verified facts:

- The values are NOT markdown-mcp's built-in defaults — `constants.py` in the markdown-mcp source repo (`~/Development/NotA/markdown-mcp/src/markdown_mcp/constants.py`) has `SECTION_READ_CAP = 5000`, `DISK_READ_CAP = 50000`. (The CLI at `~/bin/markdown-mcp` is a sh shim exec'ing that repo's `.venv`.)
- markdown-mcp has NO config write-back: `config.py` never saves TOML. So the section was an unattributed MANUAL edit (mtime 17:37 that day), not tooling-added boilerplate.
- Not load-bearing: `markdown-mcp lint` is clean both WITH and WITHOUT the section (verified via git stash A/B). The caps only shift read/truncation thresholds nothing in gromozeka relies on.
- Rationale for revert: contradicts the file's own header ("Minimal on purpose (zero-config dogfood): everything not set here uses the built-in defaults") with zero demonstrated benefit.

If an identical `[read]` section reappears in the future: treat as unattributed drift; re-verify with the same recipe (diff vs `constants.py` defaults, lint A/B, check mtime/provenance) and revert unless someone claims it deliberately.

title: rg -r flag is --replace: `rg -rn "pat"` silently mangles output by substituting matches with "n"
content: Agent mistake made (and self-caught) during Phase 7 docs closeout, 2026-09-06: running `rg -rn "pattern"` instead of `rg -n` makes ripgrep REPLACE every match with the literal string "n" in its output (`-r`/`--replace`), so search results come back mangled — e.g. `SECTION_READ_CAP: Final[int] = 5000` displayed as `n: Final[int] = n`, and `docs/docs-playbook/` displayed as `docs/n/`. This silently corrupts grep-based evidence and can lead to wrong conclusions about file contents. Always use `rg -n` for line-numbered search; reserve `-r` for intentional match replacement. Any surprising "replaced-looking" grep output should trigger an immediate re-run without `-r`.

title: Verbatim docs content-move workflow: scripted slicing + diff proof + lint baseline
content: Proven workflow for splitting/moving large markdown verbatim (used for the developer-guide → docs/guides/ split): (1) script extraction with ./venv/bin/python3 from repo root, locating section boundaries by exact heading text and slicing line ranges — never retype content by hand; (2) apply only sanctioned link transforms: bare-relative docs-internal links gain `../` when moving into a subdirectory (`llm/architecture.md` → `../llm/architecture.md` from docs/guides/); leading-slash repo-root links and `:NN` line-suffix links unchanged; repoint in-file `#anchor` links whose target section moved to another file (same-file anchors stay); (3) prove verbatim-ness by diffing extracted blocks against source (byte-identical except sanctioned transforms); (4) when other agents edit concurrently, capture a whole-tree `markdown-mcp lint` baseline BEFORE changes and diff after (tree lint is advisory/global, not per-file); (5) sweep inbound anchors repo-wide with `rg -n '<file>\.md#'` — file-level inbound links may keep resolving via a stub and need no repointing. Multi-agent gotcha seen during this task: git status showed modifications this task never made (`.opencode/memory.jsonl`, `.opencode/opencode.json`, `docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md`) — scope attribution explicitly in handoff reports and never touch `.opencode/*`.

title: Line-range Python script beats edit tool for >2000-char doc regions; write-tool escape gotcha

title: markdown-mcp index --force times out on full embedding rebuild — use incremental index + lint
content:
Gotcha (2026-09-06, ~108-file docs tree): `markdown-mcp index --force` (atomic full rebuild with embeddings) exceeds a 120s shell timeout — killed mid-embedding-job. Consequences and safe workflow:

title: Explicit commit scopes override ride-along convention; owner chose separate 4th commit for teamlead-memory.md
content:
Closeout session 2026-09-06 (ses_f8809b557ffex05MVU3Zi3HvUd) refined two standing conventions:

1. **Explicit commit scopes override the ride-along rule.** Memories 97f7416a ("memory.jsonl + teamlead-memory.md ride-along applies without explicit request") and 2aec456a describe ride-alongs for ordinary commits. But when the user provides EXPLICIT per-commit file scopes plus an acceptance criterion like "three clean commits with exactly their scoped files", do NOT fold ride-alongs into those commits. Here `docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md` was modified in the tree but listed in no scope, while expected final status was only the two `.opencode/*` lines. One focused question later, the owner chose **a separate 4th commit** (dbe69fa7 "Record docs arc completion in teamlead memory") over folding into any scoped commit — scope purity wins. When a modified file fits no scope and the brief expects a clean tree, ask; the recommended default is its own commit.

2. **".markdown-mcp.toml never staged" (2aec456a) means "never stage on own initiative"**, not an absolute ban: the owner explicitly scoped commit c to exactly `.markdown-mcp.toml` (9c5bf91e, restored ratified [read] caps), and that was correct. Owner instruction overrides the default hands-off.

Also a workflow lesson: the task brief described the working tree but omitted teamlead-memory.md — task briefs can mis-describe the tree. Always reconcile a brief's tree description against actual `git status` before planning commits, and reconcile explicit commit scopes against the expected final status (a file in no scope + "only X remains" = contradiction needing a decision).

title: markdown-mcp index.db files table: verify currency via sha256 (column is mtime_ns, not mtime)
content: Refines the index-currency verification recipe in memory f27e3c32 (serve auto-rescan makes `markdown-mcp index` report indexed=0 after edits): to verify the index is current, query `.markdown-mcp/index.db` directly. Schema gotcha: the `files` table is STRICT with columns `path, sha256, mtime_ns, size, title, description, index_status, index_error, indexed_at` — the mtime column is `mtime_ns` (INTEGER, nanoseconds), NOT `mtime` (`SELECT path, mtime FROM files` errors with "no such column: mtime"). Working verification: compare stored `sha256` per path against on-disk `shasum -a 256` of each edited file, and check `indexed_at` is after the edit time. When `markdown-mcp serve` is running with `writable = true` and `rescan_interval = 30` in .markdown-mcp.toml, it re-indexes edits within ~30s, so a CLI incremental run right after edits legitimately reports `indexed=0 skipped=<all>` — that is success, not staleness, provided the hashes match.

title: Deleting doc sections orphans prose cross-references — check-docs can't catch them

title: Bulk H2 section deletion: heading-prefix script beats edit-tool for dense blocks
content:
Proven technique (2026-09-06, deleting 27 H2 sections / 399→199 lines from docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md) for bulk section removal when sections are dense and span many lines: write a throwaway script into the sanctioned temp dir (/var/folders/.../T/opencode), run via ./venv/bin/python3 from repo root; match sections by exact heading PREFIX, delete heading+body through the next `## ` line, and ASSERT each prefix matched exactly one heading (loud failure on mismatch). Two follow-up gotchas:
1. Trailing-blank popping during deletion strips the blank line BEFORE kept H2 headings — run a fixer pass afterwards inserting a blank line before any `## ` heading that lacks one (markdown fine, style regression otherwise).
2. Before relying on edit-tool exact-match for dense files, check for lines the read tool truncates: `rg -n '.{2000}' <file>` (read truncates at 2000 chars; a truncated line makes both edit oldStrings and wholesale rewrites silently wrong). This file had none, but docs/llm/handlers.md-style table rows do.
Verification: review `git diff` hunk-by-hunk afterwards — kept sections must show as untouched context only.

title: markdown-mcp index.db files-table paths are docs-root-relative
content: Gotcha (2026-09-06): when verifying index currency after edits by querying `.markdown-mcp/index.db`'s `files` table directly, paths are DOCS-ROOT-RELATIVE, not repo-relative — query `llm/teamlead-memory.md`, NOT `docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md` (querying the wrong form silently returns db=None/absent and misleads you into thinking the file is unindexed; 105 rows = the live-docs count, archive/ and other/ excluded). Currency check = compare files.sha256 against the on-disk sha256. title: markdown-mcp index reports indexed=0 after out-of-band file edits — verify content, not counters
content:
2026-09-06, agent-memories finisher session. After editing `docs/llm/reviewing-large-changes.md` directly on disk (filesystem edit tool, NOT MCP doc_write/doc_section_edit), the incremental `markdown-mcp index` CLI reported `indexed=0 skipped=105 deleted=0 errors=0` — i.e., it claimed nothing changed, right after a real edit.

Cause: the running markdown-mcp MCP server had already picked up the disk edit (watcher / indexing), so the incremental CLI pass correctly found no new work. `indexed=0` after an out-of-band edit is NOT evidence of a stale or broken index.

Safe workflow: never trust the index counters to prove freshness — verify the index actually serves the new content (e.g., `markdown-mcp doc_search` for the changed phrase; in this session it returned the updated "line ~639 in manager.py" snippet). Then run incremental `markdown-mcp index` + `markdown-mcp lint` as the formal gates (per the established workflow: never use `index --force`, it times out on full embedding rebuild).

title: markdown-mcp write tools likely BYPASS agent edit/write permission blocks — verify opencode MCP permission semantics before adoption
content:
Key governance finding of the 2026-09-14 markdown-mcp adoption research:

Agent `permission:` frontmatter blocks gate opencode's `edit`/`write` TOOLS — they are different tools from `markdown-mcp_doc_write`/`doc_section_edit`/`doc_delete`, so existing denies/allows likely do NOT constrain them:
- teamlead has `edit: "*": deny` (except `docs/llm/teamlead-memory.md` allow) — but could technically edit ANY file under docs/ via `doc_write` since MCP write tools are available to it by inheritance.
- docs-writer's `*.md`/`*.txt` allow + `.opencode/**`/`.agents/**` edit denies also don't map onto MCP tool names (the path denies are moot anyway — markdown-mcp paths are docs-root-relative so those dirs are unreachable).
- Mitigating structural fact: markdown-mcp file_path args are resolved relative to `docs_root = "./docs"`, so the MCP tools can only touch `./docs/**` — which matches docs-writer's charter.

UNVERIFIED (as of 2026-09-14): whether opencode `permission:` blocks can target MCP tool names (e.g. `markdown-mcp_doc_write: allow/deny`). This is the load-bearing unknown — verify with a sandboxed probe BEFORE flipping any write-path instruction defaults or granting MCP write tools to teamlead/architect. Until then, do not assume `edit:`/`write:` blocks contain MCP writes.

Upside noted: CAS gating (expected_sha256/expected_text) makes MCP doc edits SAFER than raw edit for concurrent agents (teamlead + docs-writer).

title: CI runs only make check + make test — no check-docs, no markdown-mcp; adoption recommendations for CI integration
content:
Verified 2026-09-14 during markdown-mcp adoption research:

- CI (`.sourcecraft/ci.yaml` → single task runs `sh scripts/ci.sh`) = apk deps → `make venv-alpine` → `make install` → `make check` (flake8/isort/black-check/pyright/import-main) → `make test`. **`make check-docs` is NOT in CI. No markdown-mcp lint/index in CI.**
- `make check-docs` (Makefile:110-112 → `./venv/bin/python3 scripts/check_docs.py`) is a venv-Python-only link checker, zero new deps — natural candidate to add to ci.sh, independent of markdown-mcp.
- Adoption recommendations (deliberate, not auto): do NOT put `markdown-mcp index` in CI (embedding index is machine-local, gitignored, costly to rebuild); CLI `markdown-mcp lint` IS CI-able (parses tree directly, no index needed) but requires provisioning the binary in the Alpine CI image — optional future `make lint-docs` target only after image pinning.
- Index freshness stays a LOCAL concern: incremental `markdown-mcp index` after out-of-band bulk edits (rebase, scripted mass edits, edit-tool edits); serve process rescans every ~30s; never `--force` (see gotcha f5ff8191).

title: markdown-mcp A/B benchmark Phase A (read-path) results: MCP −20.7% overall, task-type-dependent
content:
READ-PHASE (Phase A) of the markdown-mcp vs manual-tools A/B benchmark, executed 2026-09-14 by a `general` subagent (glm-5.3). Compared native read/grep/glob vs markdown-mcp doc_search/doc_read/doc_outline/doc_list on 4 identical docs tasks; every call's args+result saved as exact payloads. Estimator = bytes/4 (tiktoken NOT installed in ./venv — checked, ModuleNotFoundError), same estimator both paths.

Phase A totals (~tokens): manual 9258 vs MCP 7340 → MCP −20.7% overall, but high per-task variance:
- T1 semantic locate (find LLMMessageHandler-last rule): manual 6814 vs MCP 1172 (MCP −83%; grep on broad term returned 88 matches/26 files = 19.9KB result; doc_search snippet carried the full normative rule → 1 call sufficed)
- T2 targeted section read (PK-strategy rules in sql-portability-guide.md): manual 1073 vs MCP 5344 (manual −80%; doc_outline on the 1939-line/~100-section file alone cost ~5.0k tok / 20067 B — the outline is the expensive primitive)
- T3 heading structure (llm/testing.md): manual 318 vs MCP 527 (manual −40%; grep pattern cheap despite 9 false positives; outline carries JSON metadata overhead but zero false positives)
- T4 discovery (DB-schema docs, no body loads): manual 1053 vs MCP 297 (MCP −72%)

Net heuristic: **MCP wins at finding (semantic locate/discovery); manual wins when the file + lexical anchor are already known (targeted read/structure)**. Caveats: T1 MCP finishing in 1 call was snippet-luck (protocol-conditional); T2's outline→read was protocol-prescribed — a free-strategy doc_search first would likely flip T2 to an MCP win; bytes/4 slightly undercounts dense JSON, so MCP's real overhead is marginally worse; payloads are faithful agent transcriptions, not a wire-level proxy.

Artifacts: /tmp/mmcp-benchmark/payloads/ (24 files, naming T{n}-{manual|mcp}-{seq:02d}-{toolName}.{args|result}.txt) + /tmp/mmcp-benchmark/read-phase-results.md (full per-call/per-task tables + qualitative observations). Phase B (write-path benchmark + final report) depends on these files — they are /tmp and not durable; if missing, the results-file numbers above are the record.

title: markdown-mcp vs manual-tools behavior findings: doc_outline cost on big files, index excludes archive/, weak search-score separation
content:
Empirical tool-behavior findings from the 2026-09-14 read-phase A/B benchmark (24 exact payloads in /tmp/mmcp-benchmark/payloads/), relevant to any future manual-tools vs markdown-mcp path choice:

1. **doc_outline is the expensive MCP primitive on large files**: outline of docs/sql-portability-guide.md (1939 lines, ~100 sections) returned 20067 B (~5.0k tok) — 5× the cost of the subsequent targeted doc_read. On big files, prefer doc_search-first (snippet may suffice) or a known section_slug over outline→read.
2. **doc_search snippets can carry the complete answer**: the LLMMessageHandler-last normative rule ("CRITICAL ORDER RULES: … MUST BE LAST", llm/handlers.md §6, lines 519-522) arrived fully inside the search snippet — no doc_read needed (1 call vs manual's 2 calls/6.8k tok).
3. **doc_search score separation is weak**: T1's 8 hits all scored 0.883–0.896; the TOP hit (guides/handlers.md handler-lifecycle) was a near-miss — the normative text was hit #4. Don't trust rank order; read snippets.
4. **MCP index excludes docs/archive/**: zero archive hits in both doc_search and doc_list, while manual glob surfaced 12 docs/archive/* files. Trade-off: less noise, but the index has blind spots the manual path doesn't.
5. **Manual heading greps hit code-block noise**: pattern `^#{1,6} ` on llm/testing.md matched 24 lines, 9 of them `#` shell comments inside fenced code blocks; doc_outline returned 15 headings with zero false positives (structured index beats regex here).
6. **doc_list front-matter descriptions are sparse**: only 1 of 7 `*database*` matches had a non-empty `description`; `title` had to serve as the one-liner. Discovery quality via doc_list alone is title-grade, not README-index-grade.
7. **Native read-tool traffic includes wrapper overhead**: every read result carries `N: ` line-number prefixes plus `<path>`/`<type>`/`<content>`/footer wrapper (~10-15% overhead on bounded windows) — real context cost the MCP section reads don't pay.
8. **tiktoken is NOT installed in ./venv** (ModuleNotFoundError) — token estimates in this repo must use bytes/4 unless tiktoken is added to requirements.

Benchmark-fidelity caveat: payloads are agent transcriptions of tool results, not a wire capture (one transcription slip — wrong path in a glob payload — was caught and fixed via edit).

title: markdown-mcp A/B benchmark Phase B (write-path) results: near tie (MCP +0.3%), stage pattern inverted vs read
content:
WRITE-PHASE (Phase B) of the markdown-mcp vs manual-tools A/B benchmark, executed 2026-09-14 by a `general` subagent (glm-5.3). Complements the Phase A read-phase memory (MCP −20.7%). Fixture lifecycle (create→edit→delete, 1585 B 3-section doc + Beta-body replacement) run identically on both paths; validation workflow compared (make check-docs vs doc_lint). Same estimator as Phase A: tokens = bytes/4 (tiktoken not in venv). Deliverable + 20 payload pairs in /tmp/mmcp-benchmark/ (ephemeral — these numbers are the durable record).

RESULTS — near-exact tie on write path: manual 5244 B / 1311 tok vs MCP 5260 B / 1315 tok (MCP +0.3%). Per stage (tok): create manual 445 vs MCP 583 (MCP result overhead: doc_write/doc_section_edit return ~596 B sha+outline+reindex acks vs ~25 B native acks — ~570 B per MCP write call whether wanted or not); edit MCP 654 vs manual 780 (MCP's section-scoped doc_read 705 B vs mandatory full-file native read 1795 B incl. ~5% line-number overhead; edit ARGS nearly equal: oldString duplication 1163 B ≈ expected_text duplication 1187 B); delete manual 29 vs MCP 64 (rm is 2× cheaper but leaves MCP index stale up to the 30s rescan; doc_delete removes index rows in-call, index_removed:true); validate MCP 14 vs manual 57 — but check-docs validates LINKS (repo-wide: 144 files/2902 links/0 broken) while doc_lint validates STRUCTURE (7 warning rules; returned []) — complements, not equivalents. Combined A+B: manual 10569 vs MCP 8655 tok → MCP −18%.

CAS chain worked with zero retries and zero extra reads: doc_write create needs no sha → doc_section_edit needs expected_text = exact served flat body (body only, no heading/no trailing newline) → doc_delete needs expected_sha256 taken from the doc_section_edit result. Stale-index risk did not materialize: the manually-rm'd fixture was dropped by the 30s background rescan before the MCP path began (doc_write op=write succeeded first try); final doc_list glob was empty on first check.

Key caveat: the edit-stage tie is fixture-size-dependent — manual's required full-file read scales with FILE size while MCP's read scales with SECTION size; on Phase A's 1939-line file this stage alone would flip by ~18k tok in MCP's favor. Methodology note: content-bearing args payloads (write/edit) were generated programmatically from canonical fixture files for byte fidelity and sha-verified identical across paths at create (both 0d0eaac0…).

title: doc_section_edit op=replace strips junction blank lines on ORDINARY content edits too (not just no-op trick)
content: Extension of the known doc_section_edit blank-line gotcha (memories 4b6db600 / 17d02745, which framed it around the no-op/identical-replace reindex trick): the benchmark's ORDINARY content-replacing edit hit it too. 2026-09-14: doc_section_edit op=replace swapping a section body with different text (identical old→new inputs as the native edit path) produced a file missing the blank line between heading and new body AND between body and next heading — 2×`\n` (2 bytes) stripped, post-edit sha 220837b6… vs the native edit's ebb3dbab… on otherwise-identical content. So blank-line consumption at section junctions is a property of every op=replace republish, not an artifact of the no-op trick. Practical consequences: (1) expect sha drift after any doc_section_edit — downstream CAS (e.g. doc_delete) must use the sha returned by the edit result, never a pre-edit sha; (2) outline line ranges shift after replace (observed: section 10-13 → 10-11), so cached line numbers go stale; (3) to preserve Markdown-style blank lines, include them in new_text — but note the tool may normalize, so verify bytes after (this benchmark accepted the normalization as a recorded tool-behavior finding rather than compensating inputs).

title: check_docs.py validates only markdown links; verbatim-report authoring patterns for docs/llm/
content:
Verified 2026-09-14 while persisting docs/llm/markdown-mcp-benchmark.md + docs/llm/markdown-mcp-adoption.md via markdown-mcp doc_write:

1. **check_docs.py validates ONLY real markdown links `[text](path)`** — paths written as inline code (backticked, e.g. `docs/llm/index.md:14-33`) are ignored by the checker. title: docs-writer bash allowlist lacks python/cat/head — author via write-then-doc_lint loop
content:
The docs-writer agent's bash permission is default-deny with a narrow allowlist: `make lint*`, `make check-docs*`, `rg*`, `grep*`, `ls*`, `git diff/log/show/status/ls-files*`, `wc*` (extends the granular-allowlist pattern of memory 140bc9e7). Notably NOT allowed: any python invocation (even `./venv/bin/python3`), `cat`, `head`, `find`. Chained/piped command forms outside the allowlist are denied too (see eefc752f exact-match gotcha).

Consequence for docs authoring: you cannot pre-measure section byte-sizes with a script before submitting content via `doc_write`. Workflow that worked 2026-09-14: estimate section flat-body sizes by hand, `doc_write` the file, then run `markdown-mcp doc_lint` as the feedback loop (`[]` = clean; if a section is flagged, split it via `doc_section_edit`). `wc -l/-c` via bash on repo files IS allowed for line/byte counts. For file inspection use the Read tool — `cat`/`head` are denied.

title: markdown-mcp tool contract: doc_lint now clean ([]), doc_delete can't move/extract sections, docs-root-relative paths, per-cell token rounding
content:
Tool-contract facts surfaced by the 2026-09-14 Gate-2 review of the markdown-mcp reports (complements memory c6037516, which covers doc_outline cost / archive exclusion / search-score separation — different facts):

1. **`markdown-mcp_doc_lint` on the current docs tree returns `[]`** — zero findings, NO excluded-path noise. Any doc text claiming doc_lint "shows excluded-path noise" describes pre-fix historical behavior and is now wrong. (doc_lint remains blind to blank-line stripping around headings per memory 83478fb5 — clean output ≠ perfectly formatted tree.)
2. **`doc_delete` is a pure remover; neither it nor doc_section_edit delete can implement a move or extraction.** doc_delete unlinks the file and drops index rows, creating nothing; doc_section_edit op=delete removes the section subtree AND its anchor, so a planned "delete, then replace with stub" sequence has no anchor to replace. Working alternatives: extraction = doc_write the destination file → verify → doc_section_edit replace the original section's flat body with a stub while KEEPING its heading; in-tree move = keep filesystem `mv` (docs tree is writable) or a full create/verify/delete sequence.
3. **doc_* `file_path` arguments are docs-root-relative** (`llm/index.md`), never repo-relative (`docs/llm/index.md`). Documentation examples showing repo-relative doc_read/doc_outline paths violate the tool contract — this exact error is baked into adoption.md:34-36 (see review memory).
4. **Token estimates (bytes/4) are rounded independently per cell**, so displayed token components need not sum to displayed stage totals (observed ±1-2 token discrepancies in T5b and Phase B appendix). For tool-traffic A/B accounting, raw byte totals are the authoritative numbers; state the rounding policy explicitly in any benchmark write-up.

title: markdown-mcp tool-contract semantics: doc_delete can't move, delete kills the replace anchor, docs-root-relative paths
content:
Markdown-mcp operational semantics confirmed while applying Gate-2 review corrections (2026-09-14) to docs/llm/markdown-mcp-adoption.md + markdown-mcp-benchmark.md. Three review findings were direct consequences of misreading the tool contract — recurring error class to avoid:

1. **`doc_delete` is delete-only — it cannot move a document.** Presenting `doc_delete` as a move mechanism ("archival via `mv` → `doc_delete`") is operationally wrong. In-tree/archival moves stay a filesystem `mv` + incremental reindex (excluded paths drop out of the index on rescan); reserve `doc_delete` (CAS-gated, removes index rows in-call, no backup file) for outright deletion of a live indexed doc.

2. **`doc_section_edit delete` destroys the anchor a follow-up `replace` needs.** Planning "delete on the extracted section + stub `replace`" is impossible — once the section subtree is deleted, there is no section slug left to replace. Correct patterns: stub swap = `op=replace` (swaps the flat body, heading preserved); delete only when the whole section must go. Extract-to-new-memory-file pattern: `doc_write` the destination file first (verify), THEN `op=replace` the source section's body with a stub.

3. **Tool paths are docs-root-relative, not repository-relative.** Write `doc_outline("llm/index.md")`, `doc_read("llm/index.md", section_slug=…)`, never `docs/llm/index.md`. Cite sections by name and resolve slugs at use time via `doc_outline` (slugs are re-derived per generation; dots→hyphens per memory 7cbdeb6b) — never hard-code slugs in instructions.

4. **Escaped pipes in table-cell examples:** when a proposed table row is quoted inside an existing markdown table cell, its `|` must be written `\|` or it splits the host table's columns.

Adjacent verified facts already recorded elsewhere: current MCP doc_lint builds honor [docs].exclude (memory 04bdbc5b — older builds surfaced excluded-path noise; CLI lint stays authoritative on disputes); row-level table tweaks → native edit tool, not doc_section_edit (memories eb060559, 83478fb5).

title: markdown-mcp file_glob is fnmatch: ** doesn't work, single * crosses /
content:
The `file_glob` parameter of markdown-mcp tools (doc_search, doc_list) uses Python **fnmatch**, NOT pathlib/glob semantics: `*` crosses `/`, and `**` has no special power beyond being two `*`s. Consequences (verified 2026-09-14 against docs/docs-playbook/mcp-docs-workflow.md while applying the markdown-mcp adoption plan to the skills):

- `file_glob="llm/*.md"` matches the ENTIRE `llm/` subtree, including `llm/memories/*.md` — use single-star globs for subtree scoping.
- `file_glob="llm/**/*.md"` silently MISSES top-level files like `llm/index.md`: fnmatch translates `*`→`.*`, so the pattern requires the literal `/` between the two stars, demanding an extra path segment (`llm/` + anything + `/` + anything + `.md`). This is an easy silent-empty-result trap.

The correct single-star form was deliberately encoded in the Refactor row of `.agents/skills/update-project-docs/SKILL.md` (`doc_search("old-symbol", file_glob="llm/*.md")`) rather than the intuitively-written `llm/**/*.md`.

title: MCP-first-alongside-manual authoring convention for skills and agent docs
content:
House style for writing agent-facing instructions (skills under `.agents/skills/`, AGENTS.md) that reference markdown-mcp tools, established by `docs/llm/markdown-mcp-adoption.md` and applied 2026-09-14 to `read-project-docs/SKILL.md` and `update-project-docs/SKILL.md` (14 §1.3 rows, verified by diff):

1. **Conditional-preference wording, never exclusive**: "when the markdown-mcp MCP tools are available, prefer …" with the manual tool (`read`/`edit`) always stated as an exact substitute — skills must stay valid for agents/subagents without the MCP server. When a spec row says "replace X with doc_search", implement as MCP-first-alongside-manual, not literal replacement, if it would break the MCP-less path.
2. **MCP examples use docs-root-relative paths only** (`llm/index.md`, not `docs/llm/index.md`), introduced alongside — not replacing — existing repo-relative links.
3. **Section slugs are never hard-coded** in instructions — resolve via `doc_outline` (or the edit result's returned `outline`) at use time, cite sections by name.
4. **Files outside the docs root are always marked "manual tools — outside docs root"**: root `AGENTS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, root `README.md`, inline `lib/**` + `internal/**` READMEs, `.opencode/**`.
5. **Write path discipline**: `doc_read` first (CAS token — the section's served flat body for `doc_section_edit`, file sha256 for `doc_write`), apply edit, then check `reindex.status` in the result (`error` → run incremental `markdown-mcp index`).
6. Verification pairing: `doc_lint()`/CLI `markdown-mcp lint` covers structure only (duplicate slugs, front matter), NOT links — `make check-docs` remains the link gate; CLI lint is authoritative on disputes with older MCP builds.

Known non-obvious dialect details for writing such instructions: `file_glob` is fnmatch (`*` crosses `/`; see separate gotcha memory); semantic `doc_search` is score-floored, NOT exhaustive — a raw Grep sweep stays the exhaustive-completion check after bulk out-of-band refactors.

title: Parallel-agent sessions pollute git status — attribute from tool history, not git
content:

Rules of thumb when a task says "expect only your files":
- Verify YOUR footprint against your own tool-call history (which files your `edit` calls targeted), not `git status` alone.
- Never revert or "clean up" the extra modified files — they belong to other agents/infrastructure; just report the status output with attribution.
- Parallel agents deliberately skip repo-wide quality gates (`make format lint` / `make test`) to avoid interference; serial gates run afterwards — don't run them for markdown-only edits on your disjoint slice.

title: doc_section_edit junction blank-eating: batch-all-then-repair workflow + CAS stability (15 repairs/5 files)
content:
2026-09-14 docs-writer session (applying adoption-plan §1.7 to docs/llm/index.md, tasks.md, changelog.md, reviewing-large-changes.md, markdown-mcp-adoption.md): confirmed memories 466db600/28ee0bd8 at scale — EVERY `doc_section_edit` op=replace ate BOTH junction blank lines (between section heading and body start, AND between the section's trailing `---`/last line and the NEXT heading), regardless of edit content; `doc_write` op=overwrite additionally ate the blank line after the front-matter block. 9 MCP edits produced 15 eaten blanks → repairs: index.md ×7, reviewing-large-changes.md ×4, tasks.md ×2, changelog.md ×1, adoption.md ×1.

Repair workflow that worked at scale:
1. Do ALL MCP edits first (defer repairs) — blank-line repairs outside flat bodies don't invalidate other sections' CAS `expected_text`, so subsequent `doc_section_edit` calls still pass after earlier repairs.
2. Detect eaten lines via `doc_outline` line-drift (a section span shifting UP despite gaining content, e.g. navigation 14-36 → 14-35 after ADDING a row) or via `git diff`.
3. ONE consolidated native-`edit` pass per file with disjoint unique anchors (batching same-file edits with non-overlapping anchors in one message is safe).
4. Finish with `git diff` to confirm only intended hunks remain.

CAS/serving details learned: section flat bodies as served by `doc_read` INCLUDE trailing `---` horizontal rules and leading-space artifacts (index.md nav table's first line genuinely starts with a space) — `expected_text` and `new_text` must reproduce them exactly. Markdown hard-break trailing double-spaces (§3.5 "isort␣␣" line) survive the round-trip if reproduced exactly in new_text. After native repairs, the CLI `markdown-mcp index` is NOT runnable under docs-writer bash permissions, but the serve process's 30s rescan reindexes them automatically — no manual step needed.

title: Editing preamble text (pre-first-heading) requires doc_write overwrite, not doc_section_edit
content:
Paragraphs between the H1 and the first `##` heading (e.g. the "Status:" lead in docs/llm/markdown-mcp-adoption.md) are NOT addressable sections — `doc_section_edit` has no slug for them. The MCP-native route, verified 2026-09-14 when flipping the adoption report's status from "research-only" to "applied":

1. `doc_read` the file (disk mode returns full file incl. front matter, with sha256).
2. `doc_write` op=overwrite with `expected_sha256` (full-file CAS) and the complete post-front-matter body reproduced VERBATIM with only the target paragraph changed. Overwrite preserves the front-matter block automatically — do not include it in content.
3. Verify fidelity with `git diff`: must show only the status-paragraph hunk. Verified byte-identical body on a ~14KB file, so careful verbatim reproduction is reliable. Watch unicode (§, —, →) and escaped `\|` inside tables when transcribing.
4. Safety net: if git diff shows unintended changes, `git checkout -- <file>` and re-apply the one-paragraph change via native edit instead.

This enables updating a report's status line without rewriting its historical body (the §1.7 task's hard constraint). Only known artifact: overwrite eats the blank line between front matter and H1 — restore via native edit (covered by the junction-repair workflow memory).

title: doc_section_edit eats junction blank lines on every replace — both boundaries + trailing ---; content-only diff verification; README 'For agents' item closed
content:
Refinement of the doc_section_edit blank-line series (17d02745, 28ee0bd8, 83478fb5, 4b6db600) from the 2026-09-14 §1.8/§3 application session: 7 section replaces across 4 files re-confirmed the artifact UNIVERSALLY — every single replace ate junction blank lines (~15 repairs: 7 junctions in documentation-review-process.md, 4 in gromozeka-workflow-brief.md, 2 each in mcp-docs-workflow.md and docs/README.md).

1. Stripped junctions occur at BOTH boundaries of the replaced flat body: the blank line after the section heading AND the blank line before the next heading. A trailing `---` separator kept inside the body also loses the blank line between `---` and the following heading.
2. Not every heading adjacency in the diff is an artifact: pre-existing shapes (e.g. `---\n## Appendices`) show up only as diff context lines. Repair ONLY junctions where the diff shows a removed blank line as a `-` line — don't "fix" pre-existing style.
3. Content-only verification after repairs: `git diff --check` (no whitespace errors) AND `git diff --stat` identical to `git diff --ignore-all-space --stat`. Both held after the repairs — a cheap proof the diff is purely content.
4. doc_lint does NOT flag missing junctions (re-confirms 83478fb5); only a git diff boundary inspection catches them. Workflow that worked: after every doc_section_edit → git diff the file → batch the native-edit repairs → re-verify content-only.
5. Closes 83478fb5's outstanding item: the blank line after `## For agents` in docs/README.md — this session's replace of that section ate it again and the repair restored it; boundary correct on disk as of 2026-09-14.

title: Pipes denied even when every segment is allowlisted — treat any compound bash as denied

Working patterns: run single allowlisted commands (`git diff <file>` alone, then eyeball), use the structured Grep tool for content searches, and use the Read tool for files outside the workspace (bash cat of ~/.config/... was denied; Read worked fine).

title: RESOLVED: opencode permission: config CAN target MCP tool names — exact deny syntax for markdown-mcp_doc_*
content:
Definitive answer (web research 2026-09-14) to the open question in memory d31a7cd7: opencode's `permission:` config — BOTH top-level (opencode.json/jsonc) AND per-agent markdown frontmatter — can target MCP tool names directly. Permission keys are wildcard patterns matched against the underlying tool name; MCP tools are registered as `serverName_toolName`, so `markdown-mcp_doc_write` is a valid permission key.

**Working syntax** (e.g. for a read-only analyst agent; enumerate the three write-class tools):
```yaml
permission:
  edit: deny
  markdown-mcp_doc_write: deny
  markdown-mcp_doc_section_edit: deny
  markdown-mcp_doc_delete: deny
```
Must enumerate — wildcards are ONLY `*` and `?` (no regex alternation), so `markdown-mcp_doc_*: deny` would also kill doc_read/doc_search/doc_outline/doc_list/doc_tags/doc_categories. Object form also valid per key: `markdown-mcp_doc_write: {"*": "deny"}`.

**Evidence chain:**
- Schema https://opencode.ai/config.json — `PermissionConfig` object = 15 enumerated built-in keys (read/edit/glob/grep/list/bash/task/external_directory/todowrite/question/webfetch/websearch/lsp/doom_loop/skill) PLUS `"additionalProperties": {"$ref": "#/$defs/PermissionRuleConfig"}` → arbitrary tool-name keys are schema-valid; same `PermissionConfig` referenced by top-level Config and AgentConfig.
- Decisive doc note, https://opencode.ai/docs/agents#permissions: "Permission keys are matched as wildcard patterns against the underlying tool name, so the same syntax works for built-ins, custom tools, and MCP tools — for example `"mymcp_*": "deny"` denies every tool from an MCP server, and `"mymcp_search": "ask"` targets a single one." Also: `deny` removes the tool from the toolset; legacy `tools: {name: false}` ≡ `{"name": "deny"}` permission.
- https://opencode.ai/docs/permissions — keyed by tool name; actions allow/ask/deny; most default to ALLOW; last matching rule wins; agent rules override global.
- Naming convention, https://opencode.ai/docs/mcp-servers/ — MCP tools registered with server-name prefix.
- Source (repo sst/opencode redirects to github.com/anomalyco/opencode, branch dev): `packages/core/src/permission.ts` `evaluate()` = findLast rule where `Wildcard.match(action, rule.action) && Wildcard.match(resource, rule.resource)` — no built-in-name whitelist; `packages/schema/src/permission.ts` Rule = {action, resource, effect}, action is free-form string.

**Key semantics:** `edit: deny` maps only to the write/edit/apply_patch tools — confirms the bypass recorded in d31a7cd7 + runtime-verified in fd7676de. Each MCP tool is a SEPARATE permission action defaulting to allow, so write-class MCP tools must be denied by their own names.

**Alternatives (ranked; unnecessary given native support):** (1) legacy per-agent `tools: {"markdown-mcp_doc_write": false}` — deprecated but still honored, removes tool from toolset; (2) global-off/per-agent-on inversion `tools: {"markdown-mcp*": false}` + re-enable; (3) plugin `permission.ask` hook (in `packages/plugin/src/index.ts`: `(input, output: {status: "ask"|"deny"|"allow"}) => Promise<void>`) — programmatic deny, global scope, per-agent = DIY; (4) `tool.definition` hook can only rewrite description/parameters, CANNOT remove tools; `tool.execute.before` throwing hard-blocks a call.

**Reload semantics:** config and agent-file changes are NOT hot-reloaded — restart opencode. No reload mechanism documented on /docs/agents, /docs/permissions, or /docs/config; OpenCode School (opencode.school/lessons/configuration/): "Config changes take effect the next time OpenCode starts."

**Source-lookup gotcha for future code verification:** guessed raw paths 404 — actual locations: `packages/core/src/permission.ts` (not plugin/permission.ts), hooks in `packages/plugin/src/index.ts` (not packages/plugin/index.ts). Discover paths via `https://api.github.com/repos/anomalyco/opencode/contents/<dir>?ref=dev`.

title: Preamble (pre-first-heading) edits: native edit with unique anchor is a valid surgical alternative to doc_write overwrite
content: Existing memory 907a2358 documents doc_write op=overwrite as the route for pre-first-heading preamble text (e.g., the "Status:" lead of docs/llm/markdown-mcp-adoption.md, which has no section slug). The 2026-09-14 docs-writer status-sync session validated a more surgical alternative: native `edit` on a unique anchor spanning the insertion point (e.g., "time; inferences flagged as such.\n\n## 0. Verified ground truth" → insert the new paragraph between), avoiding doc_write overwrite's whole-body rewrite and its broader normalization risk. Prerequisites and notes: (1) native `read` of the file FIRST — doc_read does not satisfy the edit tool's read-before-edit requirement; (2) none of doc_write's ops can insert mid-preamble (write=create only, overwrite=whole body, append=trailing, prepend=lands before the H1); (3) after out-of-band native edits, no explicit reindex is needed for the gates — doc_lint requires no index, make check-docs reads files directly, and the serve process's 30s rescan refreshes metadata; the preamble is not a section, so no embedded section body changes.

**Result: frontmatter `tools:` deny entries DO hard-remove markdown-mcp write tools from a subagent's toolset.** The `code-analyst` agent definition carries `tools:` denies for `markdown-mcp_doc_write`, `markdown-mcp_doc_section_edit`, `markdown-mcp_doc_delete`, and all three were ABSENT from the agent's visible toolset. **Why this matters — the two enforcement mechanisms are distinct:**
1. `permission:` frontmatter blocks (allow/deny/ask prompts) — per memory 3a1b6002 they CAN target MCP tool names by exact key (theoretical, web-research), but memory d31a7cd7 flagged doubts about whether they reliably gate MCP tools at runtime. Soft gate, model-visible as a permission decision.
2. `tools:` frontmatter denies (this probe) — remove the tools from the toolset entirely. NOT overridable by the model, no prompt surface at all. This is the mechanism that demonstrably works for hard enforcement on MCP tools.

**Operational guidance:** for subagents that must be read-only against the docs tree (e.g. code-analyst, code-reviewer), use `tools:` denies in the agent frontmatter — verified effective. Treat `permission:`-based MCP gating as unverified-at-runtime until a probe like this one exercises it. Method that worked: ask the restricted agent to enumerate its own `markdown-mcp*` tools and attempt nothing; absence of the trio in the self-reported list is conclusive.

Related: 4a70c695 (unrestricted `general` subagent sees all 10 tools — the control case), d31a7cd7 + 3a1b6002 (permission: semantics thread), 6cc1c7a3 (§1.4(b) permission rollout deferred).

title: RESOLVED: explore agent has zero markdown-mcp tools because its built-in default is `"*: deny` + explicit allow-list (H1 confirmed, H2 refuted)
content:
ROOT CAUSE RESOLVED (web research 2026-09-14, supersedes the "inconclusive" note in memory 18c8121e): opencode's built-in `explore` agent has ZERO markdown-mcp tools because its own default definition denies everything. Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anomalyco/opencode/dev/packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts defines explore as `Permission.merge(defaults, Permission.fromConfig({ "*": "deny", grep: "allow", glob: "allow", list: "allow", bash: "allow", webfetch: "allow", websearch: "allow", read: "allow", external_directory: readonlyExternalDirectory }), user)` — the `"*": "deny"` wildcard matches MCP tool names too (docs: permission keys are wildcard patterns matched against tool names, "deny" disables the tool), and no MCP tool is on the allow-list. So explore NEVER had markdown-mcp tools; observed toolset (bash, glob, grep, read, webfetch) = the allow-list minus list/websearch (build difference).

H2 (merge-semantics regression from our `.opencode/opencode.json` agent.explore.permission override) REFUTED: the same source merges config agent overrides additively — `item.permission = Permission.merge(item.permission, Permission.fromConfig(value.permission ?? {}))` — supplying `permission` for a built-in cannot strip tools the override doesn't name.

DECISION: keep the override as-is (exact-name denies of the write trio are no-ops today, zero wildcard risk, and pin the write-deny if upstream ever relaxes explore's allow-list — reads would then flow in allowed, matching the read-only matrix). Cross-refs: docs https://opencode.ai/docs/agents (Permissions + Use explore), https://opencode.ai/docs/mcp-servers ("MCP tools are automatically available to the LLM alongside built-in tools" — except where an agent's permissions deny them).

title: opencode built-in agent definitions: source path + how to locate (anomalyco/opencode dev)
content:
Research-navigation facts from the 2026-09-14 explore/MCP-tools investigation:

1. Built-in agent source location: opencode's built-in agents (build, plan, general, explore) are defined in `packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts` on branch `dev` of github.com/anomalyco/opencode (sst/opencode redirects there). Raw fetch: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anomalyco/opencode/dev/packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts — NOT under `packages/core/src/agent/…` or `packages/core/src/agents/…` (those guesses 404).

2. When the path inside the opencode repo is unknown, list the tree without auth via GitHub trees API: `https://api.github.com/repos/anomalyco/opencode/git/trees/dev?recursive=1`, then grep the JSON for candidate paths. GitHub web code-search URLs (github.com/search?q=repo:…&type=code) don't render results without JS — useless for plain fetch.

3. Permission mechanics confirmed in that file (load-bearing for the project's markdown-mcp permission matrix):
   - Permission rules evaluate LAST-MATCH-WINS. In explore's built-in `Permission.fromConfig`, `"*": "deny"` is listed BEFORE the explicit allows (grep/glob/list/bash/webfetch/websearch/read), which is why the allows beat the wildcard. Corollary for our agent permission blocks (frontmatter or opencode.json): put wildcards first, specific keys after — later keys override earlier ones for the same tool.
   - Project-config `agent.<name>.permission` merges ADDITIVELY over a built-in: `item.permission = Permission.merge(item.permission, Permission.fromConfig(value.permission ?? {}))` — supplying `permission` for a built-in never strips tools the override doesn't name.
   - `external_directory` is a permission gate (explore uses a read-only variant), not a tool.

Related memory: 1a7e136d (explore root-cause verdict).

title: opencode permission merge/evaluate mechanics: config allows override built-in deny-all (findLast), merge = flat()
content:
Mechanics behind H1 (complements memories 1a7e136d and 96bfc99b), verified 2026-09-14 from anomalyco/opencode dev branch:

1. `Permission.merge(...rulesets)` = `rulesets.flat()` — pure concatenation, nothing stripped (packages/opencode/src/permission/index.ts). Config `agent.<name>.permission` entries are APPENDED after built-in rules (`item.permission = Permission.merge(item.permission, Permission.fromConfig(value.permission ?? {}))` in packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts).
2. `evaluate()` uses `findLast` — LAST matching rule wins. Therefore config allow entries OVERRIDE a built-in `"*": "deny"` (e.g. `"markdown-mcp_doc_read": "allow"` under agent.explore.permission grants explore that tool despite its deny-all default).
3. `disabled()/visibleTools()`: a tool is hidden from the toolset when the last rule matching its permission is `pattern "*" + action "deny"`. This is why denied == invisible.
4. Built-in explore allow-list: grep, glob, list, bash, webfetch, websearch, read (+ read-only external_directory). `defaults` shared by build/general/plan starts with `"*": "allow"` — hence those agents see all MCP tools. compaction/title/summary are also `"*": "deny"`-based.
5. Docs (opencode.ai/docs/mcp-servers#per-agent): MCP tools "automatically available to the LLM alongside built-in tools"; per-agent enablement via `agent.<name>.tools`/`permission` is opt-in restriction/grant.
6. Fetch gotcha: web-search_fetch_page rejects ALL raw.githubusercontent.com URLs ("upstream_rejected"); use the webfetch tool or api.github.com contents API instead.

title: git diff vs HEAD shows cumulative uncommitted delta, not your edit's increment
content: Corollary to memory 71e750f7 (dirty-tree verification), observed 2026-09-14 while adding 7 allow entries to `agent.explore.permission` in `.opencode/opencode.json`: the task's acceptance criterion said "git diff shows the hunk is exactly the seven added allow lines", but `git diff` vs HEAD showed the ENTIRE permission block as new (plus the comma after `"model": "cheap"`) — because the 3 deny entries being built upon were themselves uncommitted work from the earlier session (3bed0942: "No commits made yet"). Rule: when a file's pre-edit state is itself uncommitted, `git diff` (and `git diff HEAD`) shows the CUMULATIVE delta since last commit, never your session's increment. To verify a session's own edit precisely in that situation: (a) compare final file content against the target state byte-for-byte, and/or (b) confirm pre-edit-content + expected-delta = final content. Don't treat a larger-than-expected diff as a failed edit without first checking whether the baseline was dirty. Report the discrepancy honestly in the handoff (what vs HEAD shows vs what the edit actually did) rather than "fixing" the diff to match expectations.

title: Models config TOML schema: [models.providers.*] + [models.models."name"], partial-override pattern
content:
Surveyed 2026-09-14 (read-only exploration for the "generate models config from models.dev with whitelist/blacklist globs + disabled-by-default" tooling feature).

LLM config lives under TWO tables under `[models]` (NOT `[llm]`):
- `[models.providers.<name>]` — only universal key is `type`; everything else is provider-specific (`folder_id`, `api_key`, `base_url`, `session_fallback`, `cache_dir`). Tracked in `configs/00-defaults/providers.toml`.
- `[models.models."name"]` — model name is the TOML key (quoted if it contains `/`). Fields: `provider` (required), `model_id` (required), `model_version` (default "latest"), `context` (code default 32768), `enabled` (default true — THE disabled-by-default mechanism; false → model skipped in `_initModels`), `tier` (free/paid/friend/bot_owner), `support_tools/text/images/structured_output/embeddings`, `embedding_dimensions`, `image_generation_api` ("openai-images"), `input_image_format` (MIME list), `customParams.*` (dotted keys forwarded verbatim).

GOTCHA — tier default drift: docs/llm/configuration.md says default `tier = "free"` but code default in `AbstractModel.getInfo()` (lib/ai/abstract.py ~line 827) is `"bot_owner"`.

KEY OVERRIDE PATTERN (essential for the feature design): gitignored `configs/common/10-openrouter.toml` re-declares `[models.models."name"]` tables with ONLY `enabled = true/false` — recursive multi-dir merge (later config dirs win per-key) makes partial overrides work. So a generated config can emit full entries while a user overlay toggles them.

Model-selector defaults are flat keys read as ChatSettingsKey members (internal/bot/models/chat_settings.py) from bot-defaults.toml: `chat-model`, `fallback-model`, `summary-model`, `summary-fallback-model`, `image-parsing-model`, `image-parsing-fallback-model`, `image-generation-model`, `image-generation-fallback-model`, `condensing-model`, `memory-refine-model`, `memory-refine-fallback-model`, `embedding-model` — values are model NAMES (config keys), e.g. `chat-model = "openrouter/free"`.

Config dirs on disk: `configs/00-defaults/` (19 tracked files; model files: openrouter-models.toml, openrouter-models-free.toml, yc-openai-models.toml, yc-sdk-models.toml, fastembed-models.toml, providers.toml), gitignored-but-present `configs/{local,common,prod,local-max,local-telegram,prod-max,prod-telegram}/`. `configs/common/01-opencode-go.toml` + `10-openrouter.toml` hold models; `configs/prod/01-ollama.toml` is a custom-openai example.

Docs to link: docs/llm/configuration.md sections `### [models]` (~line 180), `#### [models] provider types` (205), `#### [models] model configuration keys` (226), `#### [models] image generation configuration` (246). docs/llm/index.md §4 Project Map does NOT list `scripts/` at all — a new scripts doc is net-new in the map.

title: Scripts conventions: shebang, httpx2 preamble, bootstrapProxy, argparse, test pattern
content:
Established conventions in `scripts/` (verified 2026-09-14 via list_models.py, prune_unknown_chat_settings.py, clear_memory_embeddings.py) — relevant for any new tooling script:

- Shebang: `#!/usr/bin/env ./venv/bin/python3`. Module docstring with Usage/Flags/Exit codes. `from __future__ import annotations`. Repo-root sys.path shim, then `import httpx2` + `httpx2.alias_httpx()` BEFORE project imports (mandatory ordering, `# noqa: E402`) — even pure-sqlite3 scripts do this dance.
- If the script instantiates any proxy-consuming service (LLMManager, providers, httpx clients resolving ProxyConfig), it MUST call `bootstrapProxy(configManager)` from `scripts/_lib/bootstrap.py` first, else `ProxyConfig.getCombined()` raises TypeError.
- argparse everywhere (via `buildParser()`); `main() -> int` returning exit codes; `print()` for output, errors to `sys.stderr`; `asyncio.run(main())` for async. No logging output for data.
- Shell wrappers: `scripts/run-*.sh` → cd to repo root, `. "scripts/_load_env.sh"` (parses `--env=NAME`, sources `.env.NAME`, builds `$CONFIG_DIRS` from `$CONFIGS`), then run the python script with `$ENV_FILE` + `$CONFIG_DIRS`.
- ConfigManager flags convention: `--config-dir` (append, default `configs/00-defaults` + `configs/local`), `--dotenv-file` (default `.env`).
- scripts/ is an importable package (`scripts/__init__.py` exists). Tests live in `tests/scripts/test_*.py` and import script functions directly (`from scripts.prune_unknown_chat_settings import processDatabase`), using `tmp_path` throwaway DBs, `capsys` for stdout/stderr assertions, `monkeypatch` for e.g. `sqlite3.connect`, class-based grouping, camelCase names; sync tests for sync scripts (async scripts would use asyncio_mode=auto plain `async def test_...`). `tests/scripts/_lib/` holds shared test helpers. See tests/scripts/test_prune_unknown_chat_settings.py for the reference pattern.
- list_models.py output shape (the closest existing analog to the planned generator): sections "Remote models (N total):" then "Configured models (N):" comparing local `context` vs remote `context_length` → `OK`/`MISMATCH`/`NOT IN REMOTE LIST`; `--provider` required; `--verbose` dumps full JSON; exit code = mismatch count>0.
- `BasicOpenAIProvider.listRemoteModels()` uses OpenAI SDK `models.list()`; `OpenrouterProvider.listRemoteModels()` uses raw `httpx.AsyncClient` GET `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models` specifically to keep `context_length`/`pricing` fields the SDK strips — best in-repo precedent for models.dev-style raw catalogue fetching.

title: ConfigManager standalone-script gotchas: os.chdir, sys.exit on missing bot token, tomli house parser
content:
ConfigManager (internal/config/manager.py) gotchas for standalone scripts, verified 2026-09-14:

- Constructor: `ConfigManager(configPath="config.toml", configDirs=None, dotEnvFile=".env")`. Parses TOML with **tomli** (not stdlib tomllib); `${VAR}` substitution via utils.substituteEnvVars; recursive merge of every `*.toml` found by rglob in each configDir, sorted by path.
- SIDE EFFECTS that bite fetch-only tooling: it runs **`os.chdir(rootDir)`** if `[application] root-dir` is set, and **`sys.exit(1)` if `[bot] token` is missing** (manager.py ~lines 89-92, 224-226). A script that only needs the `[models]` section still triggers the bot-token hard exit — must either set a dummy token env var or avoid full ConfigManager.
- **No standalone-TOML pattern exists in scripts/**: zero tomli/tomllib imports under scripts/*.py — all current scripts go through ConfigManager. A new generator script reading its own standalone filter TOML would be a NEW pattern; house TOML parser is `tomli==2.4.1` (direct pin in requirements.direct.txt).
- HTTP client for a fetch-based script: house client is `httpx2[http2,socks]` (always with `httpx2.alias_httpx()` before project imports). `requests==2.34.2` exists only in frozen requirements.txt as a TRANSITIVE dep — not a sanctioned direct dependency. No requests/urllib usage in scripts/.
